en: The *Sūtra of the Essential Collection of All Dharmas*, Volume One.
Compiled by the Venerable Avalokita. Totaling two thousand six hundred and eighty-four verses.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, the Court-Scattered Grand Master [of the Han Dynasty].
I prostrate to the Most Victorious Honored One of the three realms of existence, Auspicious, stainless, and one who has exhausted all outflows;
For the foolish are submerged by delusions, And you are able to rescue them with impartial compassion.
Relying upon the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna*, this collection of verses has been compiled from the vast ocean of extensive sūtras to serve as an eye for the world.
One should give rise to pure faith, practice with diligence, and remain free from negligence.
Renouncing the six sense-objects, one cultivates subtle and wondrous wisdom;
delighting in generosity and upholding the precepts, as well as patience and all meditative concentrations,
one benefits and brings joy to all sentient beings through the four immeasurable minds.
If one is distracted and heedless, giving rise to violent and evil views,
and constantly uttering false speech, one shall fall into hell.
If one is stingy, envious, and hateful, and remains far removed from wholesome dharmas, [one shall likewise fall].
Those who delight in harming sentient beings will certainly fall into the realm of hungry ghosts.
Those who destroy the True Dharma, being foolish and attached to defiled desires,
and who indulge in food, drink, and sleep, shall receive the retribution of an animal.
Through the three types of body, speech, and mind, they commit various unwholesome deeds;
entangled by karma, these increase again and again.
Thus those fools proceed from one state to another without rest.
The wise who practice well shall attain the bliss of tranquility.
Understanding the fruits of karma, they abandon negligence;
discerning with wisdom, this goodness is unsurpassed.
Always delighting in the practice of giving, firmly upholding pure ethical discipline,
and feeling compassion for all sentient beings so that their aspirations may be fulfilled;
being endowed with loving-kindness and compassion, one does not give rise to expectations.
By gathering others into one’s fold, one will certainly attain accomplishment.
By being liberated from greed and hatred, by contentment and freedom from faults,
and by cherishing all sentient beings, one will certainly attain accomplishment.
With impartiality and straightforwardness, Free from notions of enemy or kin,
One is forever liberated from all evil realms And will certainly attain accomplishment.
Perfecting all dignified deportment, One skillfully and impartially teaches the Dharma.
Free from the faults of stinginess and envy, one will certainly attain accomplishment.
Delighting in serving the venerable master, upholding the precepts, and cultivating various meditative concentrations,
while clearly understanding the characteristics of sin and merit, one will certainly attain accomplishment.
Arousing courageous diligence, whether sitting in meditation or engaged in recitation,
with loving speech and free from deceit, one will certainly achieve accomplishment.
At the proper time and in the appropriate place, whether acting or resting, [one shall succeed].
All are skillfully understood and known, And certainly attained with success.
Without anger, one subdues resentment; With patience, one eliminates violence and evil.
Through the True Dharma, one abandons what is not the Dharma; With light, one extinguishes darkness.
Reality dispels the false; tranquility destroys double-tongued speech;
compassion halts reviling; freedom from bonds unties the fetters;
a heart of loving-kindness stops killing; delight in giving dissolves the stain of stinginess.
With pure virtue as the antidote, one counters improper mental attention;
with wisdom one illuminates ignorance, and with impermanence one shatters the grasping at permanence.
Like the setting sun and the waning moon, the nature of conditioned flux is fundamentally thus.
One should reflect well for oneself and observe with detachment from evil desires.
Taking the Eightfold Noble Path as the cause, one can transcend all evil realms;
abiding in the four fearlessnesses, one can subdue all terrors.
Right mindfulness dispels deluded thoughts, and supreme wisdom destroys false wisdom;
dwelling joyfully in an araṇya, one remains detached and cuts off all craving.
Just as among all mountains, Sumeru is the most preeminent, so too is this the foremost path.
Like the great ocean, deep and vast, capable of producing all manner of precious gems;
like the brilliant light of the bright sun, eclipsing all the lunar mansions and planets.
Non-arising brings an end to arising, just as fire consumes dry wood.
Just as exquisite food and drink can eliminate hunger and thirst,
and just as the lion’s every movement can subdue all the beasts,
so too is one who is content and has severed all greedy seeking fearless.
One who is kind and benevolent is praised by all the world;
yet if one abandons this, they will all despise them as indolent and ignorant. Diligence can sever such faults.
Even if there are violent and wicked people who unjustly slander them, [they remain steadfast].
The wise, through truthful speech and the power of patience, are able to dispel [obstacles].
The devas defeat the asuras because they have faith and delight in the True Dharma;
when a Buddha appears in the world, he is able to subdue all non-Buddhist paths.
If a person skillfully expounds the Dharma, able to bring about understanding in others,
acting as a guide for the multitude and leading them to the place of peace and security;
showing the true path to Bodhi and ultimately causing them to enter therein—
Within the perilous path of birth and death, one forever severs the fetters of delusion.
This Dharma is unsurpassed; it is not that which is spoken of by worldly people.
If there be those who hear this, they shall be able to cross the ocean of all existence.
If there is a person of wisdom who diligently practices this,
there are four kinds of fields of merit that can produce all manner of wholesome fruits.
If one upholds the Buddha's teachings, one will attain the full perfection of the sense faculties.
If one does not give rise to a heart of joyful devotion, one will later suffer in vain regret and distress.
If a person constantly pursues and becomes addicted to the five desires,
and remains attached to wife and children, they shall fall into the evil realms.
Arising from improper reflection, the accumulation of all faults stems entirely from one's own mind, which is bound by delusive conceptualization.
This mind is difficult to subdue, for it frequently clings to the objects of desire.
If one can skillfully restrain it, one will attain coolness and peace.
This mind is like a wild horse; tame it with the True Dharma.
Having heard this, you should remember and uphold it, examining it again and again.
If a person hears the True Dharma, Having heard it, they understand it completely;
They give rise to roots of goodness And remain far removed from all faults.
Because of hearing the True Dharma, The mind becomes pure and free from defilement.
One gives rise to leaping joy and increases luminous wisdom;
by hearing the True Dharma, one refrains from committing various evils.
Knowing that the fruits of karma are not in vain, one shall attain the path to Bodhi.
By hearing the true Dharma, one comes to know the Buddha’s manifold virtues;
that the Dharma is the cause of liberation—this is the mark of a true wise person.
By hearing the true Dharma, one knows that the characteristics of phenomena are eternally abiding.
Therefore, one should be single-minded, diligently practicing in all affairs.
By hearing the True Dharma, one is liberated from the ocean of saṃsāra;
severing various forms of craving, one shall realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).
By hearing the true Dharma, one awakens to the characteristics of arising and ceasing;
possessing these four causes and conditions, one should clearly understand and believe.
By hearing the true Dharma, one thoroughly understands the aggregates, bases, and elements.
Associated with arising and ceasing, they cause right wisdom to become obscured.
These three kinds of afflictions are the root of saṃsāra;
delighting in hearing the true Dharma, one should sever them so that they are forever exhausted.
If one delights in extensive learning, there is nothing superior to dwelling in the world;
regarding both conditioned and unconditioned phenomena, they have thoroughly investigated their very source and depth.
When such a person’s life comes to an end, they shall no longer experience any sorrow or fear.
Having thoroughly mastered that True Dharma, one does not give rise to even the slightest suffering.
By using the fire of right wisdom to burn away the fuel of afflictions,
and through delighting in extensive learning, one shall no longer undergo future suffering.
If one draws near to those of great learning, Then peace and happiness will arise;
Free from the burning of heedlessness, This is the root of all goodness.
One should serve those of venerable virtue And take joy in their teachings.
Having emerged from the causes of old age and death, one attains the state of true permanence.
Thoroughly understanding all phenomena and being liberated from all obstructive defilements, one gives rise to the bodhicitta; among these, extensive learning is supreme.
If one associates with those of great learning and desires to cultivate right wisdom,
one should always show respect and honor them through body, speech, and mind.
Those who delight in much hearing abide well within the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
By practicing with firm diligence, one can cross the ocean of the three realms of existence.
If a person possesses much learning, they are endowed with all treasures;
though one may be wealthy and abundant, if they lack learning, their ignorance makes them the same as the poor.
If a person lacks the wealth of the Dharma and remains far removed from a teacher,
they merely bear that physical form in vain and shall always harbor sorrow and shame.
If they draw near to evil associates, they will give rise to negligence and indolence.
Just as seeds sown in wasteland are cast away in vain, so too is one who possesses great learning and the eye of Dharma; though blind, they possess clear awakening.
But one who lacks both eyesight and great learning is called dull and ignorant.
If one distances oneself from the True Dharma and relies upon what is not the Dharma, it is like abandoning a skilled physician while seeking to cure a grave illness.
All dharmas are without limit; only through accumulated study can one realize and enter them.
Drops of rain form a swift current, all through gradual progression.
So too it is for the ocean of beginningless saṃsāra: from the arousal of the bodhicitta until reaching the adamantine site of enlightenment, one attains the fruit of Buddhahood.
Maintaining the True Dharma with a pure mind, one does not cling to the various meditative absorptions;
unled by the realm of desire, one is certain and ever secure.
Having wisdom, one should associate with those who possess wisdom and should abandon those who lack it.
Cultivating the body through wisdom and virtue—such a person is truly rare!
Seeking the Dharma with a faithful mind, one is always born in superior realms;
even if one should fall into perilous difficulties, the devas will constantly provide protection.
He acts as a bright lamp in the darkness, a wholesome medicine for the sick, and provides precious wealth to the destitute; he enables the blind to see.
For those caught in the torrential flood of the world, he serves as their boat and raft.
If one is intoxicated, arrogant, and heedless, one will certainly bring harm upon oneself.
This was spoken by the Buddhas of the past; you should receive it with full faith, cause right wisdom to manifest before you, and practice without weariness.
Regarding gain, fame, reputation, food, drink, bedding, and so forth—having no desire for even the slightest portion of these, what could they possibly do for me?
This body is to be loathed; it causes harm like an enemy thief.
One commits various transgressions and constantly delights in non-celibate conduct.
Furthermore, this body is the locus of manifold diseases;
it is perpetually overflowing with impurity and is truly a vessel of evil.
Abiding closely with the mind, yet devoid of thought or discernment,
at the moment of death, one’s appearance becomes foul and deeply terrifying.
The three conditions of life-force, warmth, and consciousness are all abandoned simultaneously.
Like a withered tree devoid of consciousness, its form dissolves as it exudes foul fluids.
When a fool is in the prime of youth, he is deluded and full of arrogance and indulgence;
yet without pausing for even a moment, he changes and becomes old and decrepit.
Relying on wealth and indulging in luxury, one extensively creates various evil karmas;
when such a person’s life is about to end, they undergo extreme suffering and feverish distress.
Having no delight in the True Dharma, how are they any different from those who are not human?
Turning one's back on the city of Nirvāṇa, One dwells instead upon the path of error.
By cultivating vast merit and its rewards, One is thereby born among humans;
One should then board the vessel of wisdom To forever cross the ocean of existence.
This body is like a flash of lightning, resembling a city of the Gandharvas;
why then do you repeatedly give rise to joy and anger toward others?
This body is not solid, shifting and turning for but a brief moment.
Constantly harboring a mind of flattery and crookedness, how can one avoid the terrors of old age and death?
It is a city of disease and illness, a dwelling for sorrow and affliction;
it is also like a field where the seeds of both the wholesome and the unwholesome are sown.
If a person adorns their body with generosity and precepts, and with loving-kindness and wisdom,
these alone are the virtuous causes and conditions that constitute the foremost steadfastness.
Furthermore, it is said that this body is the locus upon which all the elements (dhātus) depend.
If one can skillfully awaken to this, one will swiftly attain liberation.
This clarifies that the realms of one's own body are false and merely the result of forced conceptualization;
if one delights in the aggregates and realms of others, one remains deluded and lacks the means for deliverance.
If one possesses external wealth but lacks inner tranquility within the internal realms, yet understands the body well, one can be liberated from all suffering.
However, by guarding one's own wealth, one further increases their affliction.
Various fears arise accordingly—namely, those from officials, thieves, water, and fire.
If one stays far from wealth acquired through unrighteousness, there will be no obstacles;
by renouncing it, one constantly attains peace, whereas by grasping it, one will surely bring blame upon oneself.
One should understand, as it truly is, the characteristics of one's own and others' aggregates and elements;
by practicing meditative concentration and upholding the scriptures, one burns away the mass of afflictions.
Therefore, the wise person carefully examines the body.
Having clearly understood the nature of those realms, one is called a liberated person.
If a person constantly gives rise to craving for the five desires,
their mind will be agitated by them, and all evils will follow accordingly.
If one sees a woman’s form and takes pleasure in it, clinging to it without a moment’s let-go,
failing to realize its impermanence, all evils will follow in its wake.
Because of that greed and delusion, one increases the cycle of birth and death.
Ordinary people do not understand this; thus all evils follow after them.
Constantly delighting in heedlessness, their lifespan is not long;
lacking right wisdom and reflection, all evils follow after them.
Greed knows no satisfaction; one wears extravagant clothes and indulges in adorning the body.
Giving rise to restlessness and shamelessness, all evils follow in its wake.
Constantly besmeared by the six sense objects, one is dragged along by the five desires.
Deluded regarding the three periods of time, one lacks knowledge; thus all evils follow and turn along with this.
Delighting in attachment to one's own kin, one does not realize for oneself that death will come;
with lingering attachment giving rise to a mind of resentment, all evils follow and turn along with this.
In the past, one was addicted to the realm of desire, which later became a source of calamity;
because the mind was not tranquil, all evils followed in its wake.
Having enjoyed that wealth and pleasure, beloved ones were suddenly separated.
Failing to investigate the causes of past suffering, all evils follow and turn with them.
Deluded by defiled desires, they are like fish casting themselves into a net;
ensnared and unable to escape, all evils follow and turn with them.
Fools are constantly attached and clinging, unaware of the faults of desire;
deluded by the darkness of ignorance, all evils follow after them.
They keep many favorites and concubines, yet at the end of life, they must go forth alone.
Bound by the snare of karma, all evils follow and turn with them.
Having lost the right path and remaining ignorant of the three realms,
and failing to restrain the sense faculties, all evils follow and turn with them.
Regarding those with precepts and those without, they delight in causing harm and destruction to the True Dharma; all manner of evils follow after them.
Having heard [the teachings] concerning the loss or gain resulting from transgressions and merits, they remain as if deaf and mute.
Just as when a foolish child plays, all evils follow and turn with him; so too,
having abandoned the peaceful groves and the excellent places of flowing springs,
one delights in idle pleasures, and all evils follow and turn with him.
Leaving behind mountain caves, valleys, and palaces, and pure lotus ponds,
because of their craving for those sensual pleasures, all evils follow after them.
Though they relish exquisite food and drink, they possess neither luster nor majesty.
By creating the conditions for unrighteous karma, all evils follow and turn along with it.
Such foolish people never give rise to discernment;
blown about by the winds of karma, they revolve within the three realms.
Some may be born in a superior realm, yet through heedlessness they fall;
due to indolence and delusion, they are unable to sever their various faults.
If one abandons the five desires, one attains the highest peace and security.
Just as the Buddhas and noble ones, free from craving and free from sorrow and affliction,
practice throughout the beginning, middle, and end, and are liberated from all defilements,
they shall attain the state of the Honored Muni and the supreme bliss of tranquility.
Those who delight in the five desires will fall into the evil realms;
they possess no other capacity but to invite their own bitter retribution.
Therefore, what is there for a person of wisdom to be attached to in desire?
Because these are the causes of saṃsāra, one will certainly undergo all manner of agonizing torments.
Or, though dwelling upon peaks of celestial jewels amidst gardens, groves, and pure ponds,
one falls from those heights due to the defilement of playful delusions.
The wondrous golden mountains of the heavens, with peaks of lapis lazuli,
From these one falls due to having committed unwholesome karma.
The various jewel-trees of the heavens, with clear springs winding between them— From these one falls due to having committed unwholesome karma.
Due to the causes and conditions of craving and desire, they fall from there.
From the celestial jeweled mansions and the delightful seas of fragrance,
those who have violated the precepts and abandoned all goodness fall away from them.
The exquisite music of the heavens brings delight upon being heard;
yet, through attachment to such pleasure, one wastes time and falls from that state.
If the mind gives rise to craving, the objects of desire will constantly appear before one.
Without right wisdom and reflection, how can one attain peace and happiness?
Like an ignorant child, how could one cultivate even a small amount of merit?
Having fallen from that state, one must personally undergo the retribution of one's own karma.
If a person performs unwholesome deeds yet seeks a pleasant fruit, the cause and effect do not correspond;
the mind of the fool revolves in delusion.
Failing to give rise to the cultivation of generosity, ethical discipline, and right wisdom, [they fall into ruin].
The foolish person, attached to sensual desires, is devoured by death.
Lacking wisdom and deluded regarding the fruits of karma, they constantly commit various transgressions and evils;
the foolish person, attached to sensual desires, is devoured by death.
Burning with the fire of greed, they do not know the suffering of saṃsāra;
those fools attached to desire are devoured by death.
Bound by the weight of affection, they give rise to the anguish of separation.
At that time, the fool is devoured by death. Not weary of nor fearing saṃsāra,
with a mind racing toward the realm of forms—
the deluded person attached to desire is devoured by death.
Though afflicted by the suffering of illness, fear, and anxiety, they cannot cultivate weariness toward them;
these fools, attached to desire, are devoured by death.
Following after evil associates, they enter the perilous paths of saṃsāra.
The foolish person, attached to sensual desires, is devoured by death.
With a mind giving rise to wrong thoughts, they turn their back on the true principle;
the foolish person, attached to sensual desires, is devoured by death.
Practicing unrighteousness oneself, one creates the terrors of birth and death;
the fool who clings to desire is devoured by death.
Constantly uttering defiled speech, how could such a mind know of sin or merit?
The foolish person, attached to desire, is devoured by death.
Due to the habitual practice of craving, they take no delight in the true Dharma;
the foolish person, attached to desire, is devoured by death.
Seeking happiness for oneself, yet causing harm to the Dharma—
the fool who clings to desire is devoured by death. Therefore,
one should concentrate the mind with single-minded focus and constantly cultivate pure deeds.
One who abandons all that is unwholesome is called a wise person.
If the gods become attached to pleasure and do not delight in practicing generosity and morality,
constantly giving rise to a heedless mind, they will certainly fall.
Furthermore, there is a mountain of celestial jewels, adorned and polished with various treasures;
its peaks are made of lapis lazuli, matching in grandeur with Mount Sumeru.
Whether those devas have just been born, are currently dwelling there, or are about to pass away, [they all behold it].
If one gives rise to a heedless mind, one wanders there;
that land is entirely adorned and pure, and from its groves of trees a cool breeze rises.
If one gives rise to a heedless mind, one wanders there.
There is a wondrous lotus pond, with golden petals and lapis lazuli stalks;
if one gives rise to a heedless mind, one will transmigrate therein.
There are pure and excellent rivers, where rare birds all fly and gather.
If one gives rise to a heedless mind, one wanders through those realms.
There are sublime palanquins and carriages, and multi-storied towers of supreme loftiness;
if one gives rise to a heedless mind, one wanders through those realms.
Such is the nature of saṃsāra, all arising from delusion regarding the realm of desire;
why then is it called "human," when the mind feels no weariness or renunciation?
To delight in practicing heedless conduct is to increase the cycle of rebirth.
If one does not distance oneself from this, one shall undergo great suffering and distress.
Just as a butcher binds a herd of animals and prevents them from running away and scattering, so too are we burdened by our kin; by what means can we escape?
Furthermore, those hosts of devas are constantly attached to various sensual pleasures;
not knowing the cause of birth and death, those devas are like fools.
Thus, those sentient beings are bound and dragged away by heedlessness.
Utterly and excessively deluded, one remains unawakened until death.
Constantly committing various evils with the mind, one is subdued by death;
as the fire of desire burns incessantly, it only serves to increase one's remorse.
By delighting in unrighteous conduct, one is certain to enter saṃsāra;
at the time of death there, one is utterly terrified and without rescue.
Failing to contemplate or select wholesome dharmas, one constantly delights in worldly gatherings.
In an instant they suddenly part ways, and one suffers the pain of separation.
Days and nights hasten the end of life, passing in mere moments;
when the terror of death stands before one, know that there is no way to escape it.
When the wise behold arising and ceasing, they give rise to sighs of lamentation;
by abandoning heedlessness and folly, they attain stainless purity.
Observing the marks of cessation in both self and others, how could one permit the commission of various evils?
If the mind is free from faults, one shall attain the bliss of tranquility.
Heedfulness is supreme; this is what the Tathāgata has taught.
If a person realizes impermanence, they will abandon all that is unwholesome.
The limits of all pleasure are exhausted; nothing whatsoever is permanent.
If you give rise to attachment and delight, you should know that it must be abandoned.
This fear of death is terrifying; it is swift and difficult to guard against.
Or amidst laughter and jesting, one may suddenly pass away forever.
This law of cessation is uniform, pervading everywhere;
those who do not understand this are truly the foolish.
Whether young or old, whether impoverished or wealthy,
and whether lay or ordained, all are summoned and seized by death.
Whether experiencing joy or suffering, whether virtuous or lacking virtue, [all are likewise caught].
Whether one's conduct is pure or impure, one is seized by death.
Whether one upholds the precepts or violates them, whether one is wise or a fool,
and even whether one is high or low, all are seized by death.
Whether in heaven or in hell, or as hungry ghosts or animals—
whether awake or deluded— all are seized by death.
Whether born in the realm of desire or dwelling in the realm of form, [all are likewise caught].
The formless realms are likewise subject to being seized by death.
This body is assailed by old age and sickness, as if beaten and bound with staffs and ropes.
Death possesses great power; it offers no compassion or protection to any being.
There are various terrors, and the fear of death is most perilous;
the gods, blinded by ignorance, respond to this with both weeping and laughter.
Falling away from the celestial realm, they experience the suffering of separation.
Or one may fall into hell, where that suffering is without end;
or one may experience the pleasures of heaven, yet these only extinguish themselves by giving rise to sorrow and pain.
Like delicious food mixed with poison, they must therefore be abandoned.
When that celestial merit is about to be exhausted, all kinsmen abandon him;
at the moment of his downfall, there is suffering like no other.
Because his merit has diminished, he is like a lamp that goes out when the oil is spent.
When life here draws to a close, it only increases one's distress.
Ensnared by craving and desire, the mind becomes agitated with grief;
speech falters and the body trembles—this is the terror of falling away.
Constantly attached to those pleasures, they are deceived by desire;
when they are even temporarily separated from them, they give rise to suffering and distress.
The suffering of the gods' fall is still lighter than that of the hells.
Among sixteen parts, it does not equal even one.
Fearing extinction and disappearance in the heavens, and the grief and distress of death in the human realm, one does not feel weary of or loathe them; how much less so the fires of saṃsāra!
Through attachment to pleasure one falls away; thus one knows that the world is impermanent.
If one awakens to its cause, the mind should perform all manner of wholesome deeds.
That which is high must surely fall; the cycles of worldly existence ultimately come to an end.
Union must end in separation; death is the ultimate limit of life.
All phenomena are impermanent; arising and ceasing follow one another in turn.
As for that which arises without ceasing—where in the three realms has such ever been seen?
Some are reborn into other clans; some perish within the womb;
some wander through successive births; some engage in the affairs of desire.
Just as one sees the light of the sun, once it has risen, it is certain to set.
All that is born must perish; once perished, it remains as before.
Fools do not understand this: that which they delight in arises and then perishes.
Lacking the means for liberation, they shall in the end only await death.
One should seek that eternal bliss; while life has not yet ended, one should diligently cultivate goodness and act in accordance with the True Dharma—this is what is called being wise.
How can impermanence ever be fixed?
In future lives, hardships will increase; the Buddha taught that the cause of saṃsāra is this alone, which is the sole reality.
That is to say, as various states arise, they repeatedly fall into extinction.
Because the devas are attached to pleasure, they give rise to much arrogance.
Furthermore, when that celestial realm perishes, one undergoes suffering and distress;
except for those in the hells, no other suffering can equal it.
Because of their firm attachment to the five desires, they do not realize for themselves that they are falling away.
How can such a foolish person escape old age and death?
Undergoing the cycle of birth and extinction, their number is immeasurable;
yet, failing to give rise to the mind of renunciation, they only deceive themselves.
Those who dwell on high are bound to be in peril; those who hoard treasures shall surely face want.
There is separation from those one loves, and all who are born return to death.
Once born, one grows to maturity; the vigor of youth does not pause for a moment.
In an instant they are impermanent; such is the nature of co-arising phenomena.
Failing to grasp at merit, they are bound by sensory objects;
through craving and delusion, they find no protection at the time of death.
Furthermore, there is a peak of exquisite jewels, Fully adorned with every perfection;
There are various kinds of lotus flowers, And groves of trees most lovely to behold;
There are various rivers and ponds, Where waterfowl all take their refuge.
There are various exquisite named flowers, adorned with many jewels;
there are most excellent palaces, all fashioned from rare treasures.
The kalpa-trees emit golden light, their leaves spread in the color of lapis lazuli.
Nyagrodha trees with intermingled silver luster,
Lotus blossoms all in full bloom, Swarms of bees like the sound of music,
With exquisite and peerless necklaces of jewels, Of marvelous artistry and incomparable excellence.
What was cultivated by humans in the past brings forth fruits that accord with their wishes;
yet those gods, attached to pleasure, do not realize its impermanence—
it is like a city of the gandharvas, like an illusion, a bubble, or a mass of foam.
Sensual desire is like a blazing fire; by depending upon it, one is destroyed, and through this, at the end of life, one drifts and sinks into the ocean of existence.
Regarding the pleasures of the five desires, one enjoys them without weariness or renunciation.
At the time of destruction, they are consumed by it, and all the devas abandon them.
Having many desires and no shame, they are the most base and evil;
though the devas indulge in delusion and darkness, the Lord of Death seizes his opportunity.
Whether gods, humans, asuras, yakṣas, nāgas, or spirits,
none can provide rescue when ensnared by the noose of death.
Even throughout the three realms, all are encompassed by death.
How can one attain liberation while being firmly attached to greed and delusion?
Because the gods are attached to pleasure, they undergo the fear of hundreds of thousands of deaths.
Their sensory realms are like dry firewood, and their death is like a blazing fire.
If you see others pass away, why do you not awaken?
When the suffering of illness reaches its end, one personally reaps the karmic retribution.
With a mind stained by heedlessness, one remains attached to the realms of desire.
Failing to realize that impermanence is their innate nature,
those who delight in heedlessness and constantly pursue sensual pleasures are like those who consume poison; they are pursued by the armies of death.
Neither incantations nor marvelous medicines, nor even the great asuras,
can save those who are dragged by the noose of death;
with their eyes obscured by the dust of craving, they possess no awareness at all.
Those sentient beings attached to desire have only death as their destination.
If one delights in craving and greed, seeking much pleasure without giving rise to the mind of weary detachment, then death is not far off.
Those messengers of Yama possess a power that none can repel;
appearing before one in an instant, they immediately inspire great terror.

seeing this fall, there will be no difference between him and me.
These three realms are false and provisional; all phenomena are conditioned.
It revolves like a chariot wheel, as unsubstantial as a mass of foam.

this mind, like a chariot wheel, delights in conjunction and movement.

only the wholesome karma one has performed oneself can deliver one at the time of death.

If one does not cultivate superior causes, regret later will be of no benefit.
This is a base and inferior realm that can produce much sensual pleasure;
due to lack of wisdom and delusion, one does not know the limits of life.
Who are one's kinsmen? What is true happiness?
When the signs of cessation appear before them, those gods have no refuge.
Leaving behind all excellent abodes, Adorned with groves and flowers,
Dragged by the noose of death, One departs forever according to one's karma.
Like water leaping into the air, Its momentum ends as it falls and disperses.

Just as a tree that is flourishing, with its dense foliage spread wide,
will eventually, after that period has passed, be seen to wither and fall;
so too is saṃsāra like that tree, and the various devas are its leaves.
Because of attachment to sensual pleasures, one is destroyed by impermanence.
Just as during the rainy season, when rain falls everywhere upon the sky and,
once descended, does not turn back, so too is that pleasure.
Just as an echo resounds outward, Arisen from the movement of the wind, Being empty and false by nature, it has no inherent existence; That pleasure is likewise so.

The fire of death blazes most fiercely, burning all who cling to pleasure.
Throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of births, wandering back and forth in saṃsāra,

Indulging heedlessly in manifold sensual pleasures,
which are the cause of all suffering, one shall experience them for oneself once they have ceased—
namely, birth, old age, death, and the suffering of separation from what is loved.
Thus, for oneself and others alike, there is no one who can escape this fate.
Seeing even a single person fall, why do you not give rise to fear?
If you lack skillful means, I too shall become like them.
Having understood this, one should diligently practice and constantly contemplate impermanence;
when such a person’s life is about to end, they will be free from all suffering and pain.
Their kinsmen and friends, facing one another, will harbor feelings of grief.
When that great terror arises, no one can take away one's grief and suffering.
Those who dwell in life must perish; those who have not yet fallen will eventually pass away.
This power of death is firm and strong; it gathers in both the noble and the lowly alike.
If a celestial being discerns well, they will not give rise to negligence;
by accumulating those roots of goodness, they sever all delusions.
Accumulation is the root of dispersion, and youth inevitably leads to old age.
Life is assailed by death, and all beings dwell in dependence upon it.
This fire of impermanence at the end of the eon can incinerate even Mount Sumeru;
how much more so the gods and humans, who are like plantain trees or clusters of foam?
One should know that conditioned phenomena, by their very nature, do not abide;
whether in terms of permanence or happiness, how could there be even the slightest degree of them?
All sentient beings in the world know that death is not far off.
There is no skillful means for escape, nor does the path of antidotes arise.
Regarding the physical forms of oneself and others, how could they possibly endure for long?
In the darkness of delusion there is no discernment; pleasure is likewise like this.
All sentient beings, failing to cultivate pure and wholesome karma,
are all split asunder and destroyed by the wheel of birth and death;
though they possess hundreds of thousands of kinds of forms, they perish and vanish in a single instant.
One should know that all who are born are inevitably overcome by death.
If a person constantly delights in heedlessness through their thoughts and intentions,
they will lack the causes for happiness and be pointlessly seized by Yama.
Relying on one's physical form, beauty, and prowess, one loses them all as soon as one becomes attached to pleasure;
the powerful Yama, the Lord of Death, is the one such a person seeks to draw near.
If one draws near to Yama, one becomes most utterly base and inferior.
Happiness and lifespan swiftly perish.
If a deva is attached to sensual pleasures, they will long neglect the causes of virtue;
blinded and devoid of discernment, such a one is deceived by desire.
Devoid of majestic splendor and radiance, with dull faculties and a distracted mind,
one falls from that Yāma Heaven according to one's karma.
Though happiness may dwell there for a time, decay and aging constantly press upon the body.
If one gives rise to a mind of defiled attachment, that person is without eyes and without wisdom.
Regarding supreme and exquisite pleasures, they enjoy them without weariness or relinquishment;
unaware that in a mere instant, the terror of death will suddenly arrive.
The fool knows no contentment and does not contemplate old age and death;
when his life is about to end, his regret and distress are thus in vain.
Furthermore, the bliss within the heavens can be attained simply through reflection.
When it falls into destruction, where does that pleasure go?
Happiness swiftly passes away; life, too, is just the same.
Before long, within one's own person, this will certainly be realized without doubt.
If, while in a state of strength and health, one possesses pure wisdom and a clear mind, and delights in seeking the True Dharma, such a person is a possessor of true knowledge.
All pleasure comes to an end; all that is loved must be parted from.
All life has an end; before death one should practice and study.
The fear of death is extremely perilous and evil; only the Dharma can rescue and deliver one.
Therefore, always cherish and delight in it, so that you may be born in a place of peace and security.
By delighting in the True Dharma, one is born among the gods;
when that state eventually declines and ceases, there is not even the slightest suffering.
When death approaches for an ordinary person, their mind possesses not the slightest joy.
Though friends may be many, not one will follow even a single step.
Whatever was done during life will all manifest at the moment of death;
the terror is known only by oneself, while relatives merely stand around in vain.
Furthermore, as their life draws to a close, they give rise to conceptualizations toward others;
through deluded attachment, they grasp at things as "mine," and thus experience great terror regarding death and rebirth.
Their sensory objects are like the bite of a venomous snake, and the poison of craving is like a state of fainting.
The various devas do not understand that they are being violently assailed by death.
When they pass away from those celestial realms, some are reborn among human beings;
one should contemplate this with careful attention: birth and death are followed in succession by suffering.
Driven by the winds of karma, one undergoes the suffering of expedient means;
yet in this world there are those who are upright, who subdue their minds and escape death.
Neither parents nor kin, nor friends nor servants [can save one].
When such a person’s life comes to an end, they depart alone in sorrow.
Having deceived themselves by their own nature, they find no companion at the moment of death;
toward their kinsmen and wives, they fix their minds on them in vain.
Furthermore, none of those kinsmen can rescue or deliver one;
terrified and without refuge, they look upon each other like strangers.
The ignorant fool, lacking true understanding, has spent this present life in vain.
In future lives, one will experience even more bitter suffering, each receiving their own retribution for past deeds.
If you feel dread toward suffering, why not likewise feel it toward death?
If you resolve to seek the True Dharma, you shall attain eternal and true bliss.
Because the devas are attached to pleasure, they are dull-witted and lack clarity;
all things are entirely impermanent—how can happiness endure for long?
Illusory phenomena are subject to constant flux, whereas the true nature remains forever unmoving.
The devas abandon their palaces because they do not rely on the True Dharma.
If the mind is agitated and disturbed, and one is infatuated with the five desires,
failing to know the limit of life, one shall suffer its bitter poison.
Or when one passes away from that heaven, one is reborn again in another;
yet there must come a time of falling, just as day ends with night.
Day is like that life, and night is a metaphor for death.
Having thoroughly understood those two characteristics, one should practice them well within the mind.
The realm of desire binds sentient beings, depriving them of mastery for a long time;
yet that very thing becomes the death-demon, which will soon be subdued and extinguished.
Women are full of guile and seduction, offering sweet words in service;
yet when the fool faces death, he must himself undergo the retribution of his karma.
Once, in a magnificent grove, amidst fragrant breezes and pure ponds—
Indulging in much idle play—what joy can there truly be?
That pleasure is certain to change, and this body is certain to perish;
how, then, can one be called a true man?
Constantly driven by craving,
whether in suffering or in pleasure, in youth or in old age,
and whether of superior or inferior lineage— all are overcome by impermanence.
Whether handsome or ugly, powerful or powerless,
whether a relative or a stranger, all are overcome by impermanence.
Whether they be royal messengers or the attendants of elders, [all are subject to the same fate].
Whether gentle or fierce, whether impoverished or wealthy, whether virtuous or lacking virtue—
men and women alike— are all overcome by impermanence.
Whether they be guests or lords, or those dwelling by water or on land,
or those who reside upon mountain peaks, all are overcome by impermanence. Whether in sleep or wakefulness,
or in the midst of eating, drinking, and feasting, [they are likewise subject to it].
Whether going or coming, one is overcome by impermanence.
Whether dwelling in the air or on the earth, whether in the Middle Kingdom or among the frontier tribes,
like a revolving saw that never ceases, one is overcome by impermanence.
Whether endowed with wisdom and abundant wealth, diligent or negligent,
whether afflicted by illness or enjoying ease, all are overcome by impermanence.
Whether violent and cruel or benevolent and compassionate, whether frugal and austere or extravagant and luxurious—
If one awakens from delusion, yet is overcome by impermanence;
or if one falls among the denizens of hell, hungry ghosts, animals, or the human realm—
if one is indolent rather than courageous, one will be overcome by impermanence.

Because they lack power and capability, Are overcome by impermanence;
So too are the beings of the formless realm, Who abide in samāpatti.
They all lack the power to resist being overcome by impermanence.
Whatever phenomenon arises from causes is certain to disintegrate;
no created thing has ever been seen to remain eternally.
The various faults of the five desires can be severed through the power of wisdom;
if one is free from that craving and attachment, one shall emerge from the ocean of existence.
For all things, whether sentient or insentient, ultimately end in dissolution.
Having realized that the characteristics of the world are thus, one’s mind should delight in tranquility.
Though gardens, various jeweled mountains, and palaces are exquisitely adorned,
when the kalpa-fire blazes forth, all the devas shall utterly perish and vanish.
With a mind of folly and negligence, how can the realms of sensory objects ever reach their end?
Bound by the ropes of craving like one rendered mute, one falls from that state.
Thus, both life-span and joy are abandoned.
Blind and sightless, they see nothing; they have lost their way on the True Path.
Furthermore, for all sentient beings, life is like a rising bubble, tossed and shaken by the waves of desire—how can youthful beauty endure?
Those gods of Tuṣita, pressed by the fire of impermanence, are extinguished like a lamp when its oil is spent; so too is their swiftness.
The fruit of karma is like a wheel, with the twelve links as its spokes.
Each is drawn by its own causes; birth and cessation revolve together.
Having abandoned the sublime pleasures and magnificent realms of the heavens, they again undergo that saṃsāra, being overcome by extinction.
Because they are suppressed by cessation, the root of suffering increases;
revolving within the three realms, none can escape all sufferings.
Furthermore, when those gods fall, the other gods feel joy.
Because of this anger and affliction, one wanders through saṃsāra without rest.
When merit is exhausted, one falls back again, drifting and sinking in the ocean of existence;
whether the cause be pleasure or pain, one receives its fruit for oneself without fail.
Having cultivated wholesome karma in the past, one is born among the devas;
yet, becoming attached to pleasure and neglecting the causes of purity, that merit gradually wanes and is exhausted.
Since those causes do not increase further, how can such fortune endure for long?
All arise from impermanence; everything is utterly lost.
All conditioned forms and appearances are entirely false and impermanent;
sentient beings cling to deluded minds and take no pleasure in relying upon the True Dharma.
The gods are addicted to sensual pleasures, which pass as swiftly as a torrent;
their lifespan lasts but a moment, yet in their folly they do not realize it.
Having committed unwholesome deeds themselves, they bring upon themselves old age and death.
Those devas lack right understanding, constantly pursuing the realm of desire.
What joy is there in the three realms?
All things are impermanent; blinded by ignorance, they cannot seek the essential way out.
Just as when a torrential rain falls from the void,
its force is so swift that it never pauses, so too is the nature of pleasure.
Like wind-blown dust and sand, it may linger for a brief moment in the sky.
Delusion and karma form the physical body, yet one knows not where it shall fall.
Sentient beings possess no permanence, and even their happiness does not endure long.
The foolish lack correct reflection; thus, they cannot attain that bliss.
The increase of various sensual pleasures is the cause of saṃsāra;
if one does not understand them well, one will be destroyed by them.
For that suffering and pleasure abide in mutual dependence.
Just as a beautiful garland of flowers may cover a venomous serpent,
or as poison mixed with delicious food leads to death upon consumption, so too,
if one is attached to sensual pleasures, one will surely sink into the evil realms.
All conditioned phenomena possess the characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing;
their pleasure is likewise so. The mind delusively gives rise to craving for them.
Through this delusion, greed is born, and one thus flows and transmigrates moment by moment.
Happiness and lifespan are soon cast aside;
if one joyfully practices various virtues, without slackening in the beginning, middle, or end,
then through the tranquility of the mind, one shall face death without sorrow or regret.
Form and appearance must surely perish; affection ends in separation.
The fool lacks reflection and remains ever attached to the realm of desire.
Old age and death revolve like a wheel, swift and impossible to ward off.
Sentient beings lacking the eye of wisdom are thus torn asunder;
when those gods fall, their faculties and consciousnesses become utterly deranged,
their kinsmen all abandon them, and their suffering has no equal.
Experiencing various sensual pleasures, the mind of craving knows no satiety;
when life ends here, one undergoes manifold suffering and affliction.
If a person performs wholesome deeds, they will certainly escape the evil realms.
When the time of death eventually arrives, one will have no sorrow or fear.
Until the transition to the next life occurs, one’s meritorious rewards will be fully complete;
having personally attained those great benefits, this is the foremost peace and security.
The gods call it falling; among humans, it is named premature death.
Having realized that all things are impermanent, why would you again commit various evils?
It is just as when the oil and the wick are exhausted, one knows for certain that the lamp will go out.
When meritorious deeds are exhausted, one falls away from the celestial palaces.
Just as when a wall is destroyed, how can the painted images remain?
When pleasure perishes and merit declines, one falls into ruin without a doubt.
The gods have abandoned their superior abodes; because they are so attached to pleasure, it is thus.
All sentient beings should realize the law of impermanence:
the born are swallowed by death, and the flourishing are oppressed by decay.
When the four great elements suddenly increase or diminish, how can one escape the affliction of illness?
If births are as numerous as they are, so too is their cessation without limit;
having ceased, one is born again, and once born, one immediately grows old.
In the span of a single moment, great terror is about to arrive;
conditioned phenomena flow on without a moment’s pause—why is it that people lack awareness?
Furthermore, for all sentient beings, youth swiftly undergoes transformation.
Life’s span is suddenly impermanent; why do people lack awareness?
As days pass by in succession, one perishes in an instant;
bound and entangled by karma, why do people lack awareness?
Hundreds of thousands of koṭis of devas sport with sovereign ease, yet even they shall fall; how can humans remain without awareness?
Furthermore, the devas of the six desire realms are greedily attached to pleasure.
Because of this, they pass away and perish; why do people lack awareness?
Pleasure is like a dream or an illusion, and likewise like foam or bubbles;
existing only briefly before dispersing and decaying, why do people lack awareness?
Furthermore, like that mirage, arising from false imagination,
why do fools dwelling in saṃsāra not feel weary and distressed?
This death is most terrifying, and there is no means by which to escape it.
Whether it be one's own home or a celestial palace, which among them can be a place of lasting peace?
All pleasures are abandoned; immeasurable sufferings press in from all sides;
kinsmen and relatives are all separated—this is what is called death.
Enshrouded by delusion, one's right wisdom is obscured;
One rushes toward that great terror, the most profound and vast ocean of suffering— This is what is called death.
All the faculties become dull and feeble; In an instant, life is about to be severed.
To abandon a good reputation—this is called death.
Regarding the enjoyment of sense objects and matters such as praise, because of this they are all lost; this is called death.
Possessing definitive reality, it is that upon which sentient beings rely;
that which can destroy the commonality of existence is what is called death.
Whether they be devas, nāgas, yakṣas, or various spirits and ghosts, [it is the same].
When the time arrives, all return to extinction; this is what is called death.
Like a wild horse galloping away, like a blazing fire that oppresses, nothing can withstand it; this is what is called death.
When life-force, warmth, and consciousness are all abandoned, and the aggregates and sense-bases are utterly dispersed and destroyed—
this state of ultimate equality is what is called death.
Thus do all sentient beings flow on, without a moment’s rest.
One should abandon a heedless mind and diligently cultivate wholesome deeds.
Like the wind or a soaring bird, whose nature is exceedingly swift and sharp,
the life-span of sentient beings passes even more rapidly than they.
The force of the wind may turn back, and birds that have flown away may also return;
but when the lives of sentient beings have come to an end, one cannot regain them through empty longing.
Form and color all undergo transformation and decay, and meritorious karma is entirely consumed and melted away.
Seized by the powerful force of King Yama, the suffering of death is extremely perilous;
it destroys all sentient beings with such speed that it does not pause for a moment— how can they remain without awareness?
The devas are mostly heedless; attached to pleasure and deluded by ignorance, they do not realize that great suffering and affliction will inevitably be experienced by themselves.
They fail to see that all conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛtadharma) are by nature impermanent.
Terror arises accordingly, and one shall be destroyed in turn.
Youth is assailed by old age, and life is devoured by death;
because one dwells within the causes of destruction, all manner of calamities and misfortunes arise.
Because the devas are heedless, their minds are deranged by craving and desire;
they feel no sorrow or fear regarding such evils.
With the eye of wisdom, they clearly see all the bitter fruits of suffering in the future.
The wise contemplate well, while the foolish give rise to perversity.
By committing various evils with the mind, they deceive themselves;
their merit diminished, their lives end just as a lamp goes out when the oil is exhausted.
Regarding supreme delights and the excellent realms of gardens and groves, one never tires of such enjoyments, and by this very means one falls.
Life is not solid; it is like a floating bubble.
Suddenly appearing, they immediately vanish; so too it is with the foolish.
Like wind-driven bubbles of foam that may linger for a brief moment, when the merit of those gods is exhausted, they cannot remain for even an instant.
If a person is attached to sensual pleasures, they are driven by greed;
seeking more and more in succession, they do not realize that death is approaching.
By indulging in that craving, it increases with every passing thought.
How could one know that their lifespan is gradually diminishing?
Youthfulness suddenly decays like being struck by a staff;
when happiness is invaded by illness, harm likewise occurs in this manner.
These three kinds of faults and evils can destroy both gods and asuras;
yet ordinary people, overcome by delusion, feel no alarm upon seeing them.
When observing their own and others' kinsmen, they are like a flow of saliva that never ceases.
Bound by various forms of delusion and craving, they entangle one another.
If a person covets their lineage so that sons and grandsons may succeed one another, they are like a silkworm binding itself in its cocoon; what, in the end, will they gain?
Life is difficult to protect; the enemy of death possesses great power.
Its momentum is swift and never pauses; in a single kṣaṇa, it draws near.
Neither gods, humans, nor asuras, nor ghosts, spirits, nor any other species can [avert it].
Except for the Buddha, the World-Honored One, no others have the power to subdue [the afflictions].
Having thoroughly understood strength and weakness, he reveals the true Dharma;
by not creating the causes of various transgressions, one is forever freed from those perilous paths.
If a person delights in heedlessness, this is said not to be liberation;
deluded by that ignorance, they are far from Bodhi.
Those who do not delight in heedlessness regard heedlessness as an enemy.
Because of this, the various devas immediately fall into hell.
If sentient beings are heedless, they sink into birth and death;
if the mind is free from those faults, its intrinsic nature is fundamentally pure.
Heedfulness is supreme, like partaking of ambrosia;
if one is heedless and deluded, it is like drinking poison and dying.
Furthermore, that heedless person is like a blazing fire of venom.
Because of such volitional formations, one will burn and boil for a long time.
Within all worlds, the unconditioned is most tranquil;
if a person is not heedless, they shall reach that state.
If a person lives in negligence, constantly committing various unwholesome deeds, being shrouded by delusion, how could they be born in heaven?
Negligence leads to ruin; by departing from it, one attains constant peace and security.
Base and evil, deeply loathsome—therefore, one should cast them far away.
If a person is not heedless, they will be honored and esteemed by the world;
always free from perversion, such a person is called a true man.
Why do you cling to pleasure and joy, giving rise to the fault of negligence?
If the mind is not restrained, one will be overcome by the Mara of Death.
Pleasure and joy are like smoldering smoke; negligence is like a blazing fire.
They burn countless devas, who, intoxicated by delusion, lack awareness and discernment.
If they do not sever their heedlessness, they will remain forever transmigrating beings;
deluded by sensory objects, they are unable to seek liberation.
Heedlessness drags the devas away, causing them to fall into peril and hardship;
therefore, the wise declare heedlessness to be poison.
Pleasure is like that honey, yet heedlessness is the addiction to it.
When one later experiences the bitter fruits, one personally endures that agony and torment.
Heedlessness invites peril and calamity; the wise all understand this clearly, yet the foolish feel no weariness or aversion toward it—they are no different from oxen.
If one delights in heedlessness, that person will have only suffering;
heedlessness is not a wholesome cause, and even a small measure of happiness cannot be found.
Through non-heedlessness, one shall attain the state of death where the mind is tranquil.
Heedlessness has no other power than to summon the suffering of hell.
When the gods are attached to heedlessness and indulge in the defilement of unwise intelligence, they become identical to those in other realms; their darkness and dullness are entirely alike.
Those gods are utterly heedless, delighting in various manifestations;
thinking they dwell eternally in celestial palaces, they do not realize they are falling.
Furthermore, those devas and humans who enjoy pleasures with moderation—
If one indulges excessively in lust, the resulting ruin is one's own fault alone.
While attached to the exquisite pleasures of the heavens without ceasing for even a moment, one's meritorious karma will accordingly diminish;
then one will realize for oneself that one is about to fall away.
To demonstrate the faults of negligence, it should be forever abandoned by the gods;
yet because they do not relinquish their attachment, they fall from the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.
Fools who delight in negligence give rise to all manner of faults and evils.
At the time of death there, being tormented by the fire of desire,
the five objects of sense pleasure are like the earth; from them arises heedlessness,
and constantly indulging in attachment and delusion, one does not cultivate meritorious deeds.
Sensual desire is the cause of heedlessness; it is violent, evil, and extremely swift.
The wise should restrain it, realizing that all such things are like dreams.
Dreams are not the cause of hell; rather, the five desires are the cause.
One should distance oneself from the five desires and diligently cultivate sublime practices.
Although the various devas obtain all their sensual pleasures merely by thinking of them,
it is through the excellent awakening of wisdom that one becomes heedful.
The various devas dwell in their palaces, deluded by sensory objects;
through negligence they lack the resolve for liberation, sinking into the ocean of suffering.
Negligence is the height of ignorant darkness, having nescience as its root.
Enshrouded by that delusion, though they see, they are as if blind.
Just as a blazing, surging flame arises because of fire,
so do all afflictions arise from heedlessness and originate through delusion.
If the mind gives rise to negligence, it is immediately consumed by that fire;
such a foolish person shall fall into hell.
When the gods become negligent, they become attached to the celestial maidens.
Delighting in the pleasure of union, they do not perceive the suffering of separation.
When their heavenly life is about to end, they encounter great terror;
that pleasure is not firm, and at such a time, one will only feel weary and regretful.
Those who have gathered must eventually disperse; those attached to pleasure are destroyed by suffering.
The young soon wither and decay; all things return to extinction.
Furthermore, all those sentient beings are bound by their good and evil karma.
Each wanders through the various realms of existence, like that actor;
Drawn along by the power of karma, they flow and turn within saṃsāra.
When retribution is exhausted, there is impermanence; Even the wise cannot escape it.
Heedlessness is most loathsome; one should always avoid it through skillful means.
If one can sever that fault, one will transcend the ocean of the three realms of existence.
Like a person who has fallen into a deep abyss, their life might last but a short while.
If one falls through heedlessness, even a modicum of happiness cannot be found.
Due to the fault of heedlessness, one creates immeasurable evil karma;
throughout day and night, there is not the slightest bit of virtue.
All happiness, whether worldly or transcendent, is destroyed by heedlessness;
therefore, one should abandon it. Heedlessness swiftly brings ruin; by departing from it, there is peace and security.
In future lives one will be born among the devas, Becoming a most supreme lord of gods.
If a person abandons heedlessness, They will sever the cause of saṃsāra;
therefore, one should cast it aside, And always remain free from sorrow and fear.
If a person seeks the fruit of happiness, they should eliminate its cause of suffering;
if one cuts off that heedlessness, then there will be no various hardships.
Furthermore, for those attached to heedlessness, it gives rise to sleep.
And due to the causes and conditions of wrongdoing, one shall fall from a precipice.
Heedfulness is supreme; let not even a slight amount arise.
By abandoning [heedlessness], one constantly attains peace; attachment to pleasure is its bond.
Because the devas are negligent, they become increasingly intoxicated by delusion;
like birds that know nothing, they constantly engage in the conduct of hell-beings.
Immeasurable devas and humans are fettered and shackled by desire.
Falling into the ocean of heedlessness, they are like fish cast into a net.
Furthermore, sentient beings among the gods, addicted to desire and lacking discernment, have their minds ensnared by negligence; how could their pleasures last long?
When the mind follows after negligence, objects of sense constantly appear before it;
finding no weariness or aversion toward pleasure, those gods are perpetually tormented.
That all the gods are attached to sensual conduct is entirely due to that negligence.
This dharma is not firm; it can destroy one’s lifespan.
Countless hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas of devas have been consumed by the fire of desire due to their folly and negligence.
The faults of that heedlessness can cause all sentient beings to create the causes of unwholesome deeds, which later bring about their bitter fruits.
One should truly and skillfully observe the very nature of that heedlessness.
It is like a venomous serpent, and also like a sharp sword;
heedlessness causes all the devas to follow its turn,
appearing at first like a kinsman, but later realized to be like an enemy.
Devas, humans, asuras, and likewise all those nāgas,
Due entirely to heedlessness, give rise to various obstacles and difficulties.
Deluded by heedlessness, they are unable to cultivate manifold virtues.
Such a person loses the great benefit and seeks to enter perilous and evil paths.
If one constantly delights in and clings to food and drink,
performing the deeds of an animal, they will be deceived by heedlessness.
Furthermore, those gods and humans, having distanced themselves from all wholesome karma, wander on in the indulgence of delusion; what can they gain through such negligence?
Because the gods are negligent, their merit is exhausted and they fall.
Blown by the winds of karma, they drift and sink into the evil realms.
For immeasurable hundreds of thousands [of eons], they endure the suffering of cyclic birth and death;
lacking right mindfulness and reflection, they constantly give rise to all manner of grief and fear.
The gods, through that delusion, drink the turbid water of heedlessness;
later they fall into hell, constantly surrounded by fierce fires.
If a person in this world always delights in heedfulness, [they will not suffer such a fate].
By diligently cultivating various meritorious deeds, one will certainly be reborn among the gods.
A human body is extremely difficult to obtain; yet having obtained it, one gives rise to negligence.
Negligence is utter darkness, which shall bring about the suffering of hell.
If a person delights in negligence and fails to give rise to compassion,
at the time of their death, they will undergo extreme suffering and feverish torment.
This is not burned by the fires of the world, nor severed by swords and blades.
This fierce fire of heedlessness arises from the five sense faculties.
When pleasure perishes, it becomes suffering; even one's kinsmen become like enemies—all this is born of heedlessness; therefore, one should abandon it.
Heedlessness, delusion, and craving cause greed to increase further;
these three are fearsome, for they can destroy the virtues of sentient beings.
Lacking wisdom, they abandon the True Dharma and delight in practicing heedlessness.
Driven and coerced at the time of death by the messengers of Yama,
those who are heedless fall into extreme peril; the wise always guard themselves,
so that at the moment of life’s end, they remain secure and free from all fear.
Heedlessness is the foremost suffering; heedfulness is the supreme happiness.
Those who seek that happiness should not practice heedlessness.
Regarding those realms and elements, heedlessness gives rise to calamity.
When all roots of virtue are destroyed, various obstacles arise.
Furthermore, those who are heedless, being attached to forms and colors,
and due to their excessive ignorance, will head toward perilous difficulties.
If one constantly indulges in negligence, one will certainly fall into the evil realms;
yet the fool does not perceive this, remaining within the very palm of death.
Because the merit of the gods is exhausted, it is entirely due to the arising of negligence.
Harmed by those [enemies], one falls with no means of rescue.
There is but one wholesome dharma, complete with all virtues:
it is to be ever associated with patience and to have compassion for sentient beings.
By the power of these roots of goodness, one will be free from all fears at the time of death.
Therefore, abandon negligence and apply yourself with focused diligence;
always remain far removed from ignorance and well-guard your clear wisdom.
If one realizes these two dharmas, heedlessness will be naturally severed.
This is the wealth of a man; it must certainly be cultivated.
Because one possesses that wealth, one delights in non-heedlessness.
Heedlessness is called bondage; non-heedlessness is liberation.
These two characteristics should be discerned through skillful means.
If one delights in heedlessness, one should give rise to virtuous reflection.
When their life comes to an end later on, they will then realize the fruits of their karma.
Furthermore, having renounced the household life, they always give rise to contentment;
by diligently cultivating all manner of goodness, they attain proximity to the bliss of nirvāṇa.
Detached from worldly攀緣 (objects of attachment), they devote themselves solely to the ultimate truth;
they are not disturbed even slightly by the deeds of Māra.
If a person’s mind is tranquil, always free from all longing, [they shall attain liberation].
When supreme wisdom arises, how could there be suffering for one?
By observing with right discernment, one shall escape all terrors of the past and present,
and be liberated from the immeasurable bonds of afflictions in the future.
If one delights in heedfulness, one will never encounter calamities;
through wisdom, one leaves behind defilement and shall realize the state of true permanence.
This heedlessness can destroy the exquisite five sensual pleasures of the gods.
How much more so for that fool, who is addicted to ignorance!
If one delights in practicing heedlessness, that person is close to death;
yet one who can abandon those faults will properly sustain their life of wisdom.
Heedlessness and heedfulness—these two have been thus described.
To be near the former is the root of suffering; to abandon it is to distance oneself from death.
Devas and worldly people alike are constantly attached to sensual pleasures.
Just like those birds, there is no difference between these two types.
Failing to comprehend that True Dharma and not knowing the cause of liberation,
such gods and humans are therefore similar to them.
Those sentient beings who abandon negligence and always delight in superior conduct are truly wise. The gods,
however, delight in play and constantly indulge in negligence.
Though one may receive the karmic rewards of heavenly bliss, if one is of the same kind as those birds,
there will be differences in various actions and thus differences in rebirth;
only the wholesome Dharma can be relied upon, for it ensures that one certainly does not fall even slightly.
If one does not awaken to the cycle of rebirth, all things will eventually come to an end;
those gods are utterly deluded, and through their perversity they only bring harm upon themselves.
If a god relies on the True Dharma, they shall abide in a stainless realm.
One who does not engage in heedless conduct is revered by the world.
Realizing that both suffering and pleasure arise from causes and conditions,
such a celestial being possesses excellent discernment and does not perform what is unwholesome or disadvantageous.
Bound to one another by ties of kin and friends, they feel no weariness or fear toward saṃsāra; when have they ever sought liberation?
Drinking alcohol gives rise to heedlessness—this the wise should understand.
Once drunk, it vanishes immediately; yet heedlessness is difficult to destroy.
Heedlessness gives rise to madness and causes one to race through the five realms of existence;
therefore, it is taught as a skillful means that its affliction exceeds even drunken stupor.
If a person acts with heedlessness, they will suffer for ten million eons;
though the drinker may sober up each day, heedlessness leaves one perpetually intoxicated.
Those who distance themselves from heedlessness shall not fall into such ruin.
If one is dragged away by them, one will always sink into the various realms of existence.
Those who delight in benefiting others should abandon all negligence;
this is taught by the Buddhas as the supreme affliction.
Led astray by heedlessness, their minds become light and fickle;
for this reason, the gods fall into indolence and fail to practice abandonment.
If one does not distance oneself from heedlessness, the resulting lack of wisdom is deeply terrifying.
One will certainly fall into peril and difficulty, and later undergo that burning affliction.
Falling from the celestial realm, one then experiences all manner of hardships;
know that such negligence is not to be approached even for a moment.
If one constantly delights in heedlessness, they possess no share of happiness;
know that such heedlessness is the foremost root of suffering.
Countless devas and humans have all, because of heedlessness, [fallen into ruin].
One falls into the hells for hundreds of thousands of koṭis of kalpas;
heedlessness is the foremost enemy, while heedfulness is like a friend.
Therefore, one should draw near to it and always act for one's own benefit.
