Chao San Dafu Yu Shandang, for the purpose of reverent practice: Seeing evil as one would poison,
this negligence is therefore said to be the foremost perilous path.
Those heedless beings, deceived by sweet words, have their minds perpetually deluded and intoxicated; they experience suffering as their own lot alone.
They do not fear affliction, nor do they seek celestial happiness.
Due to observing through ignorance, they are no different from animals.
With regard to food, drink, and sexual desire, their minds never for a moment let go;
such sentient beings are identical to the class of beasts.
Those who delight in and cling to play remain within the mouth of Yama;
death confronts them immediately, and that suffering is difficult to endure.
When the minds of sentient beings are heedless, they perish prematurely as their pleasures crumble.
Because of that negligence, one is ultimately ground down by death.
There is but one wholesome dharma that makes life secure and peaceful, and can lead to rebirth among the devas; it is called non-negligence.
Heedlessness and heedfulness give rise to faults and virtues;
both good and evil stem from the mind, and liberation from bondage is likewise so.
Sentient beings do not understand this, whereby their happiness becomes like a source of harm.
Their minds are utterly deluded, far removed from the wisdom of the Buddha.
Heedlessness is like a poisonous tree with three towering trunks;
it constantly relies upon and dwells within old age, sickness, and death.
Fully perfecting right practice, one cannot be harmed by others;
the wise person dwelling in saṃsāra always delights in heedfulness.
If one delights in heedfulness, then one is free from all faults.
Liberated from all terrors, one attains the highest bliss.
If one is possessed of heedlessness, I feel fear;
yet if such a person were to attain liberation, there would be no need to abandon pleasure.
Through greed one gives rise to negligence, and shall fall into the Lotus Hell;
there, having mastery over desire, one dwells within it forever.
If one abides in negligence, the four kinds of perversions arise.
They can destroy virtuous conduct, like an enemy in this world who inflicts harm.
Immeasurable doubts and fears constantly oppress them;
their wandering through the cycle of birth and death is entirely due to heedless conduct.
This one practice of negligence, constantly delighting in various sensual pleasures,
causes one to remain far removed from all untainted and pure dharmas.
Because the devas are negligent, they revolve in succession without end.
If one is deluded and does not feel weary of [suffering], by what means can one attain tranquility?
By abandoning defiled thoughts, the mind becomes tranquil;
thus one is able to benefit oneself and others, and will no longer experience the various torments of feverish affliction.
The gods are attached to sensual pleasures, yet what they have attained has never been seen [to last].
This pleasure arises from conditioned phenomena; it is impermanent and does not endure for long.
These conditioned forms and characteristics are destined to perish.
When that pleasure perishes, then suffering and affliction arise.
If a person, regarding the objects of desire, becomes heedless and their mind deranged,
separation is certain, and they will later experience burning anguish.
Regarding the objects of the five desires, one attains mastery through craving and attachment;
those desires deceive the devas, and thus they revolve according to heedlessness.
If a person practices heedlessness, it is the root of all calamities.
Giving rise to greedy craving for wealth, one extensively commits various unwholesome deeds.
If a person is born in this life endowed with all manner of happiness,
they should act in accordance with wisdom, just as a fish follows the flowing current.
If the gods are heedless and become subjugated by female forms,
they will be consumed by them and constantly experience suffering. Therefore,
all gods and humans should, with a single mind, keep far away from them.
If one’s mind is always content and not bound by desire,
yet remains deluded by ignorance regarding vice and merit, and does not know what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma,
such a person will not attain even a small portion of Nirvana.
Regarding the light and heavy rules of discipline, And the most profound essential teachings,
If one constantly delights in practicing them, Then one shall obtain that peace and happiness.
Always delighting in proclaiming the True Dharma, One washes away all defilements and impurities.
By practicing without negligence, one will always obtain sublime bliss.
Those who formerly delighted in negligence and were constantly deluded and intoxicated by folly—
whether they be gods or humans— all should not be associated with.
Committing the fault of negligence without ever ceasing,
when that person’s life comes to an end, they shall proceed to the evil realms.
This is said because such negligence is not in accord with the truth.
The gods are perpetually deluded and shall fall into hell.
The gods are infatuated by desire; they conceive love for what is not dear.
Shrouded in the darkness of ignorance, they lack awareness; how could there be even the slightest happiness?
The gods, regarding the five sensual desires, Are constantly delighted by, attached to, and intoxicated by them;
Like those born blind, they do not see the true path.
Because their minds are distracted, they do not give rise to true vision.
Heedlessness constantly burns; therefore, one should keep far from it.
The wholesome qualities of the mental ground are destroyed by heedlessness, so that the Eightfold Noble Path, though radiant, can never be seen.
This negligence is a poison that can destroy the ten wholesome dharmas;
such a negligent person loses the four kinds of meditative concentration.
All Buddhas have transcended the five desires and always praise non-negligence.
This body is invaded by old age and death; one should therefore grow weary of and renounce heedlessness.
Heedlessness brings only suffering, while freedom from it is liberation.
Those who are dragged away by heedlessness lack the wisdom to sever it.
Heedfulness is supreme; the gods delight in its proximity.
If one is heedless, know for certain that one shall fall away.
All sentient beings wander in saṃsāra, finding no liberation.
Bound by the noose of heedlessness, one finds it difficult to escape;
Committing evil brings no merit, while performing good incurs no fault.
Sentient beings who are heedless constantly give rise to inverted views.
What constitutes sin and merit is not as described by worldly people;
the wise understand this clearly and do not praise negligence.
If the gods become heedless, they will lose their wholesome karma;
know that this evil cause will certainly bring about the fruit of suffering.
If the mind is attached to various desires, it produces a small amount of pleasure for a brief moment.
Thus they are destroyed by it, falling away and giving rise to great suffering.
Though sensory objects constantly appear before them, the fool is never satisfied;
deluded and attached to women, he is seen to fall.
Through greed one gives rise to negligence, Associating closely with women;
When one's own life comes to an end, They all merely look on.
When the devas fall from their realm, They depart alone without a companion.
Only wholesome and unwholesome karmas follow one in the future.
Stay far away from those evil deeds and devote yourself exclusively to all virtuous practices;
abandon these faults and always delight in heedfulness.
Heedlessness is the root of saṃsāra; freedom from it is tranquility.
These two distinctions are here explained according to their own characteristics.
The wise constantly reflect upon them and delight in cultivating all that is virtuous.
When a person of integrity acts in accordance with the Dharma, they shall not experience even the slightest suffering.
Since all sentient beings dwelling in saṃsāra follow their own karma,
why is that world destroyed by heedlessness?
Heedlessness is the foremost bond; it can further destroy all virtues.
It is the cause of one’s downfall and the root of suffering in hell.
To demonstrate this, heedlessness alone is the cause of all afflictions and distress.
Those who delight in benefiting others always remain free from such faults.
If one is free from heedlessness, one shall reach the deathless state;
through the absence of heedlessness, one draws near to the path of enlightenment.
If one delights in non-heedlessness, one dwells in the supreme nirvāṇa;
therefore, heedlessness is said to be the cause of one's downfall.
For a person who acts with heedlessness, there is no evil greater than this.
Deceived and despised by the world, one falls into the realm of hungry ghosts upon death.
If one delights in heedlessness, one will be born into that state of perversion;
through such karmic results, one wanders along the stream of birth and death.
The blazing fires of that hell constantly burn those who are heedless;
therefore, one who delights in liberation should abandon heedlessness.
If a person is free from heedlessness, then clear wisdom will arise.
Having forever severed all afflictions, one constantly experiences that sublime bliss.
Sentient beings have distracted minds and are bound by karma;
as they transmigrate through the three realms of existence, they should delight in heedfulness.
What is suffering is called pleasure; when pleasure perishes, suffering arises.
A husband dies and becomes a wife; one should therefore delight in heedfulness.
A wife dies and becomes a mother; a mother dies and becomes a wife.
Within this cycle of saṃsāra, one should delight in heedfulness.
Heedlessness gives rise to craving; from craving, anger arises again.
As the source of all calamities, it causes one to sink and revolve within the evil realms.
Whether in heedlessness or in heedfulness, the wise attach themselves to neither;
this is the supreme peace, ascending the pavilion of wisdom.
If one can leave heedlessness behind, one will dwell securely in the place of bliss.
To become a man of great wisdom, one must swiftly realize the fruit of true permanence.
To demonstrate the faults of negligence is to be utterly at odds with the Path;
it severs the bridge of Dharma and destroys the seeds of the virtuous mind.
They can destroy the dharma of liberation and give rise to all manner of deluded thoughts;
falling into those perilous and evil realms, it all originates from heedlessness.
Seeking no benefit for oneself, one is abandoned by others.
Speechless and inactive, they are like the dead;
though possessing celestial forms, their folly is equal to that of beasts.
Constantly dwelling in negligence, they engage in song, dance, play, and laughter.
If a person is attached to heedlessness, they will immediately head toward the ocean of the three realms of existence;
having been extinguished, they are born again, and all see their own ruin.
Because of this, they commit various transgressions and become entangled by their karma.
Heedlessness turns into an enemy, Contradicting all wholesome dharmas.
This karma does not abide within, Nor does it exist without;
one should know that those who are heedless Are all destroyed by their own minds.
Regarding the supreme realm, their minds know no satiety;
delighting in song, dance, and play, they do not know the place of downfall and extinction.
Those who are foolish and negligent take what is terrifying to be a source of joy.
Those gods are like those born blind; they do not know the path from the non-path.
Due to their heedless conduct, they fall from the various meditative absorptions and, transmigrating within the realm of desire, they rush and flow through the five destinies.
If one dwells in the formless realm and attains the four kinds of emptiness-concentrations,
yet due to the practice of negligence, one wanders through the world;
circulating within the three realms, one is deluded and lacks discernment.
Heedlessness is a shackle, and the tether of craving binds one fast.
If one falls into the various evil realms, constantly suffering from hunger, thirst, and terror,
it is because of those heedless actions that no remorse or distress arises.
If the mind gives rise to suffering and distress, it is due to separation from what is loved;
therefore, the Tathāgata has rebuked this, and one should always remain far from negligence.
From that sprout of negligence, old age, sickness, and death flourish and grow.
These three kinds of suffering and affliction can destroy all sentient beings.
Just as that great earth can produce medicinal herbs,
so too does that heedless fool increase all delusions.
Heedlessness is like a poisonous sprout; it gives rise to all forms of indolence.
Drinking alcohol, being attached to women, and sporting together in sensory realms—heedlessness is the ultimate suffering, while heedfulness is the supreme bliss.
Regarding heedlessness and heedfulness, distinguish them well herein.
Even if one were to fall into the evil realms and undergo extreme suffering for hundreds of thousands of koṭis of kalpas, one should therefore never be heedless;
thus, one will transcend to the other shore just like all the Buddhas.
Sensual desire is the foremost deception; To lack right attention toward it is the cause of all hells, A binding that is deep and perilous within saṃsāra.
If a person is attached to various desires, They will undergo boundless suffering.
Constantly harmed by the serpent of desire, how could there be even the slightest pleasure?
It would be better to use a sharp sword to sever one’s own tongue than to speak even a few words concerning matters of desire.
Sentient beings are deceived by greed, Constantly scorched and boiled by anger, And subjugated by ignorance; They always praise sensual desires.
Though they commit many evil deeds, They obtain but little flavor from those desires.
Because they indulge in greed and delusion, they do not understand suffering as suffering.
That desire is formless, its pleasures are impermanent, and it is the cause of the utmost evil;
therefore, one should subsequently distance oneself from it.
Sentient beings, through the arising of craving, constantly fall into evil realms;
if one can distance oneself from that fault, then there will be no fear of hell.
The fierce fires within hell are entirely equal to the fire of desire.
Therefore, one should be single-minded, constantly giving rise to weariness and fear [of saṃsāra].
Always delighting in liberation, one should distance oneself from those desires and destroy unwholesome dharmas, just as the sun dispels the darkness.
Those foolish worldlings, whose faculties are attached to sensory objects,
give rise to craving through the mind and thus fall into the evil realms.
Due to those five objects, the five faculties produce attachment.
In an instant the fire of craving blazes; there is no satisfaction in desire.
Furthermore, those sentient beings give rise to the fire of craving:
when combined it burns fiercely, but when separated it ceases to exist.
If one is separated from the realm of desire, it has no means by which to arise;
this fire is extremely perilous and evil, and one should always cultivate detachment from it.
Like wood that lacks discernment, it flows along the river of craving.
That craving is like clarified butter; when poured upon it, the flames increase.
This fierce and virulent fire of greed can burn the entire person;
only by abandoning name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) will that fire be extinguished.
Furthermore, just as people in the world feel dread upon seeing a fire,
why do you not feel alarm at the blazing conflagration of craving?
Arising from those five sense-faculties and surrounded by the five objects of the senses, [it burns].
The power of craving is as swift as the wind, burning those who are full of greed.
Sense objects are like a dense forest, deep and perilous, difficult to escape;
scorched by that craving, they are like dry wood consumed by fire.
This fire of craving blazes, increasing as it encounters its objects;
those who crave are ignorant, taking suffering to be pleasure.
While worldly fire increases in brightness, the fire of craving increases in darkness.
These sense objects are like enemies; the wise should keep far away from them.
If a person regards sense objects as poison upon seeing them—knowing they produce but a momentary slight pleasure followed by extreme suffering—they will be safe.
Neither in this world nor in another, nor in the beginning, middle,
or end— how can there be any happiness in such objects of desire?
These deluded ones take great pleasure in amusements and play.
Never wearying of sense objects, they are like fire consuming grass and wood.
Because they never tire of sense objects, they are deceived by them;
dwelling perpetually within birth and death, they do not recognize their faults.
Those who act like birds driven by desire are certainly deluded;
such gods and humans do not even equal the likes of birds.
Just as at the end of an eon, the sun’s heat dries up the ocean, so too [is their fate].
For hundreds of thousands of koṭis of kalpas, one may gaze upon forms without weariness;
yet even that ocean may eventually dry up, and the rain from heaven can fill it once more,
whereas the eye’s beholding of various forms and appearances has never known satiety.
If one is never satiated with desire, how can one distinguish it from pleasure?
If one is content and free from greed, then one is far removed from sorrow and affliction.
Just as Mount Malaya produces nothing but sandalwood, so too does contentment yield only peace.
The foolish cut it down for firewood, and further use it to cultivate their fields.
Desire is the foremost deception; it is false and lacks solidity.
It is like a city of Gandharvas, and also like a dream.
Like an illusion, like a mass of foam, like the *pūga* fruit which briefly produces a sweet taste— attachment to desire is just like this.
The wise see it as it truly is; by departing from craving, there is no suffering.
For the sake of those who are deluded, I reveal their evil fruits:
desire is like worldly poison; it brings about every kind of transgression.
Just as one contemplates what has been obtained, it later brings about one's own destruction.
The mind clings to desire without satiety, and yet it takes that very desire as its enemy;
when their life in heaven comes to an end, they immediately fall into hell.
Desire is a poison for the world, just like a flash of lightning.
The fool, attached to female form, Is like a fish turning with the waves.
Constantly dwelling on thoughts that increase [defilement], Unwholesome in both the past and future,
Attached to desire as if to a blazing fire— The wise should keep far away from this.
If one follows after what one associates with, then those very things will increase;
the fire of desire burns most fiercely, and contact brings only bitter suffering.
Understanding this fire of desire, the wise always keep far from it.
If one is free from those desires, one will certainly attain peace and security.
Those countless hundreds of thousands of nayutas of celestial beings,
because they delight in the five sensual pleasures, are scorched and boiled by the fires of hell.
Desire is like fire, like poison; one should abandon it to seek peace and happiness, for it is the cause of those hells. Therefore, one should renounce it.
To attain mastery over desire, one should act as if neither seeing nor hearing it.
Because one does not cling to them, there is no suffering and no affliction.
One should not engage in sensual desires, nor should one even contemplate them with the mind;
for the gods and humans who cling to desire are harmed by that fire.
From beginningless saṃsāra, the enemy of desire arises from the mind;
if one is liberated from craving, that desire will no longer exist.
Those defiled and bitter fruits arise from craving and desire.
If one seeks liberation from desire, one will attain supreme and wondrous bliss.
The wise rely upon desire yet harbor no craving for it;
because they have abandoned that delusion, they realize the state of true permanence.
Though it produces a momentary pleasure, one later undergoes manifold agonies;
by giving rise to defiled attachment toward sensual desires, one proceeds to hell.
To find delight therein is to find no joy even for a single kṣaṇa.
If one is free from defilement and attains tranquility, reaching the state of non-extinction;
since the wise adorn themselves with desire throughout the beginning, middle,
and end, why do those fools become so attached to desire?
This desire is like a poisonous sprout; when touched, it produces blazing fire.
To give rise to love and delight for it is to be harmed by that poison.
Just as when fire is added to fuel, its flames never cease.
If one delights in those desires, then one increases one's feverish affliction.
Just as a moth sees the flame of a lamp and does not know it will burn its body,
so too are those deluded beings who are attached to desire.
If a person is attached to sensual desire, they are constantly scorched and boiled by it;
ultimately lacking awareness, they are like moths drawn to a lamp.
Therefore, those gods abandon desire and seek the wisdom of the Buddha.
Heedlessness will surely bring you ruin; do not let this present life be cast away in vain.
Constantly delighting in and clinging to various desires, you diminish and lose your wholesome karma;
deceived by ignorance, you shall later fall into hell.
Just as when a poisonous tree blooms, wandering bees compete to gather its nectar,
so too do those deluded and attached to desire enjoy it as a pleasure.
Since those bees consume poison, how can they have any life remaining?
The poison of desire harms sentient beings, for a long life is exceedingly difficult to obtain.
Furthermore, the fires of that hell are ignited by desire;
these fires fill its interior and burn all classes of gods and others.
Hungry ghosts, oppressed by hunger and thirst, are further scorched by fire;
among those in the animal realm, they delight in seeking out harm.
All other worlds likewise abide entirely dependent upon desire.
This fire arises everywhere, burning all those deluded by desire.
When the mind is constantly attached to sense objects, it becomes further mired in delusion and easily stirred;
if the fool were to attain clarity, he would be able to escape that perilous suffering.
This mind is attached to various desires, unaware of their dangers and hardships;
constantly dwelling within the torrential flood of desire, it gives rise to suffering and affliction.
The devas are by nature timid and weak; attached to desire, they give rise to madness and confusion.
Because the mind wavers due to this, one does not realize the great terror.
The gods are addicted to the five desires and are constantly engrossed in protection;
lacking wisdom, they do not renounce them, and later they shall give rise to sorrow and regret.
This mind is perpetually deluded and dark, lacking clarity regarding its objects;
that desire is an extreme affliction, yielding only a fleeting moment of pleasure.
Amidst hundreds of thousands, even countless koṭis [of lifetimes], it remains thus.
All arise from the desire to destroy, through failing to guard the mind.
Bound by the objects of desire, one shall receive the retribution of hell;
therefore, by skillfully cultivating the mind, one should ultimately remain far removed from them.
Having first given rise to lustful defilement, one further engages in acts of hatred;
deluded by ignorance, such a person is no different from the beasts.
The fool sinks into the midst of desire, and through that desire, becomes further intoxicated by folly.
Just as those moths are ultimately destroyed by fire,
so too the forms and colors of those gods, though they delight in pleasure,
are ruined; overcome by desire, they will certainly fall.
Sentient beings, deceived by desire, give rise to delusion;
led astray by the ropes of craving, they fall into the evil realms.
If you fear those dangers and evils, create for yourself the benefit of virtue.
Because the mind is tranquil, no feverish distress arises.
If one delights in the realm of sensory objects, doubt will increase;
thus various afflictions gradually arise, like wind fanning a fire.
The fire of desire constantly burns; that pleasure swiftly passes away.
By always reflecting with true reality, one does not become attached to sense objects.
If a person’s mind becomes deluded regarding the realm of desire, [it will suffer].
When sense objects constantly appear before one, this is the conduct of the deluded.
Lacking wisdom, they cling to these objects and fail to give rise to weary detachment;
like wood cast into a fire, it blazes even more fiercely when fanned by the wind.
The gods, through that craving, are constantly attached to sensual pleasures;
out of folly they do not renounce them, and because of this they fall away.
If a person constantly gives rise to thoughts of attachment toward the objects of desire, [they likewise fall].
Afflicted by the suffering of separation, they are scorched and boiled for a long time.
Even the exquisite sensual pleasures of the heavens must end in the pain of parting from those one loves;
this suffering exceeds that of the human world, such that the latter does not equal even a small fraction of it.
The various devas experience sensual pleasures like fish dwelling in water;
if both mind and objects were absent, that craving would not arise.
If a person constantly loves, delights in, and draws near to the realm of desire, [craving will persist].
With a mind that offers no protection, one’s long-standing suffering remains unceasing.
Because of attachment to various sensual desires, one does not fear their bitter fruits;
being dull-witted and ignorant, one later undergoes extreme peril and hardship.
Sensual desire is a grievous affliction; though it may briefly produce a small measure of pleasure, it is an impure practice that leads one toward the evil realms.
If a person lacks the eye of wisdom and constantly cherishes sensual desires, [they will suffer].
Just like those blind men who fall into a precipice with no rescue,
so too are sentient beings attached to desire; they experience little flavor but much terror,
like the city of Gandharvas, which exists for a moment and then vanishes without a trace.
Laxity gives rise to delight, and through that succession they find pleasure;
the devas, deluded by ignorance, do not give birth to awakening.
Greed arises toward sense objects, and their desire follows after them.
Not knowing that they will receive the retribution of great suffering, they will inevitably experience it themselves.
If a person constantly delights in and clings to the play of the five desires, they shall fall into those evil realms; their folly will lead only to regret.
If one leaves the realm of delusion, is not burned by the fire of desire,
and diligently cultivates right practice, then one attains the supreme bliss.
When compared with the objects of worldly desire, the pure and wondrous bliss [of liberation] is unsurpassed.
Among sixteen parts, it does not equal even one.
If a person’s mind is attached to desire, this desire is truly not pleasure;
it leads swiftly to the hells, where one shares in suffering.
Even if one were to spend hundreds of thousands of eons attached to desire, one would never find satisfaction;
constantly seeking the realm of desire, when has there ever been a place of true joy?
If one directs the mind toward desire, it increases in every single moment.
Devas and worldlings alike fall away because of this.
Constantly addicted and deluded by desire, which is most extremely perilous and evil,
they will be destroyed by it unless they give rise to detachment.
This eye is like the ocean, never satiated in beholding forms;
the tongue craves the most exquisite flavors without weariness;
the nose smells various wondrous fragrances, never ceasing its pursuit of them.
From contact, pleasure arises, and that mind is inexhaustible;
regarding exquisite sounds, the ear hears them with extreme delight;
the mind is attached to the objects of the mind (dharmas), never for a moment letting go.
These six sense faculties are light and restless, comparable to those wicked horses;
attached to the realm of desire without satiety, they are always like one who suffers from hunger and thirst.
The devas' attachment to the five desires is like adding dry wood to a fire.
The nature of fire is inherently blazing, and the same is true for that which has no feet.
These fires of the six sense faculties have been burning constantly since beginningless time;
yet the foolish have no awareness of it, remaining deluded by craving as if in a state of fainting.
Know that those sensual pleasures are the cause of hell;
when one beholds desire and gives rise to a greedy mind, it is like a snake flickering its tongue.
Furthermore, it is like a blind man who, lacking eyes, is devoid of all desires.
If one gives rise to seeking, one will fall into hell.
It is not by being sightless that one can leave the realm of desire;
rather, it is by possessing the eye and practicing right conduct that one transcends those evil destinies.
Delighting in what is unrighteous and harmful, performing various unwholesome deeds,
and having no satiety in the mind for sensual desires— such a person falls into the evil realms.
If a person is attached to desire, all manner of sufferings arise from it.
To abandon them for a moment only to pursue them again—such people lack discernment and wisdom.
Desire is like a friend at first, but later it becomes an enemy;
it is like the fruit of the *kapittha* tree: once eaten, it brings immediate harm.
Countless sentient beings, attached to desire, fall away like flowing water that never returns; their pleasure is no different [from that of others].
They enjoy all manner of delights within the sublime realms of gardens and groves.
If one is free from craving for those things, one will always be born in a place of peace and security.
But if a person indulges in the taste of desire, their mind becomes deranged through heedlessness;
when pleasure perishes and suffering manifests, they do not feel remorse.
Due to the power of their prior virtuous karma, they have obtained such beautiful forms and colors;
therefore, those gods each give rise to love and delight.
Yet these objects of desire are impermanent and will certainly come to dissolution.
Those wise people who possess true knowledge are not disturbed by sensual desires.
What can this body possibly endure?
Those lacking wisdom give rise to attachment and constantly create the causes for unwholesome karma; how much more so will they suffer in the future.
Those foolish worldlings are constantly craving the flavor of desire;
though there may be a slight pleasure at first, in the end there will be only harm.
Thus, these sounds and forms, by their very nature, give rise to delusion.
The fool, led astray by them, proceeds upon a perilous path.
If a person’s mind constantly gives rise to craving for the taste of sensual desires, that is only suffering and not happiness; the wise should keep far away from it.
Just as rain falling from the sky can nourish the rivers,
yet for those gods submerged in desire, it only increases their burning intensity.
Like a fish dwelling within water, they still experience thirst and craving.
Those gods who are attached to pleasure are likewise insatiable.
Just as the realm of empty space has no perceivable boundary,
how could the objects of those who give rise to craving for desire ever come to an end?
Just as the ocean surges with waves, its waters ever full,
so too the mind of the foolish person attached to desire is never satisfied.
The fool constantly dwells on thoughts of sensual objects not yet attained.
Once obtained, one clings to it firmly, like one who craves flavor and drools.
Desire gives rise to feverish affliction and is an extremely evil calamity;
as this ceases, that arises again—it is not a state of tranquility.
This desire is nothing but harmful; one who abandons it is called a great man.
When one faces decline or peril, all such [desires] abandon him.
There is no satiety regarding sense objects, nor is there any fulfillment in pleasure.
The wise contemplate well and should always cultivate detachment.
Sense objects are the cause of suffering; tranquility is the root of happiness.
Leaving behind the venomous snakes of sense objects, one should draw near to tranquility.
Desire can give rise to great terror—execution, slaughter, and grievous illness;
through the causal conditions of that greed, one wanders along the flow of saṃsāra.
Through immeasurable hundreds of thousands of births, having gathered together, one disperses once more.
Only the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, truly know and see all things:
the worldly and the supramundane, and all varieties of happiness.
Because of their attachment to desire, all these are utterly destroyed and ruined.
The foolish person’s mind is attached to desire; Clinging and longing, they cannot let go.
Blinded by delusion, how could they give rise to clear wisdom?
Their harsh words are heard like those of an enemy; Everyone fears such a person.
The realm of desire is like a deep-seated enemy; why do you not distance yourself from it?
When fools are attached to that desire, they are scorched by the fire of desire;
failing to give rise to a mind of weary revulsion, they later undergo bitter retribution.
Just as a great mass of fire causes all who see it to feel fear, the realm of desire is ever-blazing; how could one take pleasure in approaching it?
This body, held together by a network of tendons, is something for which one should deeply cultivate weary detachment.
Furthermore, one is deluded by desire, as if bound and entangled by a rope.
Like the *kapittha* fruit— red in color and sweet in taste—
which brings harm and affliction when eaten, so too is it with attachment to desire.
Just as a moth that flies into a lamp’s flame is consumed by it,
so too are all sentient beings who are attached to desire destroyed by it.
Those ignorant fools praise such desire.
This desire is like a blazing fire; it burns as soon as it is touched.
Like a deer driven by thirst, rushing toward a mirage, one follows that greedy mind and falsely seeks after pleasure.
The devas, attached to exquisite desires, never know satiety;
from this, all afflictions arise—how then can they attain tranquility?
Though they experience slight pleasure in the present, it becomes suffering in the future.
Dragged by the sensual realms of the devas, their minds are constantly distracted.
Amidst various objects of perception, their hearts become stained and intoxicated with delusion;
when life ends, karma follows them—of this there is no doubt.
When the death of sentient beings approaches, none fail to give rise to fear and terror;
because they are attached to the realms of desire, at the time of death they have no refuge.
The suffering of separation from what is loved arises entirely from desire.
All you gods, you should understand this: you must not harbor attachment in your hearts.
This desire brings no benefit; it gives rise to the terror of impermanence.
Yet those foolish worldlings delight in it and draw near to it.
Due to the intensification of delusion, scorched by the fire of craving,
lacking right mindfulness and reflection, one feels no weariness or fear toward sensual desires.
If one delights in the realm of desire, one will certainly undergo all manner of suffering.
Whirling within the three realms, by what means can one attain liberation?
Sentient beings, due to ignorance, constantly undergo all manner of suffering and affliction;
therefore, it is said that desire is like lightning, not remaining for long.
One should know that this craving is like a dream or an illusion;
having realized it as suffering, empty, impermanent, and devoid of a real self-mastery,
the Buddhas have therefore taught that the intrinsic nature of the five aggregates is emptiness.
If one understands things as they truly are, one will not be attached to desires.
Out of compassion for all sentient beings, one severs the bonds of afflictions,
leads them to the further shore, and attains the peace of nirvana.
Those who delight in practicing the five desires will sink and drown within the three realms of existence;
their minds are constantly deluded, so by what means could they attain tranquility?
If a person is attached to desire, they will forget and lose the True Dharma.
Seeking after those sensory realms, one swiftly hastens toward hell.
This desire is purely destructive, like a sharp sword;
if one does not give rise to weary detachment, there shall be nothing but suffering hereafter.
If one acts in this way, then one grows in this way;
finding no satisfaction therein, one constantly gives rise to all manner of feverish afflictions.
Seeking the pleasures of the heavens, one shall be consumed by desire.
By not creating the causes of suffering, one always attains happiness.
Fools are firmly attached to the objects of desire and do not abandon them;
yet these are like flashes of lightning, flickering for but a moment.
If a person craves the five sensual desires, continuing them without interruption,
that person will be burned by the fire of desire without rest.
The various devas give rise to even greater delusion regarding the objects of desire.
In that which is free from joy yet possesses sublime bliss, one finds no further attainment;
apart from liberation there is no bliss, nor is there nirvāṇa.
Since it is contrary to the objects of desire, it should therefore be abandoned.
If one dwells within the realm of desire, the sense faculties will never find satiety;
because of that lack of satiety, by what means could liberation be attained?
If one can give rise to fear toward the ocean of saṃsāra, [one may seek deliverance].
One should abandon those unwholesome states, as well as the perils of craving.
The realm of desire does not remain still for a moment; it is like the sun that rises and then sets.
One should delight in relying upon mountain forests, practicing dhyāna to seek liberation.
Sensual desire is not the dharma of liberation; it is merely a plaything for the foolish.
Only the seven kinds of noble wealth bring ultimate peace and happiness.
This desire is no place of treasure; it is the wilderness of saṃsāra.
If one delights in and draws near [to them], one will be unable to transcend [suffering].
Not being struck with awe at transgression, such a person is profoundly ignorant;
they mistake what is not wealth for wealth, and there is only suffering, no joy.
If a person stays far removed from desire and does not give rise to craving, this is a state of excellent abiding; they cannot be harmed by the fire of desire.
For those who find no satisfaction in desires, their minds are not at peace.
Associated with craving, it is like a fire leaping up in flames.
Devas, asuras, humans, and non-humans alike—
who do not feel revulsion for desire— are all destroyed by it.
If a person, regarding the objects of desire, becomes deluded and their mind deranged,
they will deceive themselves and thereby perish.
All ignorant sentient beings do not know the characteristics of sin and merit.
The sensory realm is called desire, and therein one constantly gives rise to attachment and delight.
Drawn by these desires, the gods' minds become deluded and distracted;
if you would delight in the Buddha's virtues, you should leave that realm behind.
These present five desires can give rise to all manner of calamities;
one who is not stained by attachment to such pleasures is called a wise person.

The realm of desire is like a dream, and also like a city of Gandharvas;
it blazes fiercely like a flame, and by this the gods fall.
If one gives rise to craving for desire, one will later be harmed by it.
Crooked and perverse, devoid of right reflection, by this the devas fall.
Most wretched and loathsome, flowing forth like the source of a river,
comparable to a deep and perilous pit— by this the devas fall.
The nature of desire is inherently restless, like wind, waves, or the moon reflected in water;
it flickers like the tongue of a snake, and by this means the gods fall.
Desire whirls like a flash of lightning and is also like a mirage.
Like a mass of foam, it is not solid; by this, the devas fall.
Desire is like a swift river, like an elephant’s ear that is constantly moving, and like a plantain tree that has no core; by this, the devas fall.
Desire is like a magical illusion, like the fruit of the *kimpāka* tree, or like a fish swallowing a hook; it is because of this that the gods fall.
One should, by means of true wisdom, sever the objects of desire.
One who is liberated from unwholesome fruits and all that is disadvantageous,
yet gives rise to conceptual thoughts and finds delight in sensual desires,
will be caught in the snare of desire; how could such a person’s life endure for long?
The minds of sentient beings are light and restless, all of them pulled by desire;
being ignorant and lacking discernment, they deceive themselves.
If one is moved by the objects of desire, that is the very root of all suffering.
Like a city of the gandharvas, one should know it does not endure for long.
If one gives rise to craving for sensual desires, hatred will follow in its wake;
such sentient beings quickly hasten toward the evil realms.
Therefore, that true person abandons desire and eliminates hatred;
free from delusion and other such faults, they manifest clear wisdom.
If a person grows weary of the realm of desire and realizes it to be like a deep-seated enemy, [they shall attain liberation].
Taking wisdom as one’s true friend, one swiftly realizes the fruit of the true and eternal.
By not giving rise to attachment toward desires, one attains freedom from all defilements;
such a person is one endowed with wisdom, whom all devas reverently honor.
Skillfully transcending the mire of desire, you are able to bestow happiness upon sentient beings;
with a mind free from bonds and tranquil, you have subdued all the hosts of Māra.
When the fire of craving arises within the heart, the deluded take it to be refreshing coolness.
It surpasses even the fires of hell, for it pervades the three realms.
Furthermore, within those hells, it can produce the kalpa-ending fire;
though that fire is most fiercely blazing, all such flames arise from craving.
Sentient beings suffering in the hells shall surely emerge once their karma is exhausted;
yet for all sentient beings within the three realms, the fire of craving never ceases.
Bound by this craving, they wander in saṃsāra without end.
How much more so within the hells— how can the fire of craving arise there again?
Furthermore, while the fires of karmic retribution in hell can only burn that body,
the fire of craving harms sentient beings by burning both their minds and their physical forms.
These two kinds of distinctions shall now be analyzed:
though the fires of hell blaze fiercely, the fire of craving exceeds them even further.
Arising from the three types of karma, it burns throughout the three realms of existence.
It harms the causes of virtue; the fire of craving alone is the poison.
The fire of greed burns the gods, and the fire of hatred does likewise;
the fire of delusion pursues the fool, while the fire of craving follows wherever one goes.
Envy and pride are further like fire, born from the fuel of self-grasping;
the fire of craving burns the world, blazing perpetually even without fuel.
Through attachment arising toward objects, one is wounded by the serpent of craving.
Gazing upon and welcoming [others] increases [craving] further and further;
like fire fed by fuel, it continues without interruption.
While the fire of the world may still be prevented, the fire of craving cannot be restrained.
If one is deceived by craving and wanders through the flow of the world,
that craving is like a mortal enemy, against whom none can prevail.
Enshrouded by craving, one goes to the ocean to seek various treasures.
Amidst the terrifying ranks of the army, they penetrate deep to engage in battle.
Kings cherish their kingdoms, yet they mutually invade and compete;
even between mother and son, disputes arise over wealth.
If one is liberated from that craving and relinquishes all precious playthings,
regarding them as mere rubble, then one draws near to the path of enlightenment.
Because of attachment to wealth, one falls into the realms of hell.
That heat and affliction are difficult to endure; therefore, one should distance oneself from them.
One should douse them with the water of wisdom so that they are forever extinguished;
for if the fire of craving is not removed, one remains far from Bodhi.
If one distances oneself from craving and does not cling to precious things,
that person will have not even the slightest suffering in this world.
Just as a net catches fish while leaving behind all the snails and clams, so it is with those who are detached.
Craving binds those sentient beings; none are able to escape it.
Like a deer struck by a poisoned arrow that flees in all four directions, the poison follows everywhere; how can one flee from such suffering?
The fire of craving is likewise; that poison constantly pursues and burns the foolish worldling—by what means can one escape it?
Though it may briefly produce a sense of pleasure, its retribution is a constant conflagration.
Those who seek the bliss of transcendence should eliminate their craving.
Just as a fish that swallows its bait will surely meet its death, so too a person led by craving will perish prematurely; of this there is no doubt.
Falling into the realm of hungry ghosts, they run about everywhere in feverish distress;
as for sentient beings in the hells, it is mostly due to the love arising from the mind.
Even going to the gates of others, they beg for alms to sustain their lives.
All this is caused by craving; this is what the Buddha has taught.
The fire of craving burns the devas without requiring even a small amount of fuel;
it arises from attachment to sense objects through the six sense faculties.
Experiencing the pleasure of sensory gratification, their minds are perpetually deluded and intoxicated;
they fall without realizing it, led astray by craving.
All causes for saṃsāra are derived from craving.
The fetters of craving bind sentient beings, causing them to fall into the evil realms.
Furthermore, the fire of craving within the heavens is constantly surrounded by the objects of desire;
through the power of delusion, it burns those who are attached to sensual pleasures.

Just as fire, upon obtaining dry fuel, blazes forth with ever-increasing intensity, so too when sensual pleasures satisfy the mind, one's craving grows even more. Though the fire of the world is extremely fierce and hot, all people are able to keep their distance from it; yet this fire of craving, though subtle and difficult to perceive, consumes beings for a long time. Therefore, one should abandon desire and cultivate the path of liberation. Just as a fire that has not been kindled does not burn, so too one who is free from craving does not suffer. Thus, by abandoning craving, one attains peace and is no longer subject to rebirth. This is called the "Dharma of the Noble Ones. Having heard this teaching, the Licchavi youth attained the fruit of stream-entry. He then rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and departed. The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus: "Among my disciples, the Licchavi youth is foremost in being swift to attain realization. At that time, the bhikṣus asked the Buddha: "World-Honored One, what karmic causes and conditions did the Licchavi youth create such that he was born into a wealthy family, possessed great merit, and was able to quickly realize the fruit of stream-entry? The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "In the past, during the time of the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, there was a householder who had an only son. When the son grew up, he took a wife and lived together. Later, the father fell ill and died. Before passing away, he entrusted his property to his son, saying: 'I have now entrusted this wealth to you. You must manage it well and do not let it be lost. After his death, the son lived in comfort and enjoyed all manner of pleasures. However, he was naturally lazy and indolent, and thus failed to manage the household affairs. Consequently, the wealth was gradually exhausted. His wife, seeing this, spoke to him: 'You were born into a noble family and possess great wealth. Why do you remain idle and fail to manage the estate? If you do not act, we shall soon be destitute. The husband replied: 'I am weary of managing these affairs. I wish to go forth and practice the holy life under the Tathāgata Kāśyapa. His wife said: "If you truly desire to leave the home life, I shall accompany you. We shall both serve the World-Honored One and cultivate the path together. The husband then went to the Buddha and requested ordination. The Buddha granted his request, and he became a monk. His wife followed him to the monastery and likewise requested ordination. The Buddha granted her request as well, and she became a nun. Subsequently, they both applied themselves diligently to the practice and attained arhatship. Because of these roots of goodness, he has now been born into a wealthy family, possesses great merit, and has been able to quickly realize the fruit of stream-entry. The Buddha then spoke in verse: "If one gives rise to a single thought of faith toward the Buddha, one will never again fall into the evil realms. Even if one were to wander through the three thousand worlds, seeking out the Buddhas of the ten directions, one would find none superior to the Buddha. Therefore, one should always revere the Buddha. The Buddha then told the bhikṣus: "The Dharma I have taught is profound and subtle, difficult to understand and difficult to enter. It is not something that can be easily realized by those who hold wrong views or those who follow heterodox paths. Only those who have planted roots of goodness in the past and possess sharp faculties can understand it. Therefore, you should all listen attentively and practice accordingly. The bhikṣus received the Buddha’s instruction with joy and respectfully put it into practice. Thus ends the Sūtra on the Licchavi Youth. 203. The Sūtra on the Elder Mahānāma. ① Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the Garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time, the elder Mahānāma approached the Buddha, paid homage at his feet, and sat to one side. Sitting there, he addressed the Buddha: "World-Honored One, how should a lay follower dwell in order to be called a lay follower who is well-established in the Dharma and possesses the seven factors of a lay follower? The Buddha told the elder Mahānāma: "A lay follower should dwell with unwavering faith in the Buddha, thinking: 'The Blessed One is an Arhat, perfectly enlightened, endowed with knowledge and conduct, the Well-Gone, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed Leader of Men to Be Tamed, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One. This is called a lay follower who is well-established in the Dharma and possesses the first factor of a lay follower. Furthermore, a lay follower should dwell with unwavering faith in the Dharma, thinking: 'The Dharma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, to be realized by the wise each for themselves. This is called a lay follower who is well-established in the Dharma and possesses the second factor of a lay follower. Furthermore, a lay follower should dwell with unwavering faith in the Saṃgha, thinking: 'The Saṃgha of the Blessed One's disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals. This Saṃgha of the Blessed One's disciples is worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, and worthy of veneration; it is an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. This is called a lay follower who is well-established in the Dharma and possesses the third factor of a lay follower. Furthermore, a lay follower should dwell possessing the precept of restraint in accordance with the Dharma, a precept of restraint that is unbroken, flawless, unblemished, untarnished, liberating, praised by the wise, ungrasped, and leading to concentration. This is called a lay follower who is well-established in the Dharma and possesses the fourth factor of a lay follower. Furthermore, a lay follower should dwell possessing abundant learning, having heard much, retained, collected, and mastered many teachings—those discourses in prose, in verse and prose, in prose and verse, in verse alone, as solemn utterances, as sayings, as birth stories, as marvelous events, and as established instructions. This is called a lay follower who is well-established in the Dharma and possesses the fifth factor of a lay follower. Furthermore, a lay follower should dwell possessing the faculty of wisdom, which is noble, penetrating, leading to the complete destruction of suffering. This is called a lay follower who is well-established in the Dharma and possesses the sixth factor of a lay follower. Furthermore, a lay follower should dwell possessing the faculty of faith, which is noble, penetrating, and leads to the complete destruction of suffering. This is called a lay follower who is well-established in the Dharma and possesses the seventh factor of a lay follower. Mahānāma, if a lay follower dwells possessing these seven factors, they are called a lay follower who is well-established in the Dharma and possesses the seven factors of a lay follower.
