The fire of craving burns the world; none can escape this harm.
If a person does not give rise to craving, they attain supreme tranquility, emerge from the dense forest of afflictions, and are able to transcend the ocean of suffering.
Free from the fault of attachment, one severs the cords of craving;
liberated from all defilements of sin, such a person is truly free from sorrow.
For hundreds of thousands of koṭis of eons, one is constantly deceived by craving.
Fools do not abandon it, for they are bound by the snare of illusion.
Believing themselves shrouded by craving, they delight in intimacy and service,
like a laborer who drinks salt water when thirsty.
Having drunk, thirst is briefly stilled; yet in a moment the throat dries again.
Thirsty craving dwells within the heart—how could it cease except through the Way?
Therefore, one should keep far away from it, for all evils arise because of it.
Those who are overcome by craving sink into the depths with no time of escape.
Though they receive the most excellent and sublime pleasures of the five desires within the heavens,
in the end they are dragged by the ropes of craving and fall once more into the evil realms.
If a person is close to craving, they are constantly filled with suffering and distress;
as clarified by the authentic teaching, this is certainly not beneficial.
If one is attached to the objects of craving, there will be no satisfaction.
One who is able to abandon that craving will have no sorrow or affliction.
Because of craving, the gods give rise to negligence;
through attachment and further pursuit, they later fall into hell.
When the gods fall from their celestial state, it is the greatest of shame;
because they were attached to supreme delights, they now undergo extreme suffering.
When love obscures one's own mind, that mind becomes deranged.
They do not fear saṃsāra, remaining heedless for a long time.
Through sensual pleasures, sentient beings further increase their craving;
the fire of craving and the fires of hell burn them in various ways.
If that craving increases, it will proliferate endlessly;
having already attained birth, one guards it, and for what is not yet attained, one constantly pursues it.
Because of this pursuit, the mind is never satisfied.
Such a person has no share in happiness; this is what the Tathāgata has certified.
Because their minds never grow weary of it, they constantly contemplate the flavor of desire;
thus, by the fire of craving, they are continuously consumed.
If one feels fear toward sensual desires, And leaves behind the oppression of the fire of craving,
One is liberated from the defilement of attachment And shall no longer fall into the evil realms.
Through one's own wrong reflection, The dust of the three poisons arises.
Falling into the deep abyss of heedlessness, they are constantly craving the beauty of women and the exquisite sounds of song and music; this gives rise to distraction,
so that their minds never rest for a moment, like a swift-flowing torrent.
Craving is like a deep and treacherous river; desire is like a leaking boat.
When the foolish board it, they are immediately submerged and lost.
Craving is like a fierce, blazing flame; the three poisons are like dry firewood.
Heedlessness is like a swift wind; it consumes the gods without their realizing it.
The gods, attached to sensual pleasures, are thus overcome by craving;
in the blink of an eye, for even a brief moment, they find not the slightest leisure.
Craving is the basis for desire; it gives rise to hundreds of thousands of obstacles.
Because the gods are attached to pleasure, they are unable to perform wholesome deeds.
The serpent of craving has five heads, and its nature is extremely violent and evil.
The sting of those who harbor greed and desire is a suffering difficult to endure.
The river of craving is exceedingly deep and vast, born from the five sensual desires;
for one who wishes to reach the further shore, how could they cross it without virtue?
Craving is like a phantom actor, pervading the three realms of existence;
it deceives all gods and humans, providing not the slightest benefit.
The five faculties seize their objects of desire, never once feeling weary or satiated.
Like clarified butter cast into a fire, it increases with every passing thought.
Furthermore, that craving can open the gates to the evil realms;
one thus constantly wanders back and forth among the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals.
Fools, through the arising of craving, fall into the mouth of the Lord of Death;
those who skillfully abandon this fault are not devoured by him.
Those wise people who possess discernment are able to subdue that craving.
Free from sorrow, affliction, and fear, one sits and lies down always in peace;
if one is free from the entanglements of craving, then no sufferings will arise.
The fool has many desires and constantly gives rise to harm.
Throughout day and night, their hearts give rise to no compassion;
regarding the precious wealth of others, they desire to seize it all.
Such people are like the fire at the end of an eon; their nature is perpetually fierce and treacherous.
They distance themselves from virtuous people, like a venomous snake dwelling in its hole.
Due to the intensification of craving, they are scorched and boiled by feverish affliction;
after death they fall into hell, and are reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts.
Having emerged from the evil realms, one may be born among humans;
yet for five hundred lifetimes, one constantly begs from others.
With an inferior appearance and always speaking with humility, one is oppressed by a mind of deprivation.
Suffering alone is one's own lot, all of which arises from craving.
If a person cuts off that craving and constantly seeks the Buddha’s wisdom,
such a person is truly upright and shall attain supreme tranquility.
If one dispels the craving within the mind, like driving a snake out of its hole,
yet the poison of craving has not been eliminated, one will certainly be destroyed.
If one persists in creating [karmic conditions], that craving will constantly manifest before one.
Just as when dry firewood is cast into a fire, its flames blaze all the more intensely;
so too, sentient beings who crave precious wealth accumulate it without ever reaching satiety,
yet at the time of their death, it all becomes the property of others.
The faults incurred through craving cause wealth to dissipate while sins remain undiminished;
dragged by the force of karma, one approaches hell with sorrow.
While others enjoy the wealth, the sin falls upon one’s own person.
Falling into those evil realms, one’s subsequent regrets will be but a feverish torment.
The dispersal of wealth is called decline; the ruin of pleasure is suffering;
and friends suddenly become like enemies—all these arise from the shifting power of attachment.
The wise do not give rise to craving;
the fire of craving is ever-blazing, harming all sentient beings and causing them to fall into evil realms.
To amass wealth like a mountain, one must constantly guard it with anxiety and fear.
How could one commit various transgressions and employ them unrighteously?
One who does not delight in hoarding wealth has neither fear nor need for protection;
such a wise person, free from greed, dwells in constant peace wherever they may be.
Seeking the pleasures of wealth, they suddenly disperse and perish;
prosperity and decline do not endure for long, like the revolving wheel of the sun.
Those in honor and wealth are as if bound; those who are destitute are as if punished.
All are driven by craving, never wearying of sensual desires.
Though they experience supreme and wondrous pleasures and obtain all that their hearts wish for,
when they are oppressed by the fire of craving, both their bodies and their joys perish and crumble away.
Whether gods or humans, because they find no satiety in desire, all are consumed by craving; the Tathāgata fully knows and sees this.
Hundreds of thousands of sentient beings fall into perilous difficulties because of craving.
Receiving immeasurable retribution of suffering, the wise all raise sighs of lamentation.
Life passes away with swift transience, yet the foolish do not perceive it;
their meritorious deeds are entirely extinguished, while their craving continues to increase.
If a person is attached to craving, it will constantly follow them from life to life;
being dark, dull, and ignorant, they do not comprehend the characteristics of sin and merit.
As for the fruit of wholesome karma, one is born among the various devas and experiences happiness.
Due to the causes and conditions of unwholesome karma, one falls away from that state.
By not performing wholesome or unwholesome deeds, one leaves behind the faults of conditioned association;
by turning one's back on the causes of old age and death, one dwells in supreme peace and security.
Greed is like that chariot wheel; the five desires are its spokes, and craving is the hub situated within it—of this, those in the world are ignorant.
The river of craving is exceedingly deep and vast, with the objects of desire as its surging waves.
Doubt is like a school of fish; there are none in the world who understand this.
Throughout the three periods of day and night, they commit many unwholesome deeds.
If the wise do not exercise restraint, they will immediately follow along with the flow of evil.
Beautiful forms are like illusions; by understanding them, one is not bound.
Because of craving, one constantly pursues them; thus bound, one cannot be released.
If one is entangled by craving, then one becomes attached to sensual pleasures.
When wisdom manifests before one, it can eliminate those faults and afflictions.
Attachment increases darkness, while wisdom gives rise to light;
one should abandon darkness for light, leaving suffering behind to attain peace and happiness.
Wisdom is like a sharp sword, capable of felling the forest of craving;
one should practice it well to attain the highest peace and security.
Know that the dense thicket of craving is deep and obscure, difficult to escape from.
If a person skillfully transcends, they shall emerge from the three realms.
The river of craving has three currents, filled to the brim with the water of heedlessness;
one should board the vessel of wisdom, for it can carry one to the further shore.
Craving is like a sharp blade or staff, Cutting and slicing the body of the fool;
Its suffering and distress are difficult to endure, Therefore, one should always remain far removed from it.
Craving is like a malignant ulcer, Arising from within the mind.
Throughout day and night, there has never been even the slightest happiness.
Craving is like a fierce, blazing fire, and doubt is like firewood;
fanned by the winds of karma, it burns the mind, giving rise to feverish affliction.
If a person is entangled by craving, their mind becomes light and restless;
taking wealth through unrighteous means, they shall lose both body and life.
All sentient beings in the world thus create boundless evil karma.
All this arises from craving for wealth, leading one to sink long in the ocean of suffering.
Driven by craving, one acts with courage and fortitude, free from timidity,
even treading through fire without regard for one's own life.
If a person gives rise to much craving, the fire of the mind constantly burns;
when there is no craving, the mind is cool and refreshing, like bathing in a deep abyss.
Craving is like that fierce fire: when fuel is thrown into it, the flames flare up.
It is like that greedy man, who grows ever more insatiable the more he acquires;
even with immeasurable treasures, a kṣatriya remains unsatisfied,
whereas for other sentient beings, possessing but little brings no affliction.
If a person gives rise to craving, pleasure is slight while suffering is great;
since both suffering and pleasure are clearly manifest, the wise are skillful in what they adopt and what they abandon.
Those who successfully subdue that craving attain the most supreme tranquility.
If one can always keep them at a distance, one draws near to the path of Bodhi.
Women are the root of transgression; if one can dispense with the necessities of life, yet remains submissive to them, what joy could there possibly be?
Women are often full of flattery and crookedness, constantly harboring jealousy;
they delight in committing unwholesome deeds and exercise mastery over their karma;
with clever speech they deceive others, yet always harbor thoughts of harmony.
Lacking right mindfulness and reflection, they take delight in praising sensual matters.
They may briefly show compliance, but later become mostly stubborn and fierce;
though adorned with rare and precious things, they never once think of the kindness [bestowed upon them].
Suppose there were hundreds of thousands of sentient beings who all gave rise to love and attachment;
yet their own nature is without permanence, just like that flash of lightning.
If one delights in female forms, this constitutes an unwholesome cause.
In this life and in future existences, they are all utterly destroyed by it.
If one sees even a single beautiful form, the mind becomes distracted;
delighting in that sensory object, one is tormented by craving.
Where there is union, there must be separation; from this arise sorrow and grief.
Greed and desire constantly entwine and ensnare, all because of women.
This poisonous greed of women arises simultaneously with the body itself.
Just as when fire arises in the world, its nature of heat follows along;
so should one know that this fire of craving issues forth from the mind,
burning continuously and incessantly, with no suffering to compare to it.
To destroy wholesome dharmas and to harm and afflict sentient beings is the cause for the evil realms; this is what all Buddhas have taught.
Though beautiful words may issue from the mouth, poison is constantly harbored within the heart.
Regarding those whom they cherish and desire, their resolve is never fixed.
Should they momentarily give rise to attachment, they soon cast them aside;
what they say lacks sincerity, for their intentions are not true.
Deceiving others through skillful means, they cultivate the causes and conditions for defiled desire;
toward those who have conceived lust for them, they rely on this to give rise to arrogance.
Whether among devas, humans, asuras, yakṣas, or spirits—
Falling into peril and hardship is entirely due to women.
Furthermore, those women do not recognize kindness or remember past favors;
their minds never rest for a moment, revolving like the sun.
Seeing a person in glory and prosperity, one delights in serving them;
yet when that person falls into decline or peril, there is not the slightest concern.
Like a bee gathering from a flower, it abandons the flower as soon as it withers.
One should know that those women abandon their former [husbands] in this very same way.
Women lack a heart of compassion and are constantly harboring jealousy;
this is not without cause, for it all stems from men.
Among the gods, there are only women; none other can subdue them.
Bound by the fetters of women, one falls into the evil realms.
If one takes pleasure in and clings to female beauty, this loss is beyond compare.
The fire of greed constantly burns the heart; by what means can one escape it?
If one is led astray by desire, the karmic consequences of greed are clearly visible:
the mind is perpetually muddled and intoxicated, delighting in the commission of various unwholesome deeds.
Bound by evil, women frequently harbor secret intentions;
they cast aside their former affections like a snake shedding its skin.
Women are most treacherous and deceitful; none can surpass them.
They employ many expedient means, yet long for favor and affection.
Furthermore, women by their very nature are prone to wandering;
the wise, possessing foresight, should be careful not to follow after them.
If one associates closely with women, one loses all wholesome benefits;
even if one seeks rebirth in the heavens, this too cannot be attained.
The wondrous sounds of bliss in the heavens cause all who hear them to give rise to attachment.
If one delights in and does not abandon attachment, it will lead to the arising of suffering and hardship.
The minds of women are fickle; they conceive passionate love for others.
When the fire of passion is momentarily extinguished, then the thought of renunciation arises.
Women are firmly attached to their own wills and take pleasure in base deeds;
when they see one’s decline and decay, they give rise to abandonment.
Women are full of flattery, making him like a bewildered deer.
When seeing oneself beset by calamity, one gives rise to abandonment;
women are exceedingly treacherous and evil, and one does not reflect upon their kindness and virtue—
when such misfortunes and hardships descend upon them, one gives rise to abandonment.
The female mind is scattered and distracted, giving rise to all manner of thoughts;
it can deceive and entice others like honey mixed with various poisons.
Women possess many clever words and are able to delude those who are foolish.
The wise man reflects well, and his mind never wavers.
Because of delusion and attachment to desire, he has no stinginess regarding wealth;
yet, failing to cultivate the causes of merit, he is like a mouse constantly hiding and scurrying away.
The beauty of women is like that rope, Which is foremost in its firmness;
it binds those deluded men And causes them to fall into the ocean of the three realms of existence.
This rope does not bind the body, But is able to fetter only the mind.
If the mind is ensnared by them, suffering becomes one's own;
other ropes bind a person, burning and cutting them until they are severed,
but this woman’s rope is not like that— it can drag one toward the evil realms.
The body possesses form and characteristics; thus, that rope can bind it.
The mind is fundamentally without shape or substance; therefore, the woman’s rope cannot bind it.
If one were bound by such a rope, everyone would see its dimensions.
The female fetter binds men; it is a measure of those who lack wisdom.
It produces a momentary slight pleasure, yet later its release is difficult.
It is able to bind all sentient beings, causing them to perpetually sink into the ocean of suffering born of craving.
Furthermore, that woman’s rope binds the six sense-faculties well;
though she is always a rope, she lacks such power, binding only the body and the neck.
Wife, children, and kinsmen form the most firm of bonds.
Fools give rise to deluded thoughts, And all grasp [these things] as their own.
They conceive love for female form, Yet it is but a wrapping of muscle and sinew, A locus for excrement and urine; Your love returns once more to this.
They delight in uttering clever words and phrases, deceiving others without shame;
one should know that women are no different from enemies.
Adorned with many exquisite ornaments, they cause others to give rise to love and attachment.
Their minds are constantly shifting, and what they say is mostly false.
The nature of women is full of poison, like the *kālakūṭa* venom;
they harm those attached to desire, and none can escape their calamity.
Though one possesses hundreds of thousands of skillful means, one cannot restrain women;
like wind, fire, or space, there is no one who can bind them.
By committing various unwholesome acts, one encounters illness, calamity, and premature death.
All because of women, one destroys the practice of liberation.
All sentient beings in the world who commit various sinful deeds do so because of women; they are constantly oppressed by fear.
From childhood until old age, their minds are ever distracted;
such is the nature of women, as constant as the warmth of sunlight.
The female heart lacks stability, like the flickering flame of a lamp in the wind.
One who harbors resentment does not let it go even for a moment, like a horse that bites its own wound.
Like a rope binding a weasel, though it is tied, it can still escape;
such is the woman who cannot be restrained by another.
Like a flower atop a venomous snake, like ash covering a blazing fire,
like beauty obscuring the human heart, like a woman concealing her impurities;
like a poisonous tree in bloom, those who gaze upon it can never be satiated.
These flowers are like women; in the end, they must be abandoned.
Those who constantly delight in seeking female beauty find that such objects appear before them;
yet in both this life and future existences, they possess no share of happiness.
Neither fire nor sword, neither force nor mechanical device can sever the bonds of those who are fettered by women; such evil cannot be cut away.
Thus, I have briefly described the faults and perils of desire within the realms of humans and devas.
If the wise remain far removed from it, they become lords of the Yāma heaven.
Those who delight in the beauty of women find that [such desire] arises entirely from habitual practice;
yet if there are people in the world who possess true integrity, they are able to escape such matters.
By virtue of the roots of goodness from past lives, this person, having extinguished [defilements], is born among the devas;
yet seeing the celestial women, their distraction is likewise the same.
Thus, they disparage pleasure as not being true, and censure the mind for its lack of tranquility.
One should weary of the faults and afflictions of women, abandoning them as if they were enemies.
If one associates with women, many kinds of suffering and distress arise;
therefore, one should understand this and always remain far removed from them.
If one gives rise to a distracted mind, Then various faults will arise;
Constantly beholding women, One gives rise to frivolous playfulness.
In Japan there is no darkness, And the nature of fire is not cool.
Women lack a heart of compassion; even a small measure of it cannot be found.
The great earth does not tremble, and the nature of the wind knows no rest;
likewise, women lack virtuous conduct and always delight in speaking of others' faults.
Furthermore, the minds of women are fickle and unstable, not remaining for long;
when faced with difficulty, they abandon [their husbands], like geese departing when a pond dries up.
They rely on shallow streams where herons dwell, but they are not found in the deep abyss.
The mountains and peaks may tremble, yet they possess no compassion;
they do not praise the True Dharma but delight in creating all manner of demonic obstacles.
Falling into perilous difficulties, they are deceived by them.
The scorching sun can be made cool; Grapes can be made firm.
But the woman’s heart of flattery and envy Is stubbornly attached and will not be abandoned.
She shares equally in pleasure, But not so in suffering.
Little resentment remains constantly in my heart, while I have neglected and forgotten your kindness.
Formerly, within these gardens and groves, we enjoyed ourselves together;
yet when misfortune and decay suddenly assailed us, you reviled me and cast me aside.
Women are the fetters of the world; they increase strife and contention.
They are a treasury of faults and vessels of unrighteousness.
The beauty of women deludes sentient beings, causing them to constantly harbor thoughts of desire.
Giving rise to pervasive conceptualization and pursuit, their minds do not abandon it for even a moment.
With immeasurable arrows of craving and desire, they afflict all sentient beings;
where can such pleasure go?
One sees them all being worn away and destroyed.
This desire is deeply fearsome, like a sharp blade or a raging fire;
the wise understand this well and always guard against it with a single-minded focus.
If one who maintains pure precepts should suddenly give rise to thoughts of desire,
they will incur immeasurable slander and produce manifold calamities;
like wind striking a fire, its flames will blaze all the more fiercely.
Seeing a woman and conceiving desire, one will surely be consumed by her.
If one seeks pure happiness, one should stay far away from women;
thus, in this life and in future births, one's mind will remain ever tranquil.
Arousing courageous diligence, one cultivates supreme wisdom;
abandoning desire and believing in cause and effect, such a person attains great benefit.
This teaching declares that alcohol is poison; one should keep far away from it.
Those who delight in drinking alcohol destroy wholesome qualities.
If a person associates with liquor, they will not give rise to clear wisdom;
such a person lacks the portion of liberation, and therefore one should always remain far removed from it.
This is declared by the wise to be the foremost fault;
it ruins both oneself and others, and therefore one should always avoid it.
If a person delights in drinking alcohol and is fond of discussing worldly affairs,
Excessive speech gives rise to strife and contention; therefore, one should always avoid it.
Drinking alcohol wastes wealth, causes confusion and delusion, and leads to indolence;
because such faults and afflictions exist, one should always avoid it.
From alcohol arises craving, and likewise anger;
it further increases delusion. Therefore, one should always remain far removed from it.
Alcohol is the root of calamity; it causes the sense faculties to scatter and run wild.
Later, they fall into the midst of hell, all because they were ruined by alcohol.
Whether laughing and joking loudly or uttering violent and evil words,
and disparaging those who are virtuous and good, they will subsequently give rise to sorrow and fear.
Through intoxication from drinking alcohol, one fails to distinguish between good and evil;
like a beast lacking awareness, for this reason one should keep far away from it.
If a person is afflicted by liquor, their stupor and drunkenness are like being dead.
Seeking happiness and long life—how could these not become sources of affliction!
These are the root of all hardships and the source of all calamities;
they dwell perpetually in the darkness of ignorance and serve as the gradual steps leading toward death.
Later one falls into the hells, Is reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts, And among the animal destinies; All this is brought about by alcohol.
Alcohol is the poison among poisons, The chronic malady among all diseases.
To suffer further after already suffering—this is what the wise have said.
It destroys the life of wisdom, exhausts the treasures of the Dharma, and ruins pure brahmacarya;
all this arises from a mind that delights in liquor.
Even those who are highly esteemed, once intoxicated, lose all sense of distinction;
they become objects of ridicule for the world and feel no shame.
Alcohol is like a sharp axe, capable of destroying all wholesome qualities.
Those who delight in drinking lack a sense of shame and are held in contempt by others.
If a person is deluded by wine and indulges in it without end,
failing to perform any virtuous deeds, they are neither discerning nor wise.
If a person delights in drinking alcohol, their mind becomes deranged;
they may break into laughter or give rise to anger.
In both this life and future existences, ignorance will constantly shroud their wisdom.
The Dharma of liberation is consumed by fire, for all are driven by liquor.
If one relishes its flavor, it is like eating the *kapittha* fruit:
sweet at first, but poisonous afterward; thus it has been said by the wise.
Therefore, the wise person strictly warns against alcohol;
they do not give rise to thoughts of it, for drinking produces feverish distress.
Even the gods, who are constantly intoxicated with abundance, fall further than this.
Whatever pleasures there may be, they will all eventually disperse and perish.
Sentient beings are deluded by liquor; their minds are perpetually intoxicated and distracted.
Led astray by that ignorance, they become addicted to its delicious flavor.
Know that alcohol is like a rope; its delusive craving is ever difficult to untie.

Because one touches it and smells its fragrance, the deluded person immediately delights in drinking it.
Therefore, upon seeing that liquor, one should abandon it and depart.
If one sees it, desire arises; if one touches it, its fragrance is released;
and because of smelling that scent, the mind cannot be restrained.
Therefore, alcohol is a poison; it gives rise to manifold faults.
It destroys one's complexion, strength, and reputation—all because of drinking that liquor.
One utters mad words from the mouth and stares with unsteady eyes.

Because of upholding pure precepts, one would rather drink molten copper;

Though drinking alcohol is but a single transgression, it can give rise to all manner of evils;
therefore, one should restrain it, for the precept of the mind is the foundation.
If a bhikṣu delights in drinking alcohol, he will abandon the āraṇya.
Deprived of one-pointed concentration, they do not contemplate the True Dharma.
Because they delight in drinking alcohol, their minds are constantly plagued by feverish affliction;
they associate with what is unrighteous and destroy the wholesome benefits of both worlds.
Lacking dignified conduct and the path of practice, you have abandoned the duty of preaching the Dharma;
since your words and deeds are at odds, what benefit is there in empty talk?

Uttering coarse and harsh words, this is not the teaching of the Dharma;
it contradicts correct principle and is universally ridiculed by the wise.

One has no recollection of the past, forgets the present once more,

Through wine, one is deluded regarding the three periods of time.

giving rise to all manner of faults, this is what it means to be beset by alcohol.

If one delights in the realm of desire and does not practice the True Dharma, [one will suffer].
The fool who treads the path of error shall fall into hell.
The mind is like fire within fire; it is the most difficult to subdue.
Because it is so difficult to subdue, one must undergo extreme suffering.
If one allows the mind to run wild with freedom, it will constantly give rise to various faults;
by skillfully departing from those defiled desires, one will not be oppressed by suffering.
Because such a mind is aroused, such a fruit is received.
Performing good is the cause of purity; committing evil results in bitter retribution.
Since one creates those karmas through the mind, and since karma brings about its fruit, it is because the mind and karma correspond that one undergoes saṃsāra.
If a person, by means of that mind, Commits various evil deeds, they will be burned and boiled for a long time By the fires of that hell.
Through the mind one creates all transgressions; Through the mind one experiences their fruit.
One should know that this mind arises from causes and conditions.
Deceived by the mind, sentient beings commit various transgressions at will;
they fall into the hells and give rise to profound and great terror.
One should rely upon the True Dharma and not follow the mind in creating evil;
virtuous conduct is ever serene, while evil conduct is solely unrighteous.
All things are created by the mind alone, and their fruits are likewise obtained from the mind.
If the mind arises in various ways, its fruits are likewise so.
The mind is like a painter who paints the sentient beings of the three realms;
none dwell in peace, for they do not move apart from the shifting of the mind.
Furthermore, that mind is the root, capable of producing both liberation and bondage;
through wholesome karma one is liberated, while unwholesome karma leads to entanglement.
Sentient beings fall into the net of karma, for they are subdued by the mind.
Not seeking the path to enlightenment, like the blind who do not see the way;
this mind is of but one kind, yet it is capable of creating all karma.
Whether it be karma or that mind itself, they pervade the three realms of existence.
Furthermore, just as those five colors can manifest in various ways,
so too do the objects of the five sense-faculties cause the mind to revolve accordingly in every place.
Like a painter in the world, it is beheld by all people alike.
Know that the mind is like a painter; its ingenuity cannot be seen by others.
Just as various images on a wall depend on the skill of the artist for their beauty or ugliness, so too all wholesome and unwholesome karmic conditions are created by the mind.
This mind constantly deliberates, never pausing for even a moment day or night;
according to the karma one has created, the retribution received will be exactly like it.
If one is subdued by the mind, one delights in committing various unwholesome deeds.
At the end of life, terror arises; one cannot escape suffering.
Karma is like that painting, manifesting wherever it may be;
because it is created by the mind, its fruit follows accordingly.
The various distinctions of karma, and the retribution received therefrom, are likewise so;
driven by the mind, one gallops through the three realms.
If a person follows the mind, they will create all manner of karma.
One who has well-tamed the mind realizes true, eternal bliss.
This mind follows wherever it goes; whether it be violent, evil, or restless, how excellent it is to tame that mind! When the mind is tranquil, there is no suffering.
If a person skillfully subdues the mind, they will eliminate all faults and afflictions;
being free from faults, such a wise person does not undergo suffering.
All sufferings arise from the mind; realizing this, one finds that they are not obtained from elsewhere.
Oppression and unbearable suffering all arise from the mind’s flickering movement. Devas, nāgas, asuras, yakṣas, and piśācas—
all have the mind as their master throughout the three realms of existence.
The mind can lead one to the heavens, Or cause birth in the human world, And even into the various evil realms; It revolves like a wheel, no different.
When the mind is dragged by its objects, The fool becomes deluded and confused.
Because craving arises from the mind, one dwells in immeasurable suffering and affliction.
The mind is characterized solely by delusion; it is violent and evil, possessing great power.
It is said to be invisible, yet it perishes with extreme rapidity in every moment.
The wise who skillfully subdue the mind’s various faults and afflictions transcend the net of Māra and reach the further shore.
The mind can give rise to doubt; it is crooked, deceitful, and prone to constant fluctuation.
If one relies upon that mind, one will surely seek out perilous difficulties.
One should abandon the faults of the mind, so that the sense faculties become tranquil;
by not clinging to sinful or unrighteous things, one will skillfully penetrate the true nature of reality.
One attains the most supreme meditative concentration through the causes and conditions of the mind;
yet falling into the evil realms likewise arises from that same mind.
This mind possesses such power that it can create all manner of karmic actions.
Within the realm of space, it does not dwell for even a single moment.
That mind is difficult to comprehend; it is eternally without form or appearance.
It draws forth the production of the world, yet without the mind, nothing would go forth.
The body performs various karmas; where does it go?
Where does it abide?
While its fruits can all be seen, that mind cannot be perceived.
This mind is difficult to subdue; obscured by ignorance, it sees nothing.
It can lead all sentient beings to hasten toward the hells.
This mind can commit transgressions, yet it can also cultivate meritorious deeds.
Realizing that it is like an illusion or a magical transformation, one should always rely upon the true path.
This mind departs without being known, and its arrival likewise cannot be seen;
yet it is able to lead all sentient beings back and forth through hundreds of thousands of births.
A sharp blade cannot cut it; a blazing fire cannot burn it.
Yet the foolish person, lacking wisdom, is destroyed by it.
This karmic rope is firm and strong, capable of binding deluded sentient beings.
Throughout hundreds of thousands of lifetimes, one pulls [at it] but it does not break.
In a single moment, this mind creates both wholesome and unwholesome karma.
One who can subdue that mind will always find peace and happiness wherever they go.
Entering through the gates of those six sense faculties, they take pleasure in and become attached to various objects;
the mind drags those sentient beings along, and they fall into perilous difficulties without realizing it.
Space is fundamentally luminous and clear, and the nature of water is eternally limpid and still.
If this mind is like that, it draws forth and produces sublime virtue.
It seeks out objects and constantly dwells upon their conjunction;
through the mind’s reliance upon the various faculties, it is like a king leading his retinue.
This mind is constantly rushing about, and that body follows wherever it goes;
through their mutual power and capacity, they revolve in the ocean of the three realms of existence.
All the karma one creates throughout is brought about by the mind alone.
If there are no virtuous causes and conditions, even a small measure of happiness cannot be obtained.
One should therefore seek the True Dharma and practice the various meditative concentrations;
when the mind is free from all faults and evils, it is like the sun emerging from the clouds.
If the mind is well-established in meditative concentration, then right view will arise;
if one develops pure faith while at home, one shall escape the perils of saṃsāra.
If the mind does not commit evil, then faults will not arise.
Free from afflictions and pure, one is constantly reborn in the heavens.
This mind follows the sense faculties, flowing and shifting with great speed;
those who skillfully guard the mind will subsequently be born among the devas.
If one is driven by the mind, One commits all manner of transgressions;
Relying on unrighteous conduct, One dwells long within saṃsāra.
In a single moment of this mind, There are hundreds of thousands of arisings and ceasings.
Its nature is solely lightness and movement, unreal like a magical illusion.
This mind possesses great power, rushing about without a moment’s pause;
if wisdom recognizes its stillness, then one can skillfully bind it.
This mind is difficult to subdue; it causes the sense faculties to become agitated.
When the wise skillfully maintain it, they can reach the further shore.
This mind is bound by nothing other than insatiability; contentment is the cord that can bind it.
One who skillfully governs that mind is a wise person in the world.
This mind takes objects of desire as its conditions and constantly gives rise to craving and delight;
when it is well-governed, these are extinguished, but when it acts wickedly, they increase.
If a person’s mind is tranquil, they see all desires as poison;
the fool lets his mind run wild and indulges in them as if they were exquisite.
This mind alone performs the action, and that karma follows accordingly.
Arising from the sense faculties and their objects, they cause the associated mental factors to conjoin.
Once the wise have understood this, they abandon these [distinctions] and attain pliancy;
since all those forms appear the same to them, why would they give rise to divergent perceptions?
All objects of form can cause the mind to become disturbed;
one who skillfully disciplines that mind is then free from all faults.
Just as a single grain seed may produce variations in color and fragrance, [so too does the mind vary according to its training].
Through various combinations, each arises according to the mind.
Just as a worldly craftsman skillfully repairs his mechanical devices,
so too one who governs the mind according to the True Dharma will always abide in peace and happiness.
Objects of perception pull at the mind; the fool gives rise to delight therein.
But wisdom possesses great power, swiftly causing it to become pure.
Furthermore, that mind moves and shifts, universally taking the aggregates and elements as its objects.
And within those three realms of existence, due to the absence of the vision of reality;
just as in the great ocean, waves surge when struck by the wind,
so too do mind and objects combine, flowing along with the world.
Wholesome karma leads the mind and will surely bring about superior fruit;
one should therefore practice virtuous deeds and no longer commit any evils.
When the mind is in accord with meditative concentration, it is like water undisturbed by the wind.
Each arises from causes and conditions, following the destination determined by karma.
This mind is extremely swift, traversing back and forth in a single instant;
it may take as its object the celestial realms, or it may descend into hell.
The mind can sever all evils and further create all virtues;
it leads one to the gate of liberation—thus is the mind described.
This mind is most swift and agile; there is nothing that surpasses it.
If one does not guard it well, the mind will remain constantly attached to desire.
In the space of a single moment, this mind can create both wholesome and unwholesome karma;
its nature is inherently light and restless, and though sought, it cannot be found.
This mind comes from nowhere known; where is it seen when it departs?
When conditions conjoin, it exists momentarily; when conditions disperse, it has no place of abiding.
This mind is not an accumulation, nor does it endure for long.
It is not associated with grasping, nor is it seen in any location.
The mind, too, is a mere conventional designation, arising from a combination of conditions;
cow dung and a mani jewel are both likewise of this nature.
The sense organs and so forth are likewise; each arises from consciousness.
Not a single phenomenon has ever been seen that is obtained without being a composite.
Thus, those objects of experience are difficult for sentient beings to eliminate.
If one dwells securely in the True Dharma, what can desire do?
This mind is extremely treacherous, powerful and difficult to subdue;
it delights in creating all manner of karmic actions, while the fool remains devoid of discernment.
Because one creates various karmas, they become the cause for saṃsāra;
within the three realms of existence, one long endures all manner of suffering and affliction.
Just like contracting diseases such as wind-disorders, this [karma] does not cease by merely sinking into the evil destinies.
Those with the faults of greed and the like will certainly fall into hell.
Mental transgressions are the greatest; they constantly produce all manner of evils.
Even wind-disorders are not wholesome; one should therefore cultivate superior practice.
Wind and other ailments may be cured; when the body perishes, they scatter with it.
The disease of craving is not so; it persists through hundreds of thousands of lifetimes.
One should know that the diseases such as craving differ from those caused by wind.
By skillfully cultivating sublime practices, one attains freedom from the fault of craving.
This mind is like a king of physicians, skillfully curing the afflictions of the mental faculty;
it is not like those of the world, who treat only the diseases of the body.
When the mind gives rise to wholesome reflection, then no defilements will arise;
the fool who lacks the True Dharma will fall into perilous paths.
If a person delights in meditative concentration, taking refuge in mountain forests,
The fool is not at peace, giving rise frequently to conflict and strife.
This mind is like a painter, painting all manner of forms;
driven by its own fabrications, it wanders through the five realms of existence.
Though worldly paintings may be skillful, depicting hundreds of thousands of varieties,
the painting of karma is infinitely vast, with the three realms as its canvas.
It portrays various sentient beings as they wander through the five destinies.
Because karma is vast, it pervades every place.
Furthermore, that painter of the mind can draw the net of all karmas;
all sentient beings in the world are bound by it.
Furthermore, wind, rain, smoke, and dust can all damage a painting;
yet through hundreds of thousands of koṭis of kalpas, the painting of karma remains ever as it was.
The great earth may crumble and disintegrate, and the waters of the ocean may even dry up.
Only the paintings of karma endure, manifesting wherever they may be;
all karmas constantly follow one, their fruits never failing.
Sentient beings, letting their minds run wild, wander through the various realms of existence.
If a person’s mind is attached to pleasure and seeks to pursue the realm of desire,
failing to sever unwholesome karma, they will certainly fall into suffering and hardship; therefore,
one should restrain the mind, for that [realm] is extremely evil and terrifying.
Delighting in the union with sense objects, one is constantly filled with the poison of craving;
heedless of the dangers and hardships, one perpetually pursues desire.
When pleasure perishes, it is accompanied by suffering, and one must personally undergo its karmic retribution.
If a person fears the miserable realms, their mind will always be tranquil;
through that tranquility, their life of wisdom increases.
This mind possesses great power, yet it is violent and evil, difficult to restrain.
The wise one, well-disciplined, attains freedom from all sorrow and fear.
The wise one avoids evil speech and always utters right words;
causing others to give rise to love and joy, they dwell well upon the path to enlightenment.
One should always praise pure conduct and avoid defiled speech;
those who delight in evil words shall fall into the miserable realms.
If one utters false speech, one abandons the true Dharma.
It also destroys the merit of future lives, and there is no evil that one will not commit.
If a person speaks falsely, they will be detested by others;
they will long endure the suffering of saṃsāra and have no means of being reborn among the devas.
Virtuous people all abandon them, and they become objects of the multitude's wrath;
they obstruct all wholesome dharmas solely because of their evil speech.
For such a person in this world, the mouth is like a sharp axe.
One cuts and destroys one's own body entirely because of evil speech;
it causes others to give rise to violence and malice, increases all manner of transgressions,
and can produce every kind of calamity— all because of evil speech.
Because one's speech lacks truth, one is held in contempt by others;
for this reason, one will later fall among the hungry ghosts (*preta*).
The wise person has no false words, for false speech brings retribution in return.
The breath is constantly foul and putrid, and later one receives various bitter retributions.
If one abandons true practice, one then distances oneself from the True Dharma;
because of this distancing from the True Dharma, immeasurable suffering and affliction arise.
If one utters words of truth, one will be respected by others and praised by the Tathāgata as a bright torch of the True Dharma.
Always speaking words of liberation, one does not abandon the truth.
One should know that such a person follows the gradual stages toward the state of the noble ones.
If a person lacks truthfulness and later transforms into a female body,
constantly practicing false speech, they will fall into the evil realms.
This is the true and correct path, as taught by all the Buddhas;
it is the most supreme wealth of Dharma and provides the foremost protection.
It is as truly precious as the ultimate treasure, the most excellent among all adornments.
Like a pure and stainless eye, its radiance is ever-blazing;
True as a treasury of jewels, its priceless utility is inexhaustible.
If one can practice such conduct, they shall be the most supreme among men.
Just as a worldly king is adorned with exquisite jewels,
so are the truthful words of the wise like the ornaments of the gods.
False speech is a profound fault, like the poison within poisons.
Because of this cause, one falls into the evil destinies.
Neither father nor mother, nor kinsmen and friends, can provide rescue;
only that true practice alone is able to protect, and nothing else.
If one draws near to a person of falsehood, it is like touching the fires of hell;
by failing to give rise to fear, one will be consumed and harmed by them.
These fires are exceedingly fierce and violent, capable of burning even the great ocean.
How much more so for those without wisdom?
It is like burning grass and wood.
Therefore, one should be single-minded and never speak falsely.
If one can remain far removed from it, then there will be no sorrows or afflictions.
If one delights in that false speech and constantly abandons the truth,
such a person brings only blame upon themselves, like discarding jewels to take up rubble.
If a person does not understand this and delights in uttering false words, they will fall into hell and suffer extreme pain for a long time.
Truthful speech is not difficult; it is only that the ignorant do not practice it.
It can adorn the practitioner, bringing all that is wholesome to fulfillment.
Truth is the supreme good; falsehood is a profound fault.
The foolish abandon merit and instead grasp at calamity.
The seeds of all suffering and affliction arise entirely from false speech;
if one can distance oneself from it, one will attain stainless tranquility.
If one utters words of truth, one will be pleasing to behold by others.
One should know that those who are deceitful always perform unwholesome deeds.
If a person speaks the truth, their heart rejoices like that of the devas;
yet because of false speech, the fool is constantly terrified by future suffering.
Truth is the foremost good; falsehood is the ultimate evil.
One who leaves behind faults and seeks merit is unsurpassed among men.
Constantly born in superior realms, they enjoy all manner of happiness.
Those who seek to attain enlightenment do so because of the truth.
If a person does not distance themselves from superior false speech,
they will constantly be born in difficult places and undergo all manner of bitter retributions.
Truth is the supreme path; falsehood is no cause for the good.
It does not come from another direction, nor is it obtained through another.
The Buddha has taught that truth can bring one away from all suffering and affliction.
It is the supreme bright lamp, the excellent medicine that removes disease.
Like poison and nectar, both depend upon the tongue;
poison is like false speech, while nectar is equivalent to truth.
Abiding in the certainty of reality, one should take up that nectar;
if one gives rise to falsehood, it is like a fool seeking poison in return.
Because of giving rise to falsehood, one will certainly be destroyed by it.
Like one in this world who drinks poison, One will perish before long.
It brings no peace to oneself, And how could it benefit others?
Since it harms both self and others, Of what use is such false speech?
Furthermore, the various poisons of the world, once they strike, cause death and then cease;
the poison of falsehood is not like this—it destroys one across hundreds of thousands of lifetimes.
The Buddha taught the path to liberation, which takes reality as its foundation.
Adorned with pure conduct, one is always born in sublime places.
Sentient beings follow their own karma and fall into that river of craving;
only by boarding the vessel of truth can one transcend it.
The unwholesome causes of sentient beings all arise from craving;
they fall into the evil realms, yet [the Buddha] can truly deliver them.
Like a vajra, firm and sharp, he is able to shatter all mountains.
That true and supreme capacity skillfully pacifies and eliminates afflictions.
It brings benefit in both worlds as truly as inexhaustible wealth;
by skillfully discerning all phenomena, the mind remains ever tranquil and secure.
There may be evil bhikṣus, whose nature is full of cruelty and poison,
who constantly speak false words and whose minds are merely fickle and restless;
such people are abandoned by all virtuous ones and are loathed by the world.
One should regard them as hateful enemies, because they lack any reality.
Since it is through their false speech that they bring ruin upon themselves and others,
and since there is not even the slightest benefit [to be gained], how could one not abandon them?
If a person utters false speech, their breath will always be foul;
all the devas will shun them, and they will be impoverished and without refuge.
If a person utters false speech, they will find no peace or security in their movements or stillness.
Whether worldly or supramundane, they are constantly estranged from the right path.
If one does not abandon false speech, one shall undergo the fruit of extreme suffering;
such sentient beings seek for themselves a course toward the evil realms.
One should know that the person of truth is respected by the world;
therefore, abandon false speech and constantly cultivate this supreme practice.
Through truth one does no harm, and one always gives rise to loving-kindness and compassion.
It is the treasury of the True Dharma and the essential practice for rebirth in heaven.
That sentient beings fall into hell, as well as the realms of Yama and hungry ghosts, is all due to false speech;
therefore, the wise offer it as a profound warning.
Like a sword, fire, or poison; like a snare or a messenger of death—one should know that such false speech brings about a retribution of suffering that is truly grave.
If one does not fear the fruits of karma, they will all manifest at the end of life.
One should abandon such evil speech and always delight in speaking the truth;
otherwise, one will accumulate manifold sufferings and be born into inferior lineages.
Divisive speech gives rise to further divisiveness, revolving without end.
For that evil retribution of divisive speech, one falls into hell,
constantly burning from moment to moment, experiencing its ultimate suffering oneself.
Having secretly set one's mind upon destroying the various secret teachings—
As with those who engage in double-tongued speech, their own faults are constantly concealed.
If a person abandons double-tongued speech, abiding in definitive tranquility,
they will be free from the entanglements of kinship and will no longer give rise to thoughts of social cohesion.
Divisive speech is like a venomous serpent, Always dwelling in its lair;
if one can distance oneself from that fault, Then there will be no calamities or misfortunes.
If a person utters malicious words, It is like a salty, barren wasteland.
Because poison arises from the tongue, all people abandon it;
seeing it as one would a sharp blade or staff, why do you not feel fear?
If you delight in those evil words, you will be harmed by them.
The tongue is like that blazing fire, and the mind is like its fuel;
malicious speech is like a fierce flame that incinerates all sentient beings.
If one uses words of loving-kindness, the entire world will revere them.
Those who see them feel joy, regarding them as their own parents.
Loving speech is most excellent; it can produce supreme happiness and cause all inexhaustible torments and afflictions to become cool and refreshed.
Loving speech can lead to rebirth in heaven;
it is a supreme mass of merit, like a true friend, and is the highest tranquility.
Yet, regarding the authentic scriptures, one may oppose them and fail to practice them.
As observed by all Buddhas, that tongue is but a piece of flesh;
yet for one who always delights in speaking the truth and is endowed with all virtues,
they will later be reborn among the gods, and this tongue shall be like a treasure.
If a person’s mind is filled with false imaginings, deceived by that craving,
and they covet the wealth of others for themselves, how can they be reborn in the celestial realms?
Creating various evils through false imaginings, their ignorance knows no moment of relinquishment.
One undergoes various torments and afflictions oneself, like pouring oil onto a blazing fire.
Seeking various fruits through false imaginings—how can anything be obtained when there is no cause?
All manner of suffering arises from this; one should ultimately distance oneself from it.
Furthermore, foolish sentient beings delight in causing harm and affliction;
their minds are constantly filled with resentment, making them like those venomous serpents.
Their very nature is solely treacherous and evil, and they perpetually strike down others.
Constantly scorched by the torment of fever, they find not even the slightest happiness;
lacking fame, profit, and honor, and devoid of kinsmen and friends,
because their minds delight in harming others, neither humans nor deities will protect them.
Those who delight in harming others are like a mass of darkness;
they cause others to give rise to anger and distress, and this is said to be a profound fault.
Non-harming is the supreme good, for it brings peace and happiness to all sentient beings.
By constantly cultivating such causes, one shall attain the path to Bodhi.
Though the mouth speaks the True Dharma, if the mind is solely unwholesome, one is not like a worldly thief; such a person is a great thief within the Dharma.
If one is a teacher of the sublime Dharma, they should act in accordance with what they have taught;
thus, free from the defilements of affliction, they seek to attain the fruit of ultimate reality.
Because of false speech, they speak much of worldly matters.
The immeasurable supramundane dharmas— One cannot understand even a small portion of them.
One should delight in discoursing on the ultimate truth, And not practice worldly speech;
For if one relies upon the worldly, One will be bound by saṃsāra.
"To delight in performing non-meritorious deeds is certainly without cause for happiness;
it is devoid of the wealth of supramundane dharmas—this is what the wise have declared.
When the Teacher shows words of benefit, the foolish do not accept his instruction."
Later, one will encounter suffering and hardship, and the mind will be filled with regret and distress.
If a person speaks words of truth, their heart will always be joyful;
all the devas will protect them, and the whole world will show them respect.
Because one is honored by the world, one’s good reputation increases;
by always practicing the conduct of truth, one will certainly be reborn among the gods.
If a person speaks falsely and disturbs all the masses, [they shall suffer].
Hated by the multitude, though one lives, it is as if one were dead.
If a person speaks falsely, it is like being wounded and cut by a sharp blade;
since they destroy true merit, why does their tongue not fall off?
If a person speaks falsely, it is like a mass of blazing fire and also like a venomous serpent; both emerge from their mouth.
False speech is the foremost poison, surpassing all the poisons that grow upon the earth.
Those who harm and afflict sentient beings will be the first to fall into hell.
If a person speaks falsely, all manner of evils will gather upon their tongue,
as if excrement, urine, pus, and blood were issuing forth from their own mouths.
This person’s tongue is like a rope, capable of dragging one toward the evil realms;
it destroys the bridge of the Dharma—all this arises from speaking false words.
It is neither Buddha nor pure precepts, neither father nor mother.
Because of such evil wisdom, this person cannot rescue themselves from suffering.
If a person speaks false words, they will quickly bring contempt upon themselves;
the wise will all abandon them, and the devas will all stay far away.
Failing to restrain one’s speech and constantly giving rise to anger—
such a person possesses little merit, and wherever they go, there is much suffering.
They harbor envy toward the happiness of others and cannot conceal their own faults.
You should know that such a person will certainly fall into the evil realms.
The fool speaks empty falsehoods but cannot practice accordingly;
since his words and deeds contradict one another, he shall undergo immeasurable suffering.
Those who do not abide in the True Dharma themselves, yet delight in discussing the private affairs of others,
are arrogant and devoid of wisdom in this world.
If a person opposes and does not believe in the True Teaching, [they are likewise lost].
For one hundred thousand *nibbuda* kalpas, one constantly undergoes the retribution of hell.
If a person speaks falsely and takes pleasure in committing various evils,
for fifty-six *nibbuda* kalpas, they constantly undergo the retribution of hell.
Delighting in creating the causes of that evil, seeing the turbidity of views and lacking reality—such foolish people further increase their own darkness.
True wealth is supreme; it is firm and cannot be moved.
By relying on this, one is born in the heavens and ascends to the gate of eternal bliss.
Therefore, one should be single-minded and constantly contemplate the true Dharma;
such a person shall attain the supreme state, the place of neither birth nor death.
This true merit can give rise to the bliss of tranquility;
the wise person who abstains from false speech is praised by all Buddhas.
