The various karmas that are performed— whether meritorious or non-meritorious—
bind all sentient beings, each inevitably bringing its own retribution.
The mind of the fool is like a fish, dwelling amidst the waves of craving.
Smiling as one commits various evils, one weeps in sorrow when receiving their retribution.
Having previously committed these sins together with servants and attendants, one later undergoes the bitter fruit of those deeds; they cannot take one's place.
Through kinsmen and companions, one may join together to commit many sins;
yet in the world beyond, these follow one along—nothing but the evil karma one has created.
Just as wherever a flower goes, its fragrance does not leave it behind.
So too with good and evil karma; wherever one goes, it constantly follows.
Sentient beings, by virtue of their own karma, always experience the correspondence of cause and effect:
by performing good deeds, they are born among the various devas and enjoy sublime happiness.
If there is the retribution of evil karma, one will undergo most grievous suffering,
falling into the three evil destinies where such suffering has no equal.
This is because those three types of karma have been created throughout the three realms.
Constantly giving rise to the three poisons, one falls into the three evil realms.
All foolish ordinary beings, through the conjunction of causes and conditions,
transmigrate within the three worlds, all following their own karma.
What one has not done oneself is not received by another; what another has done is not received by oneself.
One should know that the karma one creates brings forth its retribution with absolute certainty.
Although karmic actions are manifold, there are nine places where they are experienced.
Through their mutual support, they bring about forty kinds of evil.
Having created a single karma for oneself, one will surely receive its single retribution;
falling into the perilous paths, there shall be no companion.
Or if one commits evil deeds at the urging of others,
when the time comes to suffer their bitter retribution, they will be unable to save them.
When karma ripens, it does not distinguish between beginning and end, nor between this life and future lives.
That is to say, having performed these actions, one may experience their results in this life or elsewhere.
Due to wholesome and unwholesome karma, one wanders through the flow of saṃsāra,
blown by the winds of karma, thereby inviting the retributions of suffering and happiness.
The minds of fools are distracted; they always delight in and cling to sensual desires.
Lacking the discernment of right wisdom, their various evils increase.
Those beings attached to pleasure are shrouded by ignorance.
When the retribution for evil appears before one, one then falls into a place of darkness.
Because of the Buddha’s True Dharma, the mind does not give rise to joy;
thus, within that hell, one undergoes suffering for a long time.
Bound by the net of karma throughout beginningless saṃsāra,
dying here and being reborn there, all is created by the mind;
falling from the heavens, or being born in hell and then ascending to heaven.
Some are born among humans, while others receive the retribution of hungry ghosts;
that the causes of their suffering and happiness are all produced by what they themselves have created,
arising from one another, and not fashioned by a sovereign god (Īśvara).
Within the cycle of birth and death, one has created countless evil karmas;
only the Buddha can witness and know this, for no other wisdom can comprehend it.
If non-dharma were to bring about good, then such a cause would be a perversion.
One should know that the fruits one receives are all similar to their causes.
If cause and effect correspond, then it accords with the correct principle;
of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), there are none that do not arise from conditions.
One who has not seen their own faultlessness yet proceeds toward hell does so surely because of evil karma, and thus undergoes its bitter retribution.
Having resolutely committed various evils, they remain stubbornly attached to them without remorse.
Bound by their karma, they fall into the evil realms.
One has never seen an unwholesome deed that leads to a pleasant fruit;
this is the Buddha’s truthful word, which reveals the path of its remedy.
Just as there is light because of a lamp, and just as retribution is summoned by karma,
so too all that is created arises through causes and conditions.
That is to say, through various respective causes, their corresponding fruits follow in succession.
One who thoroughly understands such characteristics is said to possess true vision.
It is not like the god Maheśvara, who is established without cause;
all phenomena arise dependently—this is what the Tathāgata has taught.
Due to beginningless saṃsāra, karmic retribution is always similar;
it does not arise from inverted discrimination, but exists through causes and conditions.
Sentient beings are deluded by ignorance and remain insatiable in their craving and desire.
If one does not understand karmic retribution, by what means could one attain tranquility?
If a person within the Buddha’s teaching fails to discern the path from that which is not the path,
they will, due to delusion and a lack of right wisdom, constantly give rise to burning affliction.
Seeing the happiness of others as one’s own, know that such happiness arises from causes;
all phenomena are but mind alone, each according to its own karma.
Conditioned things are all impermanent, like water bubbles, not lasting long.
One should practice virtuous deeds for the benefit of both worlds.
Beholding the karmic retribution of the world and the falling away of the devas,
one who delights in negligence will certainly find not even a slight measure of happiness.
The noose of karma is exceedingly long, firm and difficult to escape;
it binds that foolish person, keeping them far from Bodhi.
Wisdom is like a sharp sword, capable of severing it completely.
Free from the feverish affliction of ignorance, one is led to the further shore.
Receiving those fruits according to one's karma, in accordance with what is wholesome or unwholesome,
the wise do not forget for even a moment that cause and effect are ever certain.
Through the conjunction of causes and conditions, the skeletal frame of limbs arises,
binding all sentient beings so that they circle in saṃsāra without liberation.
Because of those bonds, they are oppressed by unbearable suffering.
One should cultivate the causes of liberation to reach the end of all suffering.
That karma is called a "virtuous hook," for it can further draw sentient beings toward their respective places of birth, where they receive retribution according to their actions.
The fruit of that karma is like a wheel, revolving within the three realms of existence;
one should abandon all faults and afflictions, and constantly cultivate sublime practices.
Generosity is like a pure vessel, containing the waters of ethical discipline, diligence, and wisdom.
The wise who skillfully maintain their practice extinguish the fires of karma within the three realms of existence.
If they放任 (let loose) those three types of action, the three poisons will follow and turn;
they will gallop through the three worlds due to the three kinds of conduct born of delusion.
All sentient beings, oppressed by suffering,
constantly abide depending upon their own past actions;
if that virtuous cause did not exist, how could there be even the slightest happiness?
One receives retribution according to one's karma, just as seeds produce their respective fruits.
Furthermore, it is like the time of spring, when plants and trees flourish;
those fruits arise from causes, and without a cause, they do not emerge.
Bound by the snares of karma, they wander through hundreds of thousands of births,
revolving like the wheels of a worldly chariot driven by its mechanism.
Because those three poisons are so firm, sentient beings find it difficult to escape.
Free from the afflictions of greed and the like, one then skillfully transcends the three realms of existence.
If a person, with a joyful and delighted mind, cultivates those sublime practices,
by virtue of these causes and conditions, they will receive a magnificent and superior retribution.
Karma is like that painter who skillfully depicts all manner of forms;
whether in the heavens or among humans, there is nothing he does not paint.
Those paintings are beyond measure, for they are all produced through the transformations of karma.
Without the application of various colors and ornaments, there is likewise no one who can see it.
When the wall crumbles, the painting vanishes; ultimately, all things disintegrate and perish.
Although this body is extinguished and passes away, that karma remains forever.
Sentient beings are shrouded by ignorance and ensnared by karma;
within beginningless birth and death, they revolve constantly like a potter’s wheel.
Like wind, sun, smoke, and dust, they cause damage to a painting.
The karmic conditions they have summoned can never be temporarily cast aside.
One should observe the various unwholesome deeds committed in the past;
wherever one may be, one will experience their results according to what was done.
That which can bring about complete liberation from all subtle evil karmas— whether superior, middling, or inferior— is the supreme wise one.
Furthermore, regarding those sentient beings who perform wholesome or unwholesome deeds:
Whether it be pleasant or unpleasant, one will certainly obtain it.
If one opposes the words of the Buddha, that person is a fool;
amidst immeasurable suffering and affliction, there will be no liberation for a long time.
Devas, humans, asuras, hell-beings, pretas, and animals—all arise from their respective karma;
therefore, one should follow the practice of wisdom.
Through the defiled discrimination of the intellect, one creates immeasurable evil karma.
Each goes to their respective realms of existence, where they experience and fully perceive the retribution [of their deeds].
If one performs wholesome karma, they will later be reborn among humans or devas;
if they do unwholesome deeds, they will drown in the three miserable states, like an actor changing his costume.
The lines of karma are extremely firm and long, binding all throughout the three realms of existence.
Sentient beings, driven by their own karma, are like spokes dependent on the rim of a wheel;
some are born among the gods, while others sink into perilous difficulties.
Samsara does not pause for a moment; one receives retribution according to one's karma.
That sentient beings are born in the heavens is entirely obtained through virtuous deeds, like exquisite lotuses emerging from a pure pond.
If one performs wholesome deeds, they will certainly not perish;
one will always be born in superior realms and experience results according to one's wishes.
Fools do not cultivate the causes, yet they vainly hope for pleasant rewards.
Just as one cannot obtain ghee by searching for it in sand,
If one cultivates those virtuous causes, then happiness will arise;
To receive a reward without a cause is like seeking fruit from a tree that has been uprooted.
Sentient beings, due to their karma, receive retributions that are not fixed;
they are like sand thrown into the air, drifting and falling according to the wind.
Just as those sands gather and disperse through causes and conditions, so too do suffering and joy.
All are led by karma; one should not commit sinful deeds.
The boundless seeds of karma transform within the six realms of existence;
all arise from the mind—this is the Buddha’s true teaching.
This mind is difficult to subdue; it delights in creating various karmas.
Like sentient beings depicted in colored paintings, only a Buddha can truly know and see them.
Just as from a single grain of seed, hundreds of thousands of millions can be produced.
This net of karma is likewise; no one is able to measure it.
Just as a bird bound by thread may fly high yet still be brought back, so too are sentient beings constrained by their karma, returning again and again in this same way.
Fools lack right view and do not comprehend the nature of sin and merit;
they circulate within the three realms of existence, for which suffering alone is their own possession.
If one understands the karma of good and evil, one will then awaken to the law of arising and ceasing.
These are truly real persons, who are able to reach the further shore.
If one is separated from virtuous friends, one will instead associate with evil companions;
abandoning the Dharma, they crave worldly wealth and do not believe in the bitter fruits of future suffering.
Because they do not understand the retribution of karma, they do not know the difference between sin and merit.
Those deluded sentient beings endure long-lasting torment;
with worldly wisdom they give rise to arrogance and constantly utter meaningless words.
Failing to realize the causes and conditions of karma, one constantly undergoes the suffering of saṃsāra.
It is like a person long held in captivity who suddenly obtains release;
his kinsmen and friends rejoice together, offering mutual congratulations and consolation.
As if dwelling within hell, one attains liberation when karma is exhausted;
by the power of prior wholesome karma, one is born in the heavens.
There one experiences celestial bliss, endowed with immeasurable adornments.
If one further cultivates the causes therein, one will be reborn in an even more excellent place.
If one does not cultivate virtue, when karma is exhausted, one will immediately fall away;
signs of decay will appear before one, like a lamp going out when the oil is spent.
This ceases and that arises again, revolving within the three realms;
blown by the winds of karma, by what means can one escape?
If a person possesses mastery of wisdom, they will not cling to saṃsāra.
One will not be bound even slightly by the ropes of that karma;
even if lotus-stalk fibers were piled up to the height of Mount Sumeru,
the noose of such karma likewise would be unable to bind the wise.
The wise one dwells within saṃsāra like Mount Sumeru, unmoving;
far removed from all grief and affliction, they are liberated from all terrors.
Just as the Buddhas perceive, cause and effect are always concordant.
If the karma one performs is vast, its retribution will be equal to it.
Repeatedly creating various karmas, one receives their respective fruits;
through such actions, one becomes bound by them.
If one performs wholesome deeds, one will certainly obtain that superior retribution:
a physical form, strength, and life-span that adorn the body, and being honored by others.
Yet how long can meritorious karma endure? It vanishes as suddenly as the light of a lamp.
The retribution of those karmas is without error; all are produced in accordance with the mind’s creation.
All sentient beings, when their karma is exhausted, must surely lose their lives;
their bodies are consumed by fire, and not even the slightest stability remains.
Furthermore, those various sentient beings, due to the distinctions within the realm of the mind,
each perform various karmas and are bound by the three realms of existence.
Like the mute of the world, they proceed along unwholesome paths.
To hope for a pleasant retribution while acting thus is like churning water in search of fire.
If one performs no wholesome deeds, the fruit of happiness will not arise;
those who constantly delight in negligence will certainly possess no merit.
Dragged by the ropes of karma, dark and dull, lacking awareness, one cannot sever those ropes;
only when suffering is exhausted is there liberation.
Because of karma, sentient beings wander back and forth through saṃsāra.
Seeing this perish and that arise, all are obtained from causes.
The foolish are attached to the five desires and have never given rise to awakening;
as greed and craving support one another, when will the limits of suffering ever be reached?
The fool knows no contentment, delighting in the pleasures of desire;
because of that lack of contentment, he brings about his own ruin.
Regarding the rewards of merit in this present life, when karma is exhausted, even pleasure perishes.
Due to frequent indulgence in negligence, one only realizes it at the moment of death.
Arising immeasurable conceptualizations, one creates various kinds of karma;
each, according to the causes and conditions of their karma, undergoes its respective retribution.
Sentient beings are driven by karma; some are summoned by karma to birth in happiness, while others are summoned to the retribution of suffering.
If they are born among the devas, they experience the exquisite pleasures of the five desires.
When merit is exhausted, one falls away, and at that point, nothing can save them.
Furthermore, the causes of that saṃsāra all arise from falsehood;
the Buddha, through his vision of reality, reveals the true path to liberation.
In the past, one cultivated various wholesome karmas, In accord with morality, concentration, and wisdom;
These are not causes for saṃsāra, But lead to abiding in pure bliss.
Since this retribution of merit is inexhaustible, One should not give way to negligence.
One should maintain ultimate single-mindedness and further cultivate sublime practices.
If a person possesses the fruits of merit, they should distance themselves from all that is unwholesome;
by doing good, one ascends the path of the sages, while by committing evil, one invites calamity and retribution.
If a person performs virtuous deeds with courage and without retreat,
they will constantly obtain the bliss of tranquility and be able to proceed upon the path to enlightenment.
If a person is attached to negligence and delights in committing various unwholesome acts, [they will suffer].
Their merit will accordingly diminish, and they shall fall into the evil realms.
This karma is like a swing; it all arises from the transformations of the mind.
Deceived by the ignorance of sentient beings, they constantly revolve in dependence upon it.
Birth and death are like a wheel, with the twelve sense bases as its spokes;
revolving within the world, they are all driven by the mind.
Through the mind one creates wholesome karma, which leads to rebirth among the gods.
Deluded by sensory objects, one does not contemplate future suffering.
Whether toward pleasure or that which is not pleasure, one should act with careful reflection;
though the karmas of pain and pleasure differ, they all arise from causes and conditions.
In this world there is no true happiness; all are dragged along by karma.
When pleasure perishes, suffering manifests, for it is created by the mind.
Driven by the winds of karma, sentient beings are blown to their places of rebirth.
If one conceives attachment and delight therein, one will be bound by karma.
Only wholesome and unwholesome karma constantly follow one into future lives,
just as when one plucks a flower, its fragrance follows along with it.
Sentient beings are driven by their own karma, flowing and turning through birth and death like a swing that rises and falls without rest;
they travel back and forth among gods, humans, and asuras across the six realms of existence.
Enshrouded by delusion, they do not give rise to true insight.
Just as a worldly wheel revolves depending upon the hand,
so too are they driven by karma with a speed that has no equal.
Enveloped by karma, the twelve links converge;
this is called the wheel of dependent origination, yet no one in the world understands it.
The gods are shrouded in delusion and are constantly attached to the realm of desire.
Only the fruits of karma endure; that pleasure is not accumulated.
They do not understand wholesome karma, which—like excellent medicine or a bright lamp—removes darkness, brings ease, and can act as a refuge and salvation.
Enduring unbearable and extreme suffering, as well as various terrors— this karma possesses great power,
yet one does not grow weary. When a deva dies and is born among humans,
and when a human perishes and falls into hell, [it is due to this].
Released from hell, they become animals, and again fall into the realm of hungry ghosts.
All are driven by the winds of their own karma, drifting and turning without stability;
yet those deluded sentient beings have never once given rise to awakening.
Sentient beings ride the chariot of karma, capable of traversing the three realms;
other vehicles are not so, for their swiftness has no equal.
If one’s actions are pure, one will receive their karmic reward.
Only when it manifests in that present life does one know its own karma.
That karma is like a painted image; it all arises from the mind.
What is drawn therein is nowhere incomplete, and it endures for a long time without perishing.
That is to say, vast karmic rewards are all born from karma;
when the meritorious karma is exhausted, that pleasure then disperses and perishes.
If one does not abandon what is wholesome, that pleasure will continue to increase.
Therefore, regarding wholesome causes, one should constantly practice them through successive stages.
Throughout hundreds of thousands of births, having received bodies that are but chains of bones,
one is entangled by karma and has never had even the slightest thought of peace and happiness.
If one creates various causes, one will receive various retributions;
therefore, within this very life, one should diligently cultivate all wholesome deeds.
The paintings of karma are most skillfully crafted, for they are all created in dependence upon the mind.
When karma is exhausted, its fruit perishes; it does not abide for even a moment.
One’s own karma alone is one’s true kin; what can be gained from others?
Thoroughly subdue your mind and dwell in accordance with reality.
Adorned by one's own karma, it is not the work of anything else;
throughout hundreds and thousands of births, one has never for a moment abandoned it.
If one thoroughly understands arising and ceasing, as well as the true nature of cause and effect, [one attains liberation].
Thus, one leaves behind all defilements of sin and attains the state of non-extinction.
All karmas that have been created follow one constantly along winding paths,
like spokes depending upon a wheel, as one revolves within the world.
One should discern with wisdom and practice according to the truth;
such a person is a trainer of men who is forever liberated from all afflictions—
namely, the stains of greed, hatred, and delusion, as well as the sufferings of old age, sickness, and death.
These six are like deep-seated enemies, capable of harming all sentient beings.
Furthermore, the five sense objects are like thieves, able to plunder the wealth of merit;
at first they appear like kinsmen and friends, but in the end they become harmful enemies.
Born from the mind, heedlessness rushes wildly toward the objects of desire;
it causes all sentient beings to head toward the realms of hell and hungry ghosts.
Greed is its blazing fire, and hatred is like an enemy.
Darkness is called delusion; these three are all to be feared.
Namely, the thirty-six karmas, the forty formations, and the ninety-eight afflictions, which pervade the three realms.
Detached from the twelve links of dependent origination and the one hundred and eight afflictions,
skillfully understanding what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma, one constantly attains immeasurable bliss;
regarding the sixteen aspects of clear realization and those sixteen kinds of emptiness—
One who has understood the two characteristics of self and dharmas is called a wise person.
Skillfully penetrating the path and what is not the path, as well as those four ultimate goals,
they are liberated from the four torrents and are able to extinguish all stains of sin.
Cultivating the Noble Eightfold Path, One transcends the two kinds of birth-and-death,
Manifests those Ten Powers, And realizes the fruit of Bodhi.
Clarifying the two truths of the ultimate and the conventional, As well as those Four Foundations of Mindfulness,
Having eliminated ignorance regarding the three periods of time, one is not overcome by Māra.
These realms of the five desires are sweet at first but bitter in the end;
they cause one to fall into various perils and difficulties, and for this reason, one should always remain far removed from them.
By reflecting with right wisdom, one subdues and severs all afflictions;
such a person is one endowed with wisdom, who is always secure and at peace in every life.
Wisdom can sever all delusions, just as fire consumes dry wood.
If right wisdom increases and becomes luminous, it causes the Three Jewels to manifest.
If one delights in the realm of wisdom and dwells constantly in the dharma of tranquility,
then the afflictions, like venomous snakes, will be able to destroy all that is wholesome.
If one possesses the vision of reality, one can benefit both oneself and others;
free from the afflictions of old age and death, one dwells in supreme tranquility.
But if one delights in saṃsāra, one will be constantly bound by it.
These afflictions are enemies and bandits, Oppressing all throughout the three realms of existence.
If a person understands the Buddha’s teaching And expounds it for the sake of sentient beings,
Constantly practicing pure conduct, They shall attain rebirth in the Brahma Heaven.
If one feels weary of and detaches from the three poisons, constantly making offerings to all Buddhas,
one will destroy that saṃsāra like burning dry wood.
If a person knows the cause of suffering and does not commit various transgressions, [they shall escape].
Amidst an immeasurable mass of afflictions, nothing has the power to bind him.
Wisdom is the supreme light, while ignorance is the ultimate darkness;
one who can skillfully discern this is called a wise person.
If one is free from the fault of delusion, there will be no perils or difficulties;
yet being shrouded by delusion, how can one attain liberation?
It would be better to touch a fierce fire or dwell together with venomous snakes, than to remain thus obscured.
One who rightly seeks the bliss of tranquility should not dwell with delusion.
The fool lacks right wisdom; like a blind man in the darkness, they do not fear saṃsāra and constantly engage in unrighteous conduct.
Sentient beings, deceived by ignorance, constantly give rise to craving and attachment;
they undergo worldly poverty and are oppressed by aging and decline.
Due to the fruits of karma across the three periods of time, they pass from the hells to birth in the heavens.
Some fall from heaven into the animal realm, while others receive the retribution of hungry ghosts;
driven by that greed, sentient beings follow their karma to the various destinies,
further ensnared by the net of delusion, circling within the ocean of the three realms of existence.
Having committed various sins since beginningless time, one undergoes manifold births and deaths;
due to such habitual practice, weariness has never arisen.
The heavens are impaired by the loss of pleasure, and the human world suffers from the pain of deprivation.
In the hells there is constant burning; among animals they devour one another;
hungry ghosts are oppressed by hunger and thirst—all this is due to that delusion.
Dwelling long in saṃsāra, when has there ever been even a slight measure of happiness?
Fools, attached to sensual pleasures, experience suffering because of those very pleasures;
they do not draw near to virtuous friends and lack the protection of the True Dharma.
If a person possesses truthfulness and always delights in hearing the True Dharma, [they shall find liberation].
Cultivating all meditative concentrations, they are free from sorrow and suffering.
The Buddhas proclaim the True Dharma like a lamp that constantly illuminates;
with loving-kindness for all sentient beings, they surpass even one's own parents.
Sentient beings, due to three causes, Commit three kinds of transgressions;
Cycling through the three realms, The three types of sensation constantly pursue them.
Arisen from the three karmas, They head toward the treacherous perils of the three evil destinies.
Because sentient beings are attached to pleasure, they gallop through the three realms of existence.
If one honors the Triple Gem, one shall attain the three types of enlightenment;
by remaining far removed from the three kinds of views, one will not give rise to any suffering.
Throughout those days and nights, one should constantly observe at the three periods of the day that old age,
sickness, and death are the treasuries of these three kinds of faults.
With the three types of action free from perverse thoughts, one should dwell well in the three equalities.
Not clinging to saṃsāra, forever free from all sorrow and affliction;
regarding that which is the path and that which is not the path, as well as the characteristics of emptiness and existence,
one observes them well with a compassionate mind and shall realize the unsurpassed way.
This person’s mind is pure, untouched by any defiled desires;
forever free from all turbidity, they attain the peace and joy of liberation.
Having abandoned craving for the three realms of existence, they constantly give rise to right mindfulness.
Such a person, regarding the True Path, is certain never to regress.
Sentient beings, obscured by ignorance, do not penetrate wisdom;
they give rise to immeasurable craving and are constantly bound by suffering.
Laziness, lack of shame, and lack of remorse, Associating with evil friends—these are the seeds of hell; The wise guard against them well.
Because of that lack of shame and remorse, One constantly commits manifold transgressions.
Later, falling into perilous paths, one will give rise to regret and distress in vain.
Arising with pride and anger, along with jealousy and concealment of faults,
being foolish and lacking the root of faith— how could such a person be born into a good realm?
Addicted to wine and greedy for wealth, One gives rise to wrong views and false speech;
Constantly practicing cruel and poisonous causes, One will surely invite the retribution of hell.
Wrong views obstruct all virtues; One should not give rise to even a fraction of them.
Such foolish people cast themselves onto perilous and evil paths.
Those who give rise to false views, reckoning what is not a cause to be a cause, deceive and delude themselves; they sink and drown with no prospect of escape.
If a person clings to false views, they practice asceticism in vain;
deceiving and deluding others, their ignorance gives rise to pride.
Due to the darkness of ignorance, they sink into the great ocean of birth and death.
These people lack the correct cause; they seek to abandon suffering through suffering.
Following the teachings of those non-Buddhists, they seek liberation by burning their bodies.
The wise person, however, causes the mind to be scorched, thereby able to burn away all delusions.
If one fully cultivates right knowledge and can destroy all afflictions, they are called a true man;
such a person attains liberation from the bounds of all suffering.
But those who delight in worldly fame and mutually flatter one another—
That pure enlightenment cannot be attained through wrong views.
Failing to apply oneself diligently to the wholesome, with a mind constantly prone to restlessness,
and because of attachment to gain and offerings, one abandons that pure ethical discipline.
Delighting in the taste of wine, Craving the beauty of external forms,
And killing various sentient beings— Because of these, one falls into hell.
Associating with evil friends, Giving rise to wrong views and double-tongued speech,
Failing to attain the various modes of dignified conduct, one’s three karmas are frequently violated.
Due to pride and ignorance, what is spoken lacks truth;
how then can one find happiness in this world or in future lives?
Sunk in the midst of manifold sufferings, here they cease and there they arise again;
as the Buddhas have taught, all this proceeds from ignorance and volitional formations.
If a person gives rise to the conceit of "I," or to false pride and overweening pride, [they remain bound].
This is the root of suffering; one should ultimately and forever distance oneself from it.
Those who delight in committing various evils lack goodness in the beginning, middle, or end;
following that stream of ignorance, they enter the great ocean of birth and death.
If a person possesses supreme wisdom, skillfully pacifying and eliminating the afflictions,
they can untie all bonds and reach the state of non-extinction.
By cultivating supreme wisdom, one is then able to sever all delusions.
This explains the bondage of afflictions, which through wisdom one attains liberation.
All afflictions are like firewood; the fire of wisdom burns them away until they are forever exhausted.
If one delights in the realm of sensory objects, how can one ever escape their entanglements?
The five desires are a heavy miasma that can shroud the eye of wisdom;
they constantly cause all sentient beings to destroy the true path of the Dharma.
Toward those who skillfully preach the Dharma, you should listen with single-minded attention and profound respect.
Such a person is a general of the Dharma, capable of opposing all demonic armies.
If, regarding the four inversions and the eight worldly concerns,
one does not give rise to right wisdom within oneself, then one will be deceived by them.
The five desires are like a swift current; One is swept away and finds it difficult to escape.
One should use the boat and raft of wisdom To be able to transcend them.
Due to that deluded mind, One constantly delights in and clings to all desires.
Within the five realms of saṃsāra, how can one attain liberation?
Improper mental attention is like a fire that burns constantly;
if one acts with proper mental attention, it is like nectar that removes the fever.
That is to say, the accumulated ignorance that has arisen from time immemorial is destroyed and rendered non-apparent by the single lamp of wisdom.
If a person possesses right knowledge, they can proceed toward Nirvana.
When lacking wisdom, one gives rein to greed and delusion, and thus gives rise to indolence.
If one possesses the light of wisdom, one destroys the darkness of the three poisons;
therefore, with a single mind, one should uphold the precepts and cultivate pure knowledge.
Always with the fire of great wisdom, one burns away the fuel of all delusions;
if one lacks these roots of goodness, one will be harmed by the three poisons.
Sentient beings are entangled in chronic illness, lying prostrate as their lives draw to a close.
Deluded and without refuge, their kinfolk grieve in vain.
Because they have practiced much negligence and always delighted in ignorant conduct,
they become causes for immeasurable evil and are oppressed by manifold sufferings.
These three poisons are afflictions that harm and distress all sentient beings;
yet when one is in accord with right wisdom, they are entirely eliminated.
Know that the fire of that wisdom can incinerate the mountain of afflictions.
Since both delusion and karma are now exhausted, one shall dwell eternally in the bliss of tranquility.
It is said that because of such mental engagement, one constantly commits various evils;
being ignorant and lacking understanding, one needlessly gives rise to regret.
Sentient beings commit various transgressions And all receive bitter retributions;
Therefore, one should distance oneself from them And constantly seek the fruits of happiness.
Though at first one commits but a small sin, In the end, one falls into perilous paths.
Obscured by delusion, they emerge from meditation only to create [evil] once more;
failing to guard against even minor transgressions, these all become causes for hell,
just as a tiny spark can burn down a mountain forest.
From sin one is born into the evil realms, Where one undergoes most grievous suffering and affliction.
Since that [sin] is like an enemy to oneself, How can one attain tranquility?
If a person commits various transgressions, Then there will not be even the slightest happiness.
If you desire to seek happiness, you should cultivate all wholesome deeds.
Those who do good are praised as "well done," while those who commit evil are universally reviled.
To cultivate merit is indeed difficult; how easy it is to fall into transgression!
If one sees another commit an unrighteous act and gives rise to an inferior mind of sympathetic joy,
because of that lack of wisdom, the suffering one undergoes shall exceed even this.
If a person creates various sins and accumulates their various retributions,
This suffering is difficult to endure; one should not commit evil deeds.
Because of the many evils one has created, one will certainly receive their retribution.
Therefore, one should keep far away from them; by not committing them, there will be no fault.
If one does not fear any transgressions, one will associate with evil friends;
because of what one has created oneself, the resulting fruit is not experienced by another.
Performing good brings forth good fruit; committing evil receives an evil retribution.
If one commits various transgressions, there will be no goodness within them.
If a person clings to false views, they will give rise to all manner of sins in succession;
even swords, staves, and pits of fire cannot compare to that.
If a person leaves behind all evils, constantly cultivates virtuous conduct,
and keeps body, speech, and mind pure, they are not far from Bodhi.
If one delights in committing various evils, one will undergo extreme and heavy suffering.
One cannot obtain a pleasant fruit by committing evil deeds.
If one joyfully cultivates all manner of virtues, one will attain the highest happiness;
these virtues are not causes of suffering, for there is no experiencing them through delusion.
Since beginningless eons, performing good brings the reward of happiness;
if one creates those evil causes, one will certainly obtain the fruit of suffering.
By doing good, one becomes close to virtuous friends; by committing sins, one draws near to evil companions.
Those who harbor hatred and envy toward virtuous and good people will fall into evil realms.
If the mind delights in cultivating goodness, one remains far removed from all evils;
for such a person, awakening is no further away than the palm of their hand.
That which is well-performed in its beginning, middle, and end, can produce a joyful retribution; otherwise, it cannot.
Therefore, distance yourself from all transgressions and cause goodness to continue in constant succession.
Those who are able to distance themselves from such evil will always obtain happiness.
Within the beginningless cycle of birth and death, they have repeatedly undergone various sufferings;
yet, driven by the delusion of the foolish, they feel no weariness or revulsion.
Attached to desire, one commits various evils, unaware of their bitter fruits hereafter;
though a momentary pleasure arises, one suffers affliction for a long time.
Those who delight in committing transgressions are universally despised by the world.
Therefore, abandon all evils and do not let goodness decline.
That which is unbeneficial is not ultimate; it brings about the most supreme suffering.
For this reason, the wise person always remains far removed from transgression.
If a person possesses a mind of loving-kindness, they will not commit any transgressions;
for evil brings calamity upon oneself, and what is not done is not suffered.
Constantly creating various sins and evils by relying on false teachers and false teachings—
If one is free from those two kinds [of faults] and abides well in the true path,
the fool does not perceive this; delighting in the commission of various evil deeds,
yet if one is free from those transgressions, one will always be born in superior realms.
If one delights in committing various evils, one will certainly be dragged away by karma;
fearing not the subsequent cycle of rebirth, one finds it difficult to regain a human body.
If a person fears all evils and greatly delights in performing various virtues, [they shall attain liberation].
They can proceed toward enlightenment and attain the most supreme and wondrous bliss.
If one can distance oneself from all faults and cultivate all virtuous deeds,
such a person shall obtain the foremost reward of merit within this world.
Having well subdued the sense faculties, one is respected by the world;
upon exhausting this present physical body, one will attain rebirth among the devas.
If a person has little merit and lacks goodness in the beginning, middle, and end, [they shall not do so].
When evil constantly increases, one falls into hell.
If one commits various transgressions, one brings upon oneself their bitter fruit;
if one performs good as it is seen [to be done], one will certainly receive the retribution of happiness.
From the seeds of unwholesome deeds, one is later born into peril and hardship;
as was the karma performed in the past, so too are cause and effect alike.
That sentient beings fall into the evil realms is entirely summoned by their own transgressions.
Just as a fish that has swallowed a hook can find no way to escape, so too is sin the root of suffering; it must ultimately be severed and abandoned.
Sentient beings are constantly defiled by habitual tendencies, like those who possess impurities that follow them everywhere.
One should constantly practice what is to be cherished, for it can destroy all evil karma;
just as when sesame seeds are pressed, the fragrance of the flower does not vanish.
Those who always delight in and cling to the five sensual pleasures are distracted and lack patience.
For those who are indolent and speak falsehoods, there will certainly be no goodness.
Those who commit various evils are like the darkness of the long night;
those who abide securely in wholesome dharmas are like the rising of the sun.
If a person is free from envy, this constitutes virtuous and pure conduct;
yet the foolish commit manifold transgressions and remain constantly in a state of anger.
Just as a boat carrying few goods can float wherever it goes, so too is one who is light in burden.
If the transgressions of sentient beings are light, they shall avoid sinking into the various evils.
By staying far away from evil associates, one constantly attains all forms of happiness;
yet if one follows them, one will undergo all manner of perilous hardships.
Thoroughly understanding the retribution of karma, One leaves behind even subtle transgressions;
Such a person is not stained by faults, Just as mud cannot defile the sky.
They cause those who have not heard to hear, And having heard, they are able to remember.
If even those in the evil realms can still be reborn in heaven, how much more so for one possessed of wisdom?
