Cháo-sàn-dàfū, Míngliǎo Zuìfúxiàng; this is for those who possess wisdom.
Lacking correct understanding in this regard is the work of ignorance.
One who thoroughly masters all virtues and likewise regarding faults—
knowing both as they truly are— constantly attains a share of happiness.
If one commits various transgressions, it is like dwelling with an enemy;
if one delights in practicing virtuous benefit, it is like being near a good friend.
Through the creation of passionate attachments, objects of perception constantly manifest before one.
Wandering through the darkness of delusion, they constantly undergo all manner of agonizing torments.
The realm of desire is like a dense forest where craving constantly roams;
since the foolish do not comprehend the Dharma, by what means could they ever achieve liberation?
Falling into that hell, one undergoes manifold sufferings through union with others;
know this: had one not committed evil deeds, there would be no way to arrive here.
By practicing virtue, one obtains superior retribution, adorned with immeasurable merit.
Committing evil brings calamity upon oneself; one can certainly not escape it.
Regarding the suffering and happiness of self and others, they circulate within the ocean of the three realms of existence, driven by the winds of karma, just as waves depend upon water.
If a person is born into negligence, constantly committing various evils,
by reason of these causes and conditions, they shall fall into hell.
Once released from hell, they will be born among other realms of existence.
Furthermore, being dragged by desire, one forgets the suffering previously endured.
This mind, due to habitual practice, returns to delusion as soon as it briefly awakens;
when pleasure perishes, suffering arises again, yet one does not contemplate future calamities.
Deceived by the five faculties, they become deranged and invade the domains of others;
they undergo endless cycles of transmigration, all due to the fetters of craving.
They fall into the realms of hell-beings and hungry ghosts, or among animals and the borderlands.
Or one may briefly be born among the devas, only to fall back into calamity in an instant.
Undergoing the cycle of rebirth through the various realms, like the wheel of a worldly chariot,
all are pulled by the牵引 (karmic habituation), yet no weariness or revulsion arises.
Even if one is born among the gods and experiences the most exquisite pleasures, when merit is exhausted, one falls back down; all these are the workings of saṃsāra.
One may fall into the Lotus Hell for hundreds of thousands of koṭis of times.
They undergo immeasurable suffering and affliction, yet in their folly they feel neither weariness nor fear.
In the three realms there is no joy; all are oppressed by suffering.
Sentient beings are blinded by ignorance and have never once harbored anxiety or dread.
Fools are deluded regarding the cause of suffering and cannot comprehend it;
this suffering arises from causes, just as seeds produce their fruit.
Bound by pleasure and pain, they wander back and forth through the three realms of existence.
Except for the bliss of quiescent extinction, which forever leaves behind all sorrow and affliction;
if, wherever one is born, one is able to contemplate all sufferings,
then such suffering will not arise again, and by being free from suffering, one attains peace and security.
If one can recollect the suffering and affliction within the hells,
then one will not be attached even to the slightest portion of those worldly pleasures.
Having understood this, one realizes that the entire world is entirely false and illusory.
One should distance oneself from all faults and evils, Cultivating practice well through wisdom.
Life does not endure for long; In a mere instant, a single kṣaṇa, One must sever those evil causes And constantly practice all manner of virtues.
Realizing that the duration of life is not firm, and that all things are created by the mind through the performance of right conduct, one should not seek a wrong livelihood;
why then do you not give rise to fear regarding the suffering of future lives?
The noose of delusion constantly entangles, and the fires of hell perpetually burn and boil.
Delusion is an unwholesome dharma; it opposes pure and meritorious deeds, leading evil sentient beings to sink ever deeper into the ocean of suffering.
If a person does not fear sin and delights in committing many evils,
they will pass from one hell to another, scorched by the fires of hell.
Just as even a tiny spark of fire can burn all manner of things, so too does the fire of karma consume the sinner.
Even if a fool commits but a small amount of sin, he shall fall into hell.
If a person fears the evil realms, they will not commit various sinful deeds;
they can embrace the True Dharma, abandoning evil and following what is good.
Evil friends give rise to negligence and provoke shamelessness and lack of remorse;
the wise always distance themselves from them, for they are like fire and like poison.
Unwholesome dharmas act as demonic obstacles, while wholesome dharmas are free from all hindrance.
Through skillful discernment of these two, one attains complete penetration of all things.
Stay far away from evil associates; delight in the extensive practice of generosity and patience;
and maintain loving-kindness toward all sentient beings—these are the essential practices for rebirth in heaven.
If a person lives by wrong livelihood and commits various evil deeds,
I shall now describe their retribution: they will later fall into the hells,
namely Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, and the two Rauravas.
Blazing and fiercely burning, such as the Avīci Hell and others—
these eight hells each have one gate on every side,
and at each individual hell-gate, four hells form the city walls.
Iron walls encircle it on all sides, filled with those who have committed evil;
the hell-wardens impale the sinners like fish boiling in cauldrons;
they rain down mountains, stones, and weapons, hacking and severing their bodies into pieces.
Constantly weeping day and night, they are made to drink molten copper out of thirst;
oppressed by extreme suffering, they let out great cries and roars,
undergoing various punishments as they flee and run toward the four quarters.
If a person is shrouded by delusion, they will perversely give rise to various evil views;
the causes for that hellish realm are as deep and vast as the ocean.
These inferior and evil views bring harm to both oneself and others.
Through immeasurable causes and conditions of suffering, you have bound yourself.
Because of your attachment to false views, you rely on yourself to give rise to arrogance;
thus you fall forever into the evil realms, enduring extreme suffering for a long time.
Because you committed those evil deeds, you have now come to this place;
O base and foolish person, why do you harbor such grief and fear?
To commit evil while hoping for a good reward—such a thing is impossible.
Planting seeds in a deep abyss will surely yield no fruit or benefit.
If a person, despite being foolish, repeatedly associates with such [evil companions] for the sake of their meager pleasures, they will later undergo great suffering.
Fools falsely regard as pleasure their attachment to wife and children;
the arising of defiled afflictions is entirely due to the deluded mind of craving.
When one's own life comes to an end, not a single one among them can provide rescue or protection.
Proceeding alone upon a perilous and evil path, they depart for eternity in misery.
Furthermore, within those hells, there are originally no instruments of suffering;
these arise from the transformations of the minds of sentient beings who have committed evil.
Just as when a wondrous incense is burned, its fragrance suddenly wafts away without form;
or like a flock of birds that roost together at night and scatter again at dawn.
Or perhaps one seizes the wealth of others, or harms their bodies and lives.
The commission of these most unwholesome deeds is entirely due to delusion.
Because of that delusion, one passes from darkness into further darkness,
losing the right conduct for rebirth in heaven as well as the supreme tranquility.
Those wives, children, and kinsmen are bonds from which it is difficult to escape;
one is submerged in the ocean of birth and death, without any refuge or protection.
Driven by craving, they commit manifold evils—what can be gained for one's wife and children?
And when one personally undergoes bitter suffering, what do they each know?
Throughout immeasurable lifetimes, they have constantly craved and clung to beautiful forms;
because of this, they have committed various transgressions, base and shameless.
Having first committed those evil deeds, If one later feels no remorse,
One will certainly fall into hell, With no time of escape for long kalpas.
Though one’s relatives be numerous, How can they possibly save oneself?
Seeing others who are attached to desire, their retribution is likewise so.
When one practices wholesome deeds oneself, one will surely bring about their pleasant fruit;
yet the foolish are shrouded by delusion and have no awakening to this at all.
If one is shrouded by delusion, greed and hatred will likewise arise;
what is loved will belong to another, and one's own suffering cannot be avoided.
Internally scorched by the three poisons, one is externally surrounded by the fires of hell.
Suffering bitter torments for long eons, when will you escape the evil realms?
Having created all manner of evils with your own mind, you never felt shame;
now, scorched by the fires of hell, what is the use of weeping in vain?
You all are extremely dull-witted and delight in practicing what is unrighteous;
you need not give rise to regret, for you should endure suffering with equanimity.
When a fool commits various transgressions, he feels alarm and fear once they have been committed.
Karmic fruits always follow; all arise from causes and conditions.
If one has never cultivated what is good and cannot sever what is evil, yet manages to leave that evil behind, one will no longer see the hells.
If a person is shrouded by delusion and fails to understand the fruits of karma,
being led astray by a false teacher, their transgressions will only increase further.
Out of fear for the sins previously committed, they will constantly give rise to burning anguish.
Without the remedy of the True Dharma, one will ultimately be oppressed by suffering.
If one can distance oneself from all faults, one shall have no share in suffering;
abiding in right mindfulness and reflection, one should not commit any transgressions.
If one delights in committing various evils, one will never grow weary of suffering;
adding suffering upon suffering, by what means can one escape?
If the mind does not give rise to weariness toward affliction, how can there be any tranquility?
Toward sentient beings who commit offenses, I do not give rise to compassion.
You are bound by delusion and have performed those unrighteous deeds;
since you created those causes yourself, I am not able to save you.
Having accumulated those deluded actions, one becomes completely filled with evil;
unable to maintain pure precepts, who can escape the retribution of suffering?
If a person creates unwholesome karma, they will receive its fruit according to its cause.
One should know that the causes and conditions of suffering are created by oneself and experienced by oneself.
Bound by the snares of craving, you are maddened and devoid of shame;
as you undergo the most perilous punishments, that suffering is beyond description.
If one commits various evils, one will then undergo all manner of agonizing torments;
if one does not commit them, one will not suffer them, for without a cause there is no retribution.
Such are the various calamities, the fruit of which lies in hell.
Among all wholesome dharmas, they never gave rise to joy;
they did not cultivate meritorious deeds, but instead committed immeasurable evils.
Their retribution was likewise so; the foolish man merely suffers in regret and distress.
Abandoning all virtuous people, one practices much deceit;
failing to cultivate the cause of truth, one cannot obtain happiness.
One accumulates a multitude of karmic stains, arising from a mind of ignorance.
Suffering extreme agony for long eons, all is due to what was created in the past.
Sentient beings in the hells are seized and imprisoned by the hell-wardens;
as they are harshly rebuked, [they hear: "When your karma is exhausted, you shall depart."
Furthermore, those foolish people, deceived by their own minds, do not understand the karma they have created;
they are consumed by anxiety and filled with sorrow.
They mistake what is unbeneficial for what is good, and treat virtuous friends as if they were enemies.
They bring ruin to themselves and others, and dwell perpetually in great darkness.
Those evil deeds of the three poisons are no different from deep-seated enmity;
they are able to drag all sentient beings to the abode of Yama.
From what cause does this delusion arise?
It arises entirely from the conception of "mine.
If one does not cultivate practices such as generosity, by what means can one be delivered?
Sin is the foremost enemy; it manifests throughout the evil realms, never abandoning one in this life or in future births.
All the evils one has committed are like sharp blades, poison, and fire.
The perilous and evil are most fearsome; having committed them, you shall surely suffer their consequences.
If one’s mind is tranquil, does not cling to sensory objects, and does not follow the ways of delusion, then one will be free from evil retribution.
Hearing the sounds of suffering in hell, the ignorant and dark-minded feel no fear;
they are like those who take dry firewood and cast it into a great conflagration.
Furthermore, while the fires of the world burn, their flames will eventually be extinguished after a long time.
One should know that the fire of karma burns fiercely for a long time;
while the power of ordinary fire can be extinguished, the fire of karma continues perpetually.
If one commits evil deeds, one will ultimately be consumed by it.
Therefore, the fire of that karma constantly burns the denizens of hell;
those who do not fear the evil realms cannot escape this harm.
One should discern with wisdom and guard oneself well.
By staying far away from those evil karmas, one will not undergo various sufferings.
Covered by ignorance, one constantly commits manifold evils;
now that one undergoes this extreme suffering, lamenting in grief is but in vain.
That which pertains to the beginning, middle, and end, as well as the limit of the exhaustion of suffering—
the cause of suffering and its fruit— are all not to be relished.
Having formerly existed among humans, one extensively committed various evil karmas.
This perilous and evil retribution has been summoned; you must now undergo it yourself.
Free from inverted discrimination, cause and effect are ever in accord:
as one has acted in the past, so one receives the fruit according to karma.
Since you are able to always cherish and protect your own body,
why do you give rise to the karma of killing, waiting to sever the life-span of others?
You sought wealth and profit from them, enduring all manner of hardships.
Why do you give rise to the intent to plunder the wealth of others?
You protect your own wives and concubines with single-minded devotion;
why then do you harbor thoughts of aggression and violence toward the women of others?
You have committed the sin of speaking falsehoods, deceiving the virtuous and causing others to lose their trust; that tongue of yours is most terrifying.
You delighted in the sin of drinking alcohol, which leads to the arising of delusion and dullness.
You have invited unlawful slander; why did you not distance yourself from it?
These five kinds of evils were all committed by you in the past;
now that you undergo this evil retribution, why do you grieve in vain?
Unwholesome dharmas are like poison; one should always remain far removed from them, for they cause all sentient beings to sink ever deeper into the ocean of suffering.
Furthermore, that fire of craving blazes fiercely throughout the three realms of existence.
Seeing a beneficial opportunity yet failing to cultivate it, how can one obtain future happiness?
Speaking words of clever smiles and chatter increases craving;
this is a great fault that must be severed without remainder.
Having fallen into that hell, they raise their voices and wail loudly;
the hell-wardens all say to them:
"You receive this according to your causes."
Not distancing oneself from various evils, but committing them again after having done so, causes those causes to increase; the retribution one receives is likewise.
If you fear the suffering of the future, you should cultivate all manner of goodness in the present.
Then there would be no retribution in hell, nor would there be any lamentation.
Heedlessness is like that ground, from which all manner of unwholesome states arise;
immeasurable sentient beings are all dragged away by craving.
In the past you committed many sins, Giving rise to evil deeds such as greed;
The fool does not understand this— Who can take the suffering upon themselves for you!
Failing to give rise to a heart of compassion, You wander along with all the currents of evil.
In this boundless ocean of suffering, by what means can one be delivered?
Wealth, possessions, and those one loves—all must be abandoned at the end of life;
yet because of having committed these manifold sins, one is pursued by the wardens of hell.
A mass of most fierce and evil fires fills the entirety of space, extending even to the earth and its regions, blazing with unceasing intensity.
This suffering is unbearable to behold; in such terror, where can one go?
Sharp blades are his path; he is driven along to tread upon them.
The perils are as vast as the ocean; he journeys alone without a companion.
When shall he attain liberation? Who among us can rescue him?
Oppressed by suffering, exhausted and unable to proceed,
I am seized and bound by them and dragged away;
my wife, children, and kinsmen, upon reaching this state, all become like enemies.
Though one may possess immeasurable wealth and treasures, Even by begging for protection, one cannot escape.
Because of past negligence, What was once enjoyed turns into suffering upon its destruction.
Dragged by the snare of death, Into the dark and vast void, where shall one go?
Those jailers of Yama are extremely violent, wicked, and wrathful;
they bind and humiliate [the sinner], causing the mind to give rise to great terror.
As I observe that evil place, there are various forms of suffering and punishment.
All sentient and insentient beings are engulfed by fierce flames.
Furthermore, great venomous serpents surround them on all sides;
they wail in grief seeking liberation, yet have no refuge and no savior.
Falling into the dark hells, vast and deep as the great ocean,
how could one behold the light of the stars and planets in space throughout long kalpas?
It is because those five faculties give rise to perverted craving and attachment.
Cycling through the three realms of existence,
by what means could one attain tranquility? With every limb and member severed by sharp saws,
the immeasurable and extreme suffering cannot be fully expressed in words.
Accumulated sins are like mountains; Constantly surrounded by manifold sufferings, They increase with every passing thought; The mind creates them, and the body receives them.
Subjected to the extreme oppression of suffering, Its bitterness and acrimony are known only to oneself.
Yama commanded him, saying:
"Observe what you have done in the past.
If you fully understand your own transgressions, you will be able to endure your suffering."
Until karma is exhausted, one must contemplate each [action] accordingly.
Previously, you were shrouded by delusion; now, you produce only regret and distress.
You created such causes, and thus you yourself undergo such results.
Arising from remorse, one commits grave and heavy offenses,
falling into perilous and difficult calamities, and experiencing the most extreme suffering among all sufferings.
When a fool has committed a sin, it is like throwing fuel into a fire.
From kalpa to kalpa, one may eventually emerge once karma is exhausted;
yet neither the devas nor the asuras, nor the yakṣas, ghosts, and spirits,
can rescue me when I am ensnared by the noose of death.
Bound by those cords, they are dragged before Yama;
terrified and without refuge, they follow wherever their karma leads.
To be free from the faults of desire is the most supreme state within the three realms.
Having liberated yourself from all bonds, you shall not commit any further sins.
If [this body] is a composite of causes and conditions, first obtained from your father—
who underwent such arduous labor for your sake— why do you commit the act of killing?
Furthermore, the crime of killing one's mother is an evil karma beyond compare;
one falls into the hells and undergoes the most intense suffering.
One who has severed the fetters of the three realms of existence is called an Arhat.
Out of delusion you committed acts of killing, and now you receive this bitter retribution.
You revealed the treasury of all dharmas and the gateway to liberation;
yet you caused a schism in the Saṃgha, and now you receive this bitter retribution.
Constantly uttering false and deceptive words, pointing east while speaking of the north,
their speech lacking sincerity and trustworthiness, they now undergo this bitter retribution.
Furthermore, they gave rise to frivolous speech, destroying the treasure of truth.
Benefiting neither oneself nor others, one now undergoes this retribution of suffering.
Having given rise to the evil karma of divisive speech,
slandering one another and alienating their kinsmen and friends, one now undergoes this retribution of suffering.
Speaking meaningless and evil words is like swords, staves, poison, or fire;
it causes others to give rise to feverish affliction, and now one receives this bitter retribution.
To protect and cherish one's own body and life while harming all sentient beings—[this is the cause of such suffering].
Lacking a heart of constant compassion, one now undergoes this retribution of suffering.
Having stolen or plundered the precious wealth of others,
indulging it as a cause for the five desires, one now undergoes this retribution of suffering.
Delighting in sexual misconduct is like adding fuel to a fire;
it constantly gives rise to a mind of doubt and fear, increasing all manner of unwholesome states.
Clinging to false views damages the roots of virtue in others.
One receives endless retribution for evil, experiencing the foremost of sufferings.
These various evil realms—you, in your folly, have followed along with them;
they were all created through the body, speech, and mind acting in concert.
Having committed those various evils, when life ends, suffering manifests before them;
driven by the wardens of hell, they quickly hasten toward the hells.
This torment of the hells is extremely difficult to endure.
Even if the ocean were deep and vast, it might be consumed by fire and dried up;
yet if a person understands that all evils are undesirable because of their causes and effects,
they should always maintain right reflection and never commit a transgression.
The Triple Gem of Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha possesses all virtues in perfection;
having attained birth among human beings, why can you not draw near to them?
When one first commits even a minute transgression, it is like being burned by a small fire.
Later, you extensively created causes of evil, like casting yourself into a mass of fire.
Now, though you are filled with anxiety and fear regarding your transgressions, your mind does not cease its various evils;
you constantly contemplate receiving the retribution of suffering—what more will you do now?
One should know that even a minor offense can give rise to manifold sufferings;
only when karma is exhausted will one escape, for there is no other who can provide rescue.
Those messengers of Yama examine the case and then release accordingly.
If the retribution for evil deeds is not yet exhausted, one is dragged back to undergo manifold sufferings.
As for their bodies and limbs, they are split apart and hacked off;
countless sinful sentient beings give rise to grief and lamentation, crying out in woe.
Furthermore, there are evil sentient beings who frequently engage in divisive speech;
like a single seed that later grows into countless [plants],
all this arises from their own wicked wisdom and gives birth to strife and discord.
Toward relatives and friends, they cause total estrangement;
constantly rejecting all virtuous words, they delight in uttering evil speech.
Their tongues shall be cut off, for cause and effect are ever like unto one another.
A hundred thousand gateways of merit are destroyed by the tongue;
now one undergoes this bitter retribution—when will liberation be attained?
Having fallen into that hell, extreme heat gives rise to hunger and thirst.
It is like throwing a mustard seed into a mass of fire as large as Mount Sumeru;
likewise, the fires of that hell arise from hunger and thirst,
and when the various devas fall, they undergo retribution in this same manner.
All the various evil karmas created arise from the three poisons;
amidst their ever-turning fierce flames, there is no place to hide, conceal oneself, or flee.
Sentient beings lacking wisdom falsely give rise to conceptual discrimination.
They misrepresent the unwholesome as wholesome, and treat a true friend like an enemy.
Why is it that all sentient beings do not awaken to the true Dharma?
Even when it is revealed to them, their hearts feel no love or joy for it.
Taking no delight in hearing the True Dharma, And disparaging the teachers of the Dharma,
In this turbid and evil world, By what means could the eye of wisdom arise?
Within the realm of the foolish, Craving and desire perpetually cause delusion.
Not relying on the true Dharma and Vinaya, one cannot attain self-awakening without cause;
dragged by the ropes of delusion, one constantly delights in committing various evils;
having committed them, one undergoes extreme suffering, only to give rise in vain to grief and regret.
Due to excessive delusion, they proclaim what is not the Dharma to be the Dharma;
since their cause is inverted, they practice erroneously and study in confusion.
Lacking the wisdom of discernment, they are addicted to the five desires.
Failing to cultivate what is wholesome, they follow after evil upon seeing it.
The gods, their minds attached to pleasure, cast themselves into the fire of negligence;
failing to encounter superior and wholesome conditions, they then fall into decline.
Furthermore, those foolish people harbor envy toward the virtuous;
they feign various dignified manners to deceive others for the sake of gain.
Though their mouths speak the true Dharma, their hearts constantly watch for the faults of others.
Such a person is the most wicked in the world.
If one is attached to sensual pleasures, they are merely seeking suffering;
deceived by their own minds, it is the destruction of their own happiness that they experience, not another's.
Therefore, with right wisdom, one should constantly cultivate the ten wholesome actions;
as for all that is not meaningful or beneficial, one should ultimately and forever sever them.
Delighting in benefiting others, one should bind the mind to this task without ever abandoning it for a moment.
One should always rely on pure and wholesome dharmas and abide in them accordingly.
If a person does not practice giving, it is like seeking light without a lamp;
having abandoned virtuous karma, how could there be any joyful retribution?
Just as those blind in this world see nothing at all, so too,
without the cause of merit through giving, one shall fall into the realm of hungry ghosts.
Falling among the destitute spirits, one searches everywhere for sustenance.
Constantly oppressed by hunger and thirst, all is brought about by the influence of stinginess.
If one delights in practicing generosity, nothing can destroy it;
yet if one does not create even a small cause now, one will later give rise to regret in vain.
Due to evil karma committed in the past, one falls into the realm of hungry ghosts;
scorched and roasted by the fires of hell, one suffers hunger and thirst for a long time.
When will one leave that realm and briefly obtain happiness?
In what eon will one attain liberation and thus cast off all burning afflictions?
Failing to understand cause and effect, as well as the path and what is not the path,
one is oppressed by the fire of hunger, and the continuity of suffering remains unbroken.
With an ugly form and disheveled hair, joined together only by sinews and skin,
they long for various foods and drinks, yet upon seeing them, have no means to obtain them.
Oppressed by manifold sufferings, they fall into various evil and perilous difficulties.
There has never been a kinsman or friend who could provide me even momentary relief.
In former times among human beings, you cut off the performance of all meritorious deeds;
like reaching a treasure island and returning alone with empty hands.
If one delights in cultivating sublime practices and always remains far from those various evils,
I observe that such a virtuous person treads the gradual steps leading to rebirth in heaven.
Because they commit various unwholesome deeds through body, speech, and mind, [they fall].
All kinsmen have departed, and one dwells alone in suffering.
Seized and bound by the messengers of Yama,
one is driven away into deep darkness, to a place most remote.
In all places, I have constantly experienced various sufferings and afflictions;
even for the briefest moment, there has never been the slightest bit of joy.
That I now undergo this retribution is entirely due to what was done in the past.
When shall we be freed from this suffering and attain a place of bliss?
Driven by thirst, we labor in vain upon that high plateau;
though we see rivers and ponds, they have all dried up by the time we reach them.
In the wilderness and mountain forests, they searched everywhere;
they endured the hardships of thirst and exhaustion, yet could find no water.
Even at places where moisture might be found, they were unable to see it.
Furthermore, there are great crows and vultures with sharp beaks that peck and devour them.
Driven by the fires of hunger and thirst, their bodies are constantly tormented;
they wallow within the perilous path, crying out in search of rescue and protection.
In the past, you were close to the realm of desire; it was like an image in a mirror.
Having squandered your own precious wealth, you now alone undergo this retribution.
Because of having committed those karmic acts, you are ensnared and find it difficult to escape.
Running hither and thither in the four directions, one shall be liberated when karma is exhausted.
Born from the three poisons, this mass of most evil and fierce fire constantly blazes at every moment;
it is capable of incinerating even massive boulders.
Furthermore, when fire burns that stone, it can be extinguished by pouring water;
but the fire of my karma is like the ocean—how could it ever be extinguished, given its depth and breadth?
Evil karma is like the fuel, and the wind of craving fans it into being.
It burns those sinful sentient beings, leaving no way to escape on any side.
Having committed various transgressions and strayed from wholesome dharmas,
I have fallen into that world of hungry ghosts, deceived by my own mind.
For the sake of that hunger and thirst, I am constantly scorched by two fires;
Furthermore, wounded and mangled by blades and staves, I undergo three kinds of extreme suffering.
Having committed various evil karmas, I have fallen into the realm of hungry ghosts.
Neither kinsmen nor friends are able to provide rescue;
only those wholesome dharmas serve as my refuge— namely, generosity,
ethical discipline, and extensive learning— these three being my protection.
Even until now, I have committed various causes of extreme evil and suffering;
fallen into the net of ignorance, I have long been submerged in the ocean of misery.
Subjected to most grievous burning afflictions, it is truly difficult to endure and impossible to bear.
If I can attain liberation, I shall no longer commit even the slightest transgression.
Within that realm of hungry ghosts, one constantly gives rise to great sorrow and fear;
because this is the cause of unwholesomeness, one should therefore distance oneself from it.
Those who suffer the retribution of animal birth are bound, tethered, and beaten;
as long as they do not sever the causal conditions for killing, they will be born again to devour one another.
The deluded person, their mind clouded by craving, delights in inflicting harm.
Failing to cultivate the causes of generosity and precepts, one later receives the retribution of an animal.
Bound by the cords of craving, with the five faculties like those of a fool or a mute,
harboring anger, resentment, hatred, and jealousy, one later receives the retribution of an animal.
What should be done and what should not be done, what may be eaten and what may not be eaten—
regarding both wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, they lack complete understanding.
Beings in the human realm are full of seeking, while those in the heavens are attached to heedlessness.
Hungry ghosts suffer from hunger and thirst; hell is nothing but extreme agony.
If a person delights in killing sentient beings, they will encounter all manner of perilous suffering and shall inevitably bring about mutual slaughter.
Furthermore, all sentient beings, being largely stingy and distracted,
will by reason of these causes and conditions fall into the realms of hungry ghosts and animals.
Those afflictions of the three poisons drown all living beings.
Experiencing the cycle of birth and death, one finds it deep, perilous, and difficult to escape.
If one joyfully seeks the True Dharma, then all wholesome fruits will arise;
endowed with that luminous wisdom, one will be revered by others.
Therefore, those possessed of wisdom delight in cultivating pure karma;
attending to their thoughts in accordance with reality, they ascend the true path to liberation.
Those who delight in doing what is unbeneficial enslave and exploit all sentient beings.
Nothing compares to hunger as the cause for summoning base suffering.
Crying out in search of food and drink, fire breaks forth from their own bodies and burns those sinful beings, just like burning dry wood.
This fire pervades every direction; wherever one goes, it follows.
Even if one were to pass through a hundred kalpas, nothing but food can provide relief.
Though the fire of the world is scorching hot, the fire of hunger exceeds it even more.
Racing through the three realms of existence, one finds nothing at all when seeking food.
Furthermore, sentient beings in the world constantly give rise to various faults;
for the sake of food and drink, they sink and drown in the ocean of the three realms.
Dwelling within those three realms of existence, one is dragged away by the pull of karma;
for a long time one undergoes bitter torment, a suffering that can never be fully described.
Abiding within the womb, one is submerged in filth and impurity.
Oppressed by affliction and tormented by heat, this suffering is inexhaustible when described.
Attached to the realm of desires and delighting in exquisite adornments, they undergo hardships in their greedy pursuit; this suffering is inexhaustible when described.
Constantly visiting the houses of others to beg for food and clothing, one is treated with contempt and disdain; this suffering is inexhaustible when described.
Driven by the poison of craving, one exhausts oneself in the search.
Until the end of one's life, this suffering is said to be inexhaustible.
Clinging greedily to the objects of desire, various enemies watch for their opportunity;
the mind is constantly filled with dread—this suffering is said to be inexhaustible.
Because of one's wife and children, much sorrow and grief arise;
they are the foremost enemies, and their suffering is inexhaustible to describe.
Precious wealth is wasted in vain, and one is censured and reviled by kinsmen and friends.
From this arises sorrow and affliction; this suffering is said to be inexhaustible.
The body changes and grows old; one walks slowly, leaning upon a staff.
Physical strength suddenly becomes exhausted and frail; this suffering is said to be inexhaustible.
All that one has cherished throughout life is abandoned at the moment of death;
departing alone with nothing to rely upon, this suffering is beyond description.
Fools commit various transgressions and fall into the miserable realms.
All arise from the cause of food and drink; this is what the wise warn against.
Understanding that these are the retributions of karma, one’s mind should give rise to fear;
one should joyfully cultivate generosity and precepts, adorning oneself with manifold virtues.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master from India during the Zhao San Dafu era:
It is because of that inferior wisdom that one gives rise to indolence,
delights in practicing frivolous discourse, and remains far removed from right knowledge.
Abandoning virtuous friends and delighting in associating with evil companions,
acting as a cause for the destruction of the Dharma— this is called wrong livelihood.
Not knowing the proper time and place, nor those various difficult circumstances,
One should not say that what is being spoken is [truly] spoken; the mind constantly gives rise to sorrow and fear.
Without avoiding censure and reproach, one constantly goes out to beg for food;
yet one is despised by others and delights in praising one's own virtues.
Giving rise to excessive greed and delusion, Producing agitation, wrong pride,
and deep attachment to the five desires, The mind does not rely upon the true teaching.
Contradicting the king’s commands, They constantly harbor anger and resentment.
Mentally deranged and having lost right mindfulness, they die an untimely death.
Having distanced themselves from the teacher of the Dharma, they fail to discern what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma;
though the virtuous instruct and exhort them, they give rise to anger and revile them.
Those who crave food and drink, and are constantly attached to sleep—
such sinful beings shall fall into hell.
But those who are resolutely diligent can produce the fruit of happiness.
Therefore, relying upon the True Dharma, one should attain wholesome fruits.
If indolence is taken as the basis, three kinds of faults arise;
only diligence serves as the remedy, capable of destroying all delusions and confusions.
That is to say, those three poisons are the cause that can summon three kinds of retribution;
these three serve as the root, leading one accordingly through the three realms of existence.
If one delights in that indolence, then one abandons all wholesome dharmas.
From this all evils arise; one shall surely fall into hell.
By grasping at that, greed is born; by rejecting this, anger increases.
To be thus attached to such things—this is called delusion.
Laziness shrouds the mind, like one fainting from poison;
there is no doubt that one will fall into the deep pit of heedlessness.
If one delights in practicing diligence, one leaves behind the defilement of sloth.
Liberated from all terrors, one thus attains a share of happiness;
yet if one is heedless in thought and does not cultivate the sublime, pure Dharma,
one incurs vast faults and such a person possesses only a share of suffering.
Bound by the fetters of kin, one shall fall into peril;
therefore, in this life, do not crave those sensual pleasures.
Furthermore, that indolent person is constantly obscured by delusion.
Lacking even a small portion of meritorious deeds, they are collectively held in contempt by others.
Furthermore, those who are indolent give rise to sleep and mental dullness, which destroy the gateway to liberation;
therefore, the wise guard themselves well against them.
Furthermore, those who are indolent give rise to shamelessness and lack of remorse;
these two are the root of suffering, and later they shall encounter great terror.
Moreover, those who are indolent completely abandon their practice and cultivation.
Such a person, though living in this world, is as if already dead.
Furthermore, that indolent one gives rise to restlessness, causing the mind to lack tranquility; at the end of life, his mind will be distracted.
Without emerging from the mire of indolence, by what means could one transcend the ocean of suffering?
Only through courageous diligence can one reach the further shore.
Furthermore, those who are indolent are no different from animals.
They think only of what they eat and know nothing else;
through their greedy craving for food and drink, they delight in impure conduct.
Their desires are many and their resources are meager, so they constantly beg from others.
Even regarding one's own person, enduring cold, heat, hunger, and thirst—
all this is due to indolence, through which one undergoes every hardship.
Because of that indolence, all people hold one in contempt.
He deceives only himself; how can he reach the end of suffering?
Not studying the True Vehicle, but craving only delicious flavors, he falls into evil realms at the end of life, laboring in vain to feel regret.
If one arouses diligence and abides in right mindfulness,
forever severing unwholesome states, such a person is a wise one.
All such various sufferings arise from indolence.
Having fully understood that this is the retribution of karma, one shall never again create it.
The fire of the three poisons within sentient beings is constantly blazing in every thought-moment;
with the nectar-rain of great compassion, one extinguishes it for their sake.
That is to say, the actions of body, speech, and mind are always associated with virtue;
they reveal the three evil realms and lead beings to transcend them.
If one relies upon a compassionate heart, one can proceed toward the bliss of nirvana.
Compassionately mindful of all sentient beings, as a mother loves her own child,
he seeks out and protects those who suffer;
even those in the realm of hungry ghosts receive his blessing, attaining rebirth in the celestial realms.
If one is fully endowed with compassion and cherishes all sentient beings,
such a person is called a great man (mahāpuruṣa), revered by both humans and devas.
If a person possesses a compassionate heart, they will then be able to maintain the pure precepts.
Just as the moon illuminates the world, its radiance is ever pure;
it enables all sentient beings to leave behind sorrow, fear, and grief.
Therefore, one should always remain intimately close to the mind of compassion until the very end.
If a person is free from coarseness and rudeness, Adorned with a heart of compassion, they are called a field of merit; Their fame will spread everywhere.
Sustained by the universal nourishment of compassion, Their faculties remain untainted by defilement.
Abiding in pure right view, one is not far from Bodhi.
If a person possesses a heart of compassion, like the sovereign power of the devas,
throughout hundreds of thousands of lifetimes, they will forever be free from poverty.
If a person’s character is upright and honest, valuable as gold,
and they further abide in a heart of compassion, they are an inexhaustible treasure.
If a person possesses diligence and constantly strives to seek the True Dharma,
With the bright lamp of a compassionate mind, he expounds the Dharma to dispel the darkness of doubt;
throughout day and night, he never abandons his compassionate intent,
and wherever he goes, he delights in teaching without weariness.

Compassion is supremely cooling; it extinguishes the feverish afflictions of sentient beings, causes them to attain sublime and wondrous bliss, and leads to the attainment of the fruit of true permanence.
Therefore, it is praised by all Buddhas: compassion is an inexhaustible treasure.
It is like a pure pond that can wash away all defilements of sin;
it is the supreme adornment that destroys the darkness of afflictions,
nourishes the sprouts of bodhi, and causes one to attain the fruit of true permanence.
If a person possesses a heart of compassion, it is like cow’s ghee produced from milk;
endowed with its exquisite flavor, it dispels the feverish afflictions of body and mind.
The three realms of existence are like a vast ocean, and the three poisons are like a swift current.
Compassion is the boat and raft, upon which the benevolent person rides and treads.
Compassion is the wealth of merit, adorned with the pure and white dharmas;
that the virtuous always keep it in mind—this is what is called compassion.
Compassion abandons all harshness; within, it gives rise to every virtue.
It eliminates the afflictions and their faults, just as molten gold is extracted from ore.
A compassionate heart is like a precious vessel, filled to capacity with sublime things.
Increasing those roots of goodness, one attains peace and security through mindfulness.
A compassionate heart is like a treasury; for sentient beings, its use is inexhaustible.
It can destroy their poverty and accomplish vast benefit.
With a mind of compassion ever tranquil, delighting in the cultivation of the various dhyānas,
one leaves behind the realm of negligence and emerges from the defilements of the five desires.
Furthermore, giving rise to a heart of loving-kindness, one conceives sympathetic concern for others.
May they attain pliancy and be liberated from the bonds of suffering.
By reflecting well with the mind, may they always remain far removed from the defilements of sin;
liberated from all terrors, may they aspire to the bliss of tranquility.
Always conjoined with patience, one causes no affliction to oneself or others;
the world all delights in seeing such a person, and later they shall be reborn among the gods.
If a person can abide securely in the supreme jewel of loving-kindness and patience, [they will attain these fruits].
All sentient beings look upon them as their parents;
Their compassion is unsurpassed and is the very root of happiness.
If a person lacks this mind, In the future, there will be nothing but suffering.
If Brahmā possessed compassion, and Maheśvara possessed patience, and all the Mothers who hold wisdom and insight— none could equal the practice of loving-kindness.
Non-harming is the foremost merit; right view is the supreme goodness.
With a tranquil mind always at peace, one escapes all perils and hardships.
Therefore, one should understand this: with a mind constantly generating compassion, cultivate and perfect stainless wisdom through generosity, ethical discipline, patience, and loving-kindness.
Through the merit induced by pure giving, one attains twelve kinds of virtue,
is reborn among gods and humans, and possesses wealth beyond compare.
If a person acts contrary to this, they will incur faults just as great.
The foolish take no delight in giving, and later they fall into evil realms.
For the sake of wives, children, and kin, they give rise to stinginess and greedy attachment;
they create the causes for the suffering of deprivation, constantly longing for more yet never satisfied.
If one practices giving extensively, one is liberated from the bonds of craving,
topples the banner of self-conceit, and destroys all the darkness of ignorance.
Giving serves as the precursor that leads one to rebirth in an excellent realm.
In the human world and among the devas, one shall attract great wealth.
Giving is like that bathing pool; precepts can purify all defilements;
and by observing well with wisdom, one can transcend the three realms of existence.
Generosity, morality, and wisdom—these three are like the light of a lamp.
If a person practices them well, they will forever leave behind the darkness of all delusion.
Attachment and aversion are like a vast ocean; doubt and confusion are like its surging waves.
Desiring to cross over those perils and difficulties, one should cultivate generosity, ethical discipline, and wisdom.
Since sentient beings are largely deranged and give rise to attachment wherever they go,
if one wishes to guard their minds, one should cultivate generosity, ethical discipline, and wisdom.
These three types of practice, I declare to be the excellent medicine that thoroughly cures the disease of afflictions and brings all to attain coolness.
When the mind gives rise to improper reflection, it produces the fault of negligence.
Bound and fettered by association with lust, anger, and delusion—
these three poisons are fearsome, like fire consuming the world.
One should sever them through remedies such as generosity, so that they may be forever exhausted.
Those who do not cultivate practices such as generosity are indeed deluded;
such people are constantly afflicted by suffering, and though they seek happiness, it is nowhere to be found.
Wherever sentient beings may be, if they commit various transgressions, [they will suffer].
According to various causes and conditions, one receives diverse retributions.
All conditioned phenomena arise from causes and conditions;
never has it been seen that one suffers the retribution of suffering without an evil cause.
One whose mind finds no joy in giving, whose face constantly wears an expression of anger—this is the cause of poverty; therefore, one should distance oneself from it.
If, however, giving gives rise to a joyful heart and one is freed from the stain of stinginess, [one attains prosperity].
Later one may be born among the gods, where one plays together with all the devas.
Yet this stinginess is like an enemy; its destruction is most terrifying, for it causes all sentient beings to suffer from the hunger and thirst of the hungry ghosts.
If one delights in practicing generosity, one will experience happiness wherever one is born;
for this reason, the wise always praise giving.
Like that light, wherever it goes, it follows after.
If one is born among humans or devas, one will receive offerings and respect.
Therefore, as all Buddhas have taught, one should skillfully cultivate generosity;
abiding in that which is indestructible, one reaches the most supreme and firm state.
One who practices giving well subdues the enemy of stinginess;
by constantly observing with wisdom, do not allow it to find an opportunity.
Giving is like a fertile field, and there are three kinds of it.
When the seeds of the mind are well-perfumed, each obtains its own beneficial fruit.
First delighting in the practice of giving, later specializing in maintaining pure precepts,
and using wisdom to sever the defilement of craving— this principle is unsurpassed.
The world is entirely impermanent and further beset by many faults;
if one cannot sever that craving, by what means could one be born in a superior realm?
One should give rise to the great mind and delight in practicing extensive generosity.
If one abandons this and fails to practice it, one will later receive the retribution of a hungry ghost.
However, by relying on the foundation of generosity and further upholding the pure precepts,
such a person will, in a future life, attain the rank of a universal monarch (cakravartin).
By possessing those precepts, knowing well the proper and improper times,
and reaching the end of suffering, one draws near to the path of enlightenment.
If the devas do not practice giving, their merit will accordingly diminish.
Having understood this, the wise should delight in practicing joy and equanimity;
even throughout this very life, they shall enjoy human happiness—
all of which arises from that giving— therefore, one should always maintain mindfulness and cultivate it.
Even if one falls among the animals, one still experiences their happiness;
all this is due to that very giving—this is what the Tathāgata has taught.
If a person does not delight in giving, they will later fall into the realm of hungry ghosts.
Because of such stinginess, one constantly eats all manner of impurities.
If one delights in practicing generosity, one will obtain the fruit of coolness;
if one does not cultivate such conduct, one will be scorched by hunger and thirst.
Due to past negligence, one does not cultivate the causes such as generosity;
at the time of death, one’s own mind gives rise to burning affliction.
One who gives with a joyful heart will be loved and respected by all.
One constantly attains auspiciousness, for the fruits one experiences correspond to the causes.
If a person does not delight in giving, nor enjoys their own wealth,
but is always stingy with their riches, in the end they will be scattered and destroyed by others.
If a person possesses precious wealth and offers it to their honored parents and teachers,
this accords with right practice and is not spent in vain. Toward those who are poor,
sick, or exhausted— toward all sentient beings— [one should likewise act].
Always delighting in pure giving, one acts as their eyes.
By practicing giving in this way, after having given, one is reborn in heaven;
yet if the gods should give rise to stinginess, they will before long fall away.
When humans cultivate the cause of giving, they receive the retribution of joy among the devas;
it is not that there is no cultivated cause, yet one falsely brings about its fruit.
If one is devoid of giving and precepts, nor cultivates meditative concentration, [how could one attain such a state]?
Such a foolish person, though living, is no different from the dead.
If one does not delight in the True Dharma, then the life of wisdom is diminished and lost;
the fool who does not practice, though living, is as if dead.
If a person lacks the lamp of wisdom, their mind will not be clear;
such a one is like an animal, merely covered by human skin.
Without practicing generosity and being full of greed, their faculties are constantly distracted.
You should know that those non-humans are like hungry ghosts engaged in strife.
One who dwells in loving-kindness and observes with mindfulness, practicing generosity, ethical discipline,
and meditative concentration— such a person is truly serene, and all the devas pay them respect.
Those endowed with virtue are honored by all; those lacking virtue are universally treated with contempt.
One who understands this well is called a "human among gods.
Those who practice generosity well obtain wealth, happiness, and long life.
In this world and in worlds beyond, one should always delight in practicing joy and renunciation.
Sentient beings, according to their own karma, are born within the five realms of existence;
regarding them as parents, one should regard only virtuous causes such as giving.
Understanding the cause of giving and the superior retribution it elicits,
one should uphold the pure precepts to escape the suffering of the three realms of existence.
Morality is the most excellent wealth, shining universally like the light of the sun.
When a person's life comes to an end, only the precepts serve as their companion.
By upholding the precepts, one attains rebirth in heaven or achieves various meditative absorptions;
in this world and in worlds to come, such radiance is peerless.
If a person desires rebirth in heaven, they can attain it through even a small cause;
therefore, stay far from all evils and always uphold the pure precepts.
If one can protect those precepts and joyfully practice generosity with the mind, [they will surely attain their goal].
Later one will be born among the gods, Attaining incomparable,
sublime bliss. Wives, children, precious wealth, Relatives, and companions—
To one who maintains the pure precepts, All these appear as nothing but suffering.
If one conceives love and reverence for the precepts, guarding them as one would cherish an only child,
then one will remain free from transgressions and always be reborn in superior realms.
By practicing such pure conduct, both generosity and ethical discipline will be brought to full perfection.
Adorned with white karma, one is born in the heavens.
Precepts are like a treasury of jewels; they can produce such abundance that fame and birth in heaven arrive spontaneously, without being sought.
These three kinds of supreme rewards can even be sought by those in the realm of hungry ghosts;
how much more so for a person endowed with wisdom who upholds the precepts with a pure mind?
If a person is able to protect and maintain the pure precepts for as long as they live, [they shall attain such rewards].
One shall reach the state of non-extinction, forever ending the limit of all suffering.
Past cycles of saṃsāra were bound by the three poisons;
precepts are like pure radiance, able to shatter that darkness.
The precepts are like a celestial pond, adorned with a multitude of precious jewels;
they are also called the wealth of steadfastness, which neither water nor fire can destroy.
Therefore, that true person never transgresses the precepts.
Always generating a heart of love and respect, one attains the supreme tranquility.
With a resolute and firm mind, one remains without flaw or leakage in the precepts;
it is solely through the power of those precepts that one is constantly protected until the end of life.
If one associates closely with those who personally uphold the precepts, it is like being illuminated by the light of the sun;
yet if one draws near to those who violate the prohibitions, their own dullness and delusion will increase further.
By remaining free from the defilement of unwholesomeness, one is without the feverish distress of craving.
Such a person who upholds the precepts is praised by all Buddhas.
Upholding the precepts brings merit and wisdom; it is virtuous in the beginning, middle, and end.
One who breaks the precepts is merely a fool, no different from an animal.
If a person maintains pure precepts and is covered by the robes of morality, yet violates those precepts, they are like one who is naked. Through the observance of precepts, one is born in heaven;
there, the hosts of devas vie with one another to welcome and honor them.
Within those gardens and groves, they sport together;
having fulfilled all meritorious deeds and firmly practiced the holy life,
such people are born among the devas— of this there is no doubt.
By upholding those precepts, one increases all beneficial virtues;
toward the five sublime sensual desires, the mind gives rise to no defiled attachment.
Whether in this world or the next, the precepts serve as one’s companion.
Upon that perilous and evil path, he acts as their refuge;
amidst hunger, thirst, and fear, he provides the foremost protection.
One should observe this well: if one abandons him, where else can one turn?
It would be better to use a sharp sword to sever one's own head than to commit a transgression against the power of those precepts.
This merit of upholding the precepts is pure in both cause and effect.
It summons the joys of both the mundane and supramundane worlds, and is praised by all Buddhas.
If a person does not guard the precepts, they will lack the goodness of the beginning, middle, and end;
they will lose vast benefits as well as the most supreme tranquility.
Keeping the precepts is the foremost good, which even generosity cannot equal;
while that wealth has its limits, the efficacy of the precepts is inexhaustible.
Adorned by the virtue of the precepts, one is beloved and respected by all people.
One should know that all Tathāgatas became sages because of the precepts.
Observing the precepts is most refreshing; it removes the feverish afflictions of body and mind.
Therefore, always practice them diligently, and you shall be reborn in the heavenly realms.
Precepts are the ladder for rebirth in heaven, and are also called the ocean of bliss;
if a person abandons those precepts, they will later experience only sorrow and regret.
Precepts are like cool, clear water—deep, vast, and ever-filling.
For those who uphold the precepts, they wash away the defilements of body and mind.
That they receive the wondrous joys of the heavens, as well as supreme adornments,
is entirely due to the power of the precepts and the result of virtuous causes.
If one dwells securely in pure precepts, all virtues will take them as their foundation;
with every thought constantly increasing, there is no fear of the miserable realms.
If one single-mindedly cultivates the holy life, adorning the body with the precepts,
In this present life, such a person receives offerings and respect;
by steadfastly upholding the precepts and always remaining far from all that is unwholesome,
they attain happiness and security in every place.
If one upholds various precepts, each possesses its own specific efficacy:
one will constantly be reborn in sublime realms and attain mastery according to one's wishes.
Through these three—generosity, ethical discipline, and wisdom—one is able to give rise to a heart of loving-kindness.
Always loving and mindful of sentient beings, one gains the opportunity to draw near and serve them.
Precepts are like exquisite treasures; virtuous people always value them highly.
By forever leaving behind all faults, one attains rebirth among the gods.
Endowed with pure wisdom, like molten gold free from impurity,
always delighting in the observance of pure precepts, one is born among the gods.
One is able to bring all sentient beings peace and security in every place.
By not committing any sinful deeds, one may be born among the gods.
If a person guards those precepts, making wise and skillful discernment,
they shall remain diligent and never regress throughout day and night.
Precepts are like those fine horses, ridden and controlled by the virtuous;
through true contemplation, they do not cling to the rewards of pleasure.
Among the heavens, there is supreme and wondrous bliss, where all the devas sport together.
All are born there by virtue of upholding the precepts;
Adorned with exquisite celestial flower garlands and heavenly robes,
The various devas sport together— all these are obtained through virtuous causes.
There are exquisite lotus ponds, where pure, cool, and fragrant breezes arise;
the devas sport together therein—all of which is obtained through virtuous causes.
The various palaces in the heavens are adorned with myriad jewels.
The various devas sport together, all because they maintain the precepts.
In the wondrous gardens of the heavens, all the flowers are in full bloom;
they dwell and roam among the jewel-mountains, all because they maintain the precepts.
By possessing that pure morality, one is born in the Heaven of the Thirty-three;
like a person entering their own home, they are immediately free from all sorrows and afflictions.
If a person guards that morality, they shall obtain the most supreme lifespan.
When one who has broken the precepts reaches the end of life, they undergo immeasurable and extreme suffering.
Having understood the merit of upholding the precepts and always delighting in them,
those who skillfully guard the precepts will not commit transgressions.
By being able to guard that precept and dwelling well in patience,
through the causes and conditions of tranquility, all people delight in beholding them.
If one relies upon pure precepts, it is like boarding a boat or raft.
It can carry oneself and others, enabling one to cross the ocean of the three realms of existence.
Through the cool water of ethical discipline, it can cleanse the mind and intellect;
the flowers of Jambūnada gold are offered by the devas.
If a person’s mind is tranquil and they are constantly adorned with the precepts,
they will be born with mastery among the devas and experience boundless bliss.
By extensively cultivating sublime practices, they receive the most excellent and wondrous joy.
Sporting among the various devas is entirely due to the observance of the precepts.
If one maintains those pure precepts, it is like ascending a flight of stairs;
with wisdom and power constantly supporting one another, one attains birth in a noble and superior place.
If a person possesses a pure mind and is without flaw or leakage in their precepts,
through the purity of the dharma of precepts, they will always be born in a place of peace and security.
One who well guards the precepts should constantly contemplate and examine them.
By abandoning even subtle transgressions, one attains the state of tranquility.
Precepts can produce that bliss and cause one to cast off all stains of sin;
therefore, always guard them well, and you will ultimately eliminate sorrow and fear.
By upholding those precepts, one has no fear at the end of life;
among the three evil realms, they serve as the foremost protection.
If a person does not guard the precepts, they are like a blind person with cataracts in their eyes.
If one is impure in ethical discipline, one will constantly be reborn in inferior states.
If one seeks the happiness of gods and humans, ethical discipline alone is its foundation;
if one is impure in ethical discipline, one will later experience regret and distress.
Those who lack precepts and are foolish cannot be born in the heavenly realms;
therefore, the wise always uphold the precepts.
The five exquisite sensual pleasures in the heavens are the foremost and most sublime joys.
Because of the purity of their precepts, they obtain manifold fruits.
The golden light of Mount Meru is surpassed by the light of the precepts;
even if the mountain were divided into sixteen parts, it would not equal even one of them.
The light of the precepts constantly shines, more brilliant and pure than refined gold;
all this arises from one's own wholesome karma, enabling rebirth in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
There are three grades of upholding the precepts, namely: superior, middling, and inferior.
Just as the causes one has created, so too will the retribution one receives.
Because of upholding those precepts, one does not give rise to negligence;
dwelling securely in the True Dharma, one constantly attains all manner of sublime bliss.
The precepts can remove all defilements and constantly radiate pure light;
even if there were hundreds or thousands of suns, none could equal them.
If one maintains the precepts in the highest degree, one shall obtain seven kinds of merit.
One may enjoy things as one wishes, as taught by the Sugata.
By relying upon pure ethical discipline, right view will constantly manifest;
thus, passing from the human world to birth in heaven is not difficult to attain.
Precepts are a refreshing touch; They are never abandoned by the body.
The foolish do not draw near them, And thus constantly suffer various torments.
If a person possesses a pure mind And skillfully guards the prohibitive precepts,
One who possesses those seven kinds of wealth is certainly incapable of being destroyed.
If a person with a pure mind cultivates the holy life (brahmacarya),
they are like a bird with two wings that flies through the sky without falling.
By upholding those precepts, one attains the fruit of purity;
it is the most supreme among the supreme, and there is nothing higher than this.
If the mind is well-cultivated through practice, relying upon the jewels of generosity and ethical discipline, [one will attain the highest state].
In the heavens and among humans, in places of long life and excellence—
If one’s body does not uphold the pure precepts, And the mind does not delight in the True Dharma,
With nothing internal or external to rely upon, By what means can one escape the evil realms?
If one delights in the dharma of tranquility and is honored by others,
their inner and outer self will be as firm and unyielding as a diamond,
no different from it. Like sandalwood, aloeswood, tagara, and campaka flowers—
That which is esteemed by both humans and devas does not equal the fragrance of that precept.
If a person practices giving and precepts solely with the desire to be born in heaven,
this is a cause of defilement, like poison mixed with fine food.
Therefore, regarding that precept, one should firmly maintain it to seek liberation;
stay far away from those who break the precepts as if they were poison, a sword, or a staff.
By thus well-guarding the precepts, one shall proceed to the realms of humans and devas.
One who lacks precepts is despised by the multitude, and happiness cannot be found.
Understanding these merits, one should focus the mind on them without abandoning them for even a moment;
as the supreme protection, there is nothing that resembles the precepts.
Abiding well in patience is the foremost adornment;
this is the most excellent wealth, which no worldly treasure can equal.
If a person cultivates the practice of patience, they will be honored by the world.
Therefore, always with a single mind, cultivate this practice with steadfastness.
If a person cultivates the practice of patience, they leave behind the fault of anger;
such a person is constantly praised by the virtuous in both this world and the next.
The wealth of patience and the wealth of ethical discipline,
As well as that supreme wealth of wisdom— These various merits transcend the world.
Therefore, the wise person delights in practicing patience.
Toward all sentient beings, one’s mind never gives rise to weariness or abandonment.
Patience is like a wondrous and excellent medicine, capable of curing the poison of anger;
by the power of that patience, it prevents [anger] from arising again and again.
Fools lack the wisdom of clear understanding; like the blind who see nothing, they are led by the lamp-light of patience to ascend the true path.
Devoid of the wealth of the True Dharma, they revolve through the five realms of existence.
One who has well cultivated the practice of patience, I declare to be truly wealthy.
Anger is a profound fault, like a treacherous and desolate wilderness;
yet if a person possesses the practice of patience, they will skillfully transcend it.
If one does not cultivate the practice of patience, one will lose the way on the Noble Path;
if one wishes to escape the suffering of the evil realms, how can one avoid it without patience?
If a person practices forbearance, they shall obtain peace and security day and night.
Forever free from all sorrow and grief, one will always be handsome in future lives.
Patience is a treasury of merit; the virtuous always guard it.
With the mind well-subdued, one is not troubled by afflictions.
Patience is the ladder for rebirth in heaven; it delivers one from the terrors of saṃsāra.
If one can practice it well, one will be liberated from the suffering of hell.
Patience is the water of merit, pure and ever-filling.
It can rescue hungry ghosts from thirst and wash away the defilements of animal rebirths.
If one practices patience with single-minded dedication, one will attain auspiciousness and peace,
regarding all sentient beings as a compassionate mother of the world does.
To nurture the True Dharma, one should observe the proper time and place,
rouse courageous diligence, and seek various fruits thereof. If one is separated from the True Dharma,
as well as from the proper time, place, and activity, [there can be no attainment].
Due to the absence of such diligence, one increases many matters of indolence.
The wise are full of valor; delighting in the True Dharma of liberation, they swiftly proceed to the celestial realms in a mere instant, like the flight of an arrow.
By the power of that diligence, one skillfully manages various affairs;
in whatever tasks are undertaken, all are fully accomplished.
Whether it be the supramundane True Dharma or worldly benefits and profit, [all are achieved].
All arise from that diligence; without it, nothing exists.
If a person distances themselves from diligence, they abandon all wholesome dharmas and are held in contempt by the world, like the shadow of a hare obscuring the moon.
Abandoning the Noble Eightfold Path, pure wisdom does not increase;
only through the power of diligence can one reach the place of peace.
If a person possesses diligence, they will have mastery of power like that of a king.
If an Arhat lacks diligence, they cannot achieve Bodhi.
Understanding this merit, one should not allow the faculties to be distracted;
by arousing a mind of diligence, one becomes foremost and most excellent.
When pure wisdom manifests before one, One constantly gives rise to right mindfulness;
Far removed from that old age and death, One attains the realization of the fruit of true permanence.
If a person cultivates various meditative concentrations Without becoming attached to wisdom,
One should always maintain single-mindedness and give rise to pure aspirations.
Abiding well in one-pointed concentration, free from the fault of contradiction, one is liberated from all fears; this is called true peace and happiness.
If the mind abides in a single object, it is free from all doubt and confusion;
pure like refined gold, this is called true peace and happiness.
If a person’s mind is tranquil and their faculties are not distracted, [they shall attain liberation].
One who is certain to proceed toward enlightenment is said to possess peace and happiness.
Because the mind abides in a single object, such a person delights in cultivating the various meditative concentrations and constantly attains the bliss of *samādhi*.
Delighting in dwelling alone in seclusion, constantly cultivating that supreme concentration,
and realizing that wondrous bliss which transcends the world—
with such a pure mind, one always abides in a single state of focus.
Having escaped the net of faults, one reaches supreme tranquility.
If the mind is concentrated on a single object and the five faculties are well-restrained,
one uses the water of wisdom to extinguish the burning harm of the fire of craving.
Constantly manifesting and dwelling in pure, sublime bliss,
one enjoys it inexhaustibly through liberation from that craving.
When the mind harbors crooked thoughts, they arise everywhere.
One who skillfully maintains meditative concentration is constantly in accord with a single object.
This supreme dhyāna can lead one to the city of Nirvāṇa and destroy all demonic adversaries; therefore, it should be cultivated.
One who is well-firm in all meditative concentrations can then tame the horse of the mind;
forever free from the defilement of sorrow, they attain the supreme abiding.
One who has skillfully cultivated concentration is free from greed and remains content.
The sublime rewards thus summoned cannot be fully described.
By practicing such cultivation and abiding in one-pointedness of mind,
one can transcend the stream of birth and death and reach the state of non-extinction.
Preceded by the power of wisdom, one delights in diligently seeking the True Dharma and remains constantly in union with meditative concentration, like a mother’s love for her child;
yet worldly parents cannot follow after their offspring in such exclusive devotion.
Among the five realms of existence, they provide protection for all.
The mountain of wisdom is exceedingly high and steep; the water of precepts is ever pure.
Regarding the faults and afflictions of the three realms of existence, they clearly perceive them all.
If one truly understands the objective sphere of the eye-faculty,
relying upon wisdom as one's support, one can cross the ocean of the three realms of existence.
Having well-cultivated generosity, ethical discipline, and meditative concentration, it is said that wisdom is their prerequisite.
Through wisdom and the joy of upholding the precepts, one can escape the evil realms.
If one becomes free from defilement regarding the objects perceived by the eye through discerning wisdom,
then as the Tathāgata has taught, one dwells well upon the Noble Eightfold Path.
Regarding the Four Noble Truths, such as suffering and the rest, he first revealed them;
through the power of superior wisdom, he shattered the common folk’s view of permanence.
His knowledge is like a sharp sword, severing the creeping vines of craving and attachment.
Free from the fetters of birth and so forth, as well as the mass of those faults,
wisdom is the supreme nectar; it is the supramundane wealth,
the most excellent spiritual friend, and the foremost treasure-store.
Cultivating wisdom and precepts, venerable in age, Free from craving,
attachment, and doubt, Always relying on tranquility, He reveals the path of ultimate reality.
His wisdom is like that vajra, Its power being exceedingly firm and sharp.
Destroying all afflictions, Causing one to mount the chariot of great wisdom.
