The Venerable Avalokiteśvara,
Compiler of the Translated Tripiṭaka of the Western Heaven, Chao San Da Fu,
states: If one exhausts all afflictions, then one attains the supreme bliss.
This is the supernormal power of tranquility, as the wise have truly explained.
Furthermore, those Tathāgatas always praise the Dharma of tranquility;
by attaining the state of non-extinction, all sufferings will no longer arise.
If a person is free from negligence, devoid of the afflictions of craving,
and delights in practicing the conduct of tranquility, they are not far from Bodhi.
If one can abandon greedy attachment, the mind will not be distracted by sense objects.
And by abandoning evil associates, one is not far from bodhi.
If one can observe skillfully, remaining unattached to the wholesome and the unwholesome,
and being free from the fear of saṃsāra, one is not far from bodhi.
If one can sever all delusions, Remove the defilement of indolence,
And realize that both self and others are without self, One is not far from Bodhi.
Free from the afflictions of the three poisons, One causes the faculties to become tranquil.
One who clearly understands the Four Noble Truths is not far from Bodhi.
One who feels neither craving nor aversion toward food, whether refined or coarse,
and for whom the realm of wisdom and its objects are both like [a reflection], is not far from Bodhi.
Regarding both suffering and pleasure, one should not give rise to attachment;
having attained freedom from all fears, one is not far from Bodhi.
If a person fears all transgressions, they should abandon all negligence.
Seeking the path to enlightenment well, one attains supreme tranquility.
If a person skillfully observes the Four Noble Truths with wisdom,
they will be liberated from all saṃsāra and proceed to the unconditioned shore beyond.
If one lacks right reflection, being foolishly attached to various desires and not weary of or seeking to leave birth and death, one will be bound by saṃsāra.
Fearing neither vast suffering nor possessing the means for deliverance, [one remains in bondage].
Struck by the arrow of desire, one shall fall into the evil realms.
The fool is attached to various sensual pleasures, like a moth that craves the light of a lamp;
unaware of the great terror, there is ultimately not the slightest joy.
The Buddha taught the path of reality, Namely: suffering, emptiness, impermanence, And the absence of self and agent; By this, one can be liberated from saṃsāra.
The realm of wisdom is fundamentally equal, For all things are created by the mind.
Having realized and understood this, one does not speak of the three types [of food].
Free from the faults of food and drink, and not relying on wrong livelihood,
one gives rise to non-conceptual wisdom and realizes the supramundane Dharma.
Abiding well in true wisdom, one performs the sixteen aspects of contemplation;
thereafter, being able to understand thoroughly, one attains mastery over the sequence of all phenomena.
Forever free from the defilements of the three poisons, one emerges from the oppression of the three realms of existence.
Transcending the three evil destinies, one is called a *srotāpanna*.
With unwholesome dharmas as cause, one would certainly fall into the evil realms;
by relying on the dharma of liberation, one attains the fruit of *srotāpanna*.
Thoroughly cultivating all meditative concentrations, one gives rise to pliancy;
through association with pure karma, one attains transcendence of the ocean of the three realms of existence.
Permanently severing all doubts, one becomes free from greed and non-harming.
Boarding the vessel of white karma, one is able to reach the further shore.
That is to say, all conditioned phenomena arise from causes and conditions;
knowing those Four Noble Truths as the causes and effects of defilement and purification.
If one thoroughly understands the Four Noble Truths, one will certainly attain liberation;
the fool, however, clings to the realm of desire and revolves through the three realms of existence.
If one can abandon craving and desire, one will abide in the path of tranquility.
This path is unsurpassed, the domain traversed by the wise.
If a person always maintains a pure heart of reverence toward the Buddhas, they shall obtain happiness in every birth; apart from the Buddhas, there is no liberation.
If a person always loves and delights in the True Dharma with a pure mind, they will obtain happiness in birth after birth; apart from the Dharma, there is no liberation.
If a person always makes offerings to the Sangha with a pure mind, [they will likewise attain joy].
In birth after birth one obtains happiness; without the Saṅgha there is no liberation.
If a person, regarding the Four Truths, always maintains a pure mind of faith and understanding, they will obtain happiness in birth after birth; apart from this, there is no liberation.
If a person constantly cultivates the noble path with a pure mind, they will obtain happiness in birth after birth; apart from this, there is no liberation.
If one seeks to realize suchness, one should abide in pure wisdom.
Not delighting in or clinging to play—this is the God among Gods.
If one delights in and clings to frolics, and the mind does not give them up even for a moment, it increases all manner of sickness and affliction; this, then, is truly not happiness.
One who well understands the Dharma of the Four Truths, And practices such deeds as giving—
Know that such a person Abides in the most supreme peace and security.
Always delighting in the practice of loving-kindness and patience, They do not harm any sentient beings.
He wins the affection of all sentient beings, who revere him as they would their own father.
His physical actions are always pure, his faculties are well-coordinated,
his mind is free from stinginess and greed, and he stays far removed from taking what is not given.
One should not gaze upon painted women; having severed the firm conception of desire, one becomes a liberator of the world.
Delighting in the practice of various meditative concentrations, one attains freedom from all sorrow and fear.
Not touched by the serpent of afflictions, viewing gold as mere rubble;
with regard to suffering and pleasure, safety and peril, as well as prosperity and decline,
whose mind does not waver— this one is called a bhikṣu.
Skillfully subduing the sense faculties, one is not disturbed by external objects;
knowing things as they truly are through wisdom, one remains equanimous toward both enemies and kin.
If one possesses clear intelligence, one understands that the realm of desire is like poison.
I prophesy that such a person as this shall attain the path of Bodhi.
Possessing true and right view, awakening to the arising and ceasing of each moment,
they shall abide as steadfast as Mount Sumeru and transcend the ocean of saṃsāra.
Regarding grass and sandalwood, they view them with equal regard, making no distinction;
toward exquisite food and famous garments, they feel no attachment or delight.
Regarding gain and fame, they regard them as a blazing fire.
The mind constantly gives rise to contentment, resting and reclining upon the grass.
Regarding the various activities performed in the past and present,
by abandoning inverted thoughts, one will not give rise to defiled attachment.
Delighting in hearing the True Dharma, not following the causes of saṃsāra,
one skillfully discriminates with wisdom and constantly cultivates sublime practices.
Though the realm of desire burns fiercely, because the mind is tranquil, one remains undisturbed.
If one drives [the senses] like servants, then there will be no sufferings;
if the faculties are disciplined and compliant, then no wandering will arise.
One who is free from the fetters of desire is no different from a Muni.
A virtuous person is like gold and treasure; all who see them hold them in high esteem.
Delighting in the practice of tranquility, they cause others to give rise to joyful hearts.
Dwelling in an araṇya, they take no pleasure in residing in lofty towers or palaces.
Contented and wearing robes of coarse wool, always practicing the alms-round,
well-cultivating body, speech, and mind, one gives rise to neither notions of suffering nor pleasure;
free from conceptual discrimination and attachment, one attains the supreme peace and security.
By practicing various meditative concentrations, one can destroy those demonic enemies;
always employing truthful speech, one guides all classes of beings.
Skillfully mounting the chariot of wisdom, one crushes the greedy impulses of the six sense faculties.
One should know that such a person draws near to the path of enlightenment.
Delighting in dwelling in an araṇya, they are forever free from all faults;
like the wind in the sky, they blow through clouds without obstruction.
By purifying the three karmas, diligently cultivating all supreme practices,
and possessing true right view, one destroys the teachings of all Māras.
Regarding those activities such as greed, one remains unstained by their inherent nature.
Constantly giving rise to a mind of loving-kindness and compassion— this is what a bhikṣu should do.
Fully understanding that objects such as form are the causes of bondage,
such a person is free from sorrow and affliction, and shall reach the state of quiescent extinction.
Knowing the laws of all causes and conditions, that both good and evil are determinate,
one delights in hearing the Dharma of liberation and does not cling to greed.
Even toward wholesome deeds not yet cultivated, one constantly gives rise to love and joy.
This person is like the moonlight, pure by nature and free from defilement.
They incinerate evil dharmas as fire consumes dry wood;
having cast aside all causes of suffering, they are celebrated as supreme within the three realms of existence.
Aiming for liberation, they do not cling to worldly dharmas;
transcending all cycles of rebirth, they move through space like birds.
Knowing causes as they truly are, they certainly receive their fruits.
Within the three realms of existence, this is called true liberation.
Regarding suffering and pleasure, the refined and the coarse, there is no attachment whatsoever.
This most supreme bhikṣu contemplates the world as a mirage.
With a mind free from distraction, delighting in the quest for the True Dharma,
and diligently cultivating one's original pure karma, such a person is like an Arhat.
Delighting in proximity to virtuous friends, they remain far removed from worldly kin.
Having cast off the defilements of household life, he is like an arhat;
with wisdom his faculties are stilled, and he is unattached to sensory objects.
Walking, he looks at the tips of his own toes; he is like an arhat.
He does not go to the royal roads, nor to the crossroads and alleys of the city;
though he engages in trade, he is beyond reproach, like an Arhat.
He does not watch songs or dances, nor does he delight in mutual strife.
Dwelling in the wilderness or in solitude, he is like an arhat.
Eating but one meal a day, not seeking what he has not yet obtained,
knowing moderation and contentment— he is like an arhat.
Always wearing rag-robes, not delighting in fine garments,
and acting in accordance with the practice of alms-gathering, such a person is like an Arhat.
Because they do not create further karma and are free from all falsehood, they are truly liberated.
Neither arising nor delighting [in existence], he is like an arhat.
Without the manifestation of anger, free from greed, desire, and delusion,
liberated from all evil dharmas— he is like an arhat.
Free from all anger and affliction, transcending all fetters and latent tendencies,
dwelling in right mindfulness and reflection— one is like an Arhat.
Cultivating the Eightfold Noble Path, one abides well in tranquility.
Having destroyed the enemies that are the various afflictions, he is like an arhat.
With faculties stilled and firm, having transcended the mire of sensual desire and abiding in one-pointedness of mind, he is like an arhat.
Whether in one’s own place of practice or in the dwellings of others, knowing them as they truly are, one speaks accordingly; such a person is like an Arhat.
Knowing that both tainted and untainted phenomena arise entirely from causes and conditions—
One who is resolute and free from doubt is like an arhat.
Free from sloth and torpor, untiring, rising at the proper time,
and diligently practicing the holy life— such a one is like an arhat.
Delighting in dwelling in an araṇya, practicing vipaśyanā and the various samādhis of śamatha, such a person is like an arhat.
Relying on correct principle, the wise one always dwells in forests and wilds.
Like a bird dwelling in the empty sky, he is like an arhat;
receiving the food and drink offered by the faithful, he preaches the Dharma with equanimity,
destroying the root afflictions and secondary defilements— he is like an arhat.
One who well knows the true path, whose mind accords with the stages of practice,
and who is able to reach the further shore, is like an arhat.
If one possesses clear wisdom, they are free from fear and filled with joy.
Unattached to both [self and others], he is like an arhat.
Regarding all classes of beings, self and other, knowing aging and death as they truly are, gods and humans alike take refuge in him; he is like an arhat.
Always delighting in the cultivation of pure conduct, possessing nothing beyond the three robes, and being content with what little he obtains—he is like an Arhat.
He does not indulge in delicious flavors; relying on the proper time, he eats while seated once.
Free from the defilements of fame and profit, they are like arhats.
Endowed with compassion and equanimity, they do not conceal their many faults;
having incinerated the forest of transgressions, they are like arhats.
Violating the regulations of the Saṃgha, with a mind always indolent and lacking courageous diligence—such a person is not a bhikṣu.
The Buddha admonished his disciples: "You should not keep bedding and requisites."
If one delights in indolence, how can one attain peace and happiness?
Since indolence alone is the root of all calamities,
one will undergo immeasurable suffering within the cycle of saṃsāra.
If there are those who are indolent, no manifold virtues will arise;
though they wear the saffron robes, they are not bhikṣus.
If one does not cultivate concentration and wisdom, by what means could one exhaust all outflows?
One who possesses only the semblance of form, yet lacks the true nature of a bhikṣu;
one who delights in dwelling in monasteries, having departed from the sphere of training in the Dharma;
one who is addicted to the flavors of wine and sensual beauty—this person is not a bhikṣu.
If one has severed the bonds of Māra and distanced oneself from all sinful karma,
one should not dwell together with or share food and drink with those who have violated the precepts.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who has broken the precepts partakes of the community’s food and drink.
That is like consuming poison; it is no different from drinking molten copper.
Because they lack superior capacity, they are excluded from the common lot of beings;
later, falling into the hells, they shall find no food there.
If one has severed all afflictions, like a snake emerging from its hole,
taking no pleasure in seeing women and subsisting on alms through right livelihood—
how is it that these bhikṣus use their bodies as collateral?
They create the causes for rebirth in the evil realms and destroy the reputation of the Sangha Jewel.
Greedy for the spheres of fame and profit, they associate closely with women;
being neither laypeople nor monks, they are thieves within the Dharma.
Relying on the power and prestige of kings and ministers, they indulge freely in wine and fine foods;
being bhikṣus in name only, they deceive those who give alms.
Lacking the skillful means of wholesome discipline, they engage in worldly affairs just like laypeople.
Constantly dwelling in the royal city, like a snake in its forest lair,
if one does not give rise to weary detachment, then [defilements] will increase with every thought-moment.
One should therefore cast off the entanglements of sensual craving and delight in relying upon tranquility.
All afflictions, delusions, and karmic actions are severed through what is abandoned by vision;
one should skillfully cultivate the practice of liberation from the aggregates of form and so forth.
Delighting in the cultivation of various meditative concentrations, one awakens to all phenomena.
Thoroughly attaining the true nature of reality, One obtains the supreme peace and security.
Arousing a vast mind of great compassion, Diligently seeking the True Dharma,
And realizing that one's own body is like an illusion— Such a person is called a true bhikṣu.
Always giving rise to pure and wholesome thoughts, Eliminating greed, desire, anger, and resentment,
And departing from inverted conceptualization— Such a one is called a true bhikṣu.
Severing all fetters and bonds, Detached from all forms of association,
One who constantly has compassion for all sentient beings is called a true bhikṣu.
One who skillfully tames his own mind so that the realm of desire cannot disturb it,
like pure gold free from dross, is called a true bhikṣu.
Regarding all realms of desire, he gives rise neither to attachment nor aversion;
his mind is free from clinging—such a one is called a true bhikṣu.
Fully endowed with the dharmas of the precepts, he subdues the enemies that are the sense faculties.
Free from base slander, he is called a true bhikṣu.
Not indulging in various foods and drinks, he constantly gives rise to clear wisdom.
Delighting in the study of all dharmas, he is called a true bhikṣu.
In the wilderness or among the graves, Spreading grass upon which to sit or lie,
If one’s mind feels no weariness, Such a person is called a true bhikṣu.
Fully understanding that all evil causes Will inevitably result in their bitter retribution,
Thus, being free from that defilement and turbidity, one is called a true bhikṣu.
Through the purity of the mental faculty, having left behind all evils, perils, and hardships,
and having transcended the path of saṃsāra, one is called a true bhikṣu.
With wisdom as deep as the ocean, unmoved by praise or blame,
with no thoughts of anger or attachment arising in the mind— one is called a true bhikṣu.
Skillfully proclaiming the subtle and wondrous Dharma, free from defilement and non-attached.
With the power of wisdom firm and steadfast, acting according to the time without weariness or indolence;
knowing the realm of desire, the realm of form, and that formless realm—
all as arising from various causes and conditions— one is called a possessor of true knowledge.
One who can leave behind the faults of desire and does not cling to worldly discourse—
I call that bhikṣu one who views the objects of desire as poison.
Possessing such right wisdom, he contemplates desire as if it were mud.
These are the people who have attained liberation, Who have escaped from drowning and sinking.
They delight in practicing various meditative concentrations, And remain far removed from indolence;
They constantly read and recite the scriptures, Bringing great benefit to all sentient beings.
Possessing great eloquence, he answers according to every question;
knowing the sequence of all phenomena, he is free from inverted discrimination.
He skillfully manages the affairs of the Saṃgha and guards all its property with care.
The body feels no fatigue, nor is there any regret or distress.
One seeks not personal fame, nor does one hope for the reward of merit;
of such a bhikṣu I say that he is free from all bonds.
Furthermore, those who uphold the pure precepts do not seek rebirth in the heavens;
by means of the wholesome causes they have cultivated, they aspire solely toward the fruit of Bodhi.
They always delight in practicing correct conduct and do not associate with evil friends.
I prophesy that such a person shall be free from all faults.
Having well-cultivated the contemplation of loving-kindness, with a diligent and upright mind,
and without the slightest transgression of the precepts, they are not far from Bodhi.
Fearing birth, old age, sickness, and death, Weary of the suffering of saṃsāra,
Eliminating distraction and practicing dhyāna, One is not far from Bodhi.
Relying on the emptiness of intrinsic nature, Realizing impermanence and arising-and-ceasing,
By practicing the various dhyānas in successive order, one attains the ultimate end of suffering.
Furthermore, those who violate the precepts are a detriment to the Buddha-dharma;
though they wear the kashaya robes on the outside, there is no virtue stored within them.
Just like that mass of foam, Feeble and lacking solidity, So too are those who practice in vain, Merely stealing the name of a bhikṣu.
These violators of the precepts are destined for hell; They are cast out by the Saṅgha-ratna.
Deceived by one's own mind, at the dissolution of the body one falls into the evil realms.
Deceiving oneself regarding the rituals of the Dharma and Vinaya, one experiences the results according to one's karma;
bound by the net of karma, one suffers nothing but extreme pain.
Not donning the robe of wholesome dharmas, one is as ugly as a naked body;
later, falling into the hells, one undergoes various punishments.
Lacking the adornment of manifold virtues, one is oppressed solely by suffering and affliction.
Such a person who has broken the precepts will swiftly hasten toward the evil realms.
Because they have broken the precepts, they do not cultivate various virtuous deeds;
when the fires of hell burn most fiercely, there is certainly no way to escape them.
Abiding securely in the Dharma of ethical discipline within, And externally maintaining all proper deportment—
To abandon these is to rely on wrong livelihood, From which there is no way to escape.
Throughout those days and nights, One increases all manner of unwholesome states.
The foolish practitioner of evil deeds destroys the jewel of the precepts;
yet one who hears that all phenomena are empty, maintains this in mind without abandoning it,
and dwells in right mindfulness and reflection, is a true protector of the precepts.
Precepts can distance one from all transgressions; virtuous people always uphold them.
Broken precepts are like a defiled rope that binds those who commit evil.
If one violates the prohibitive precepts, one is joined only with sin.
Such a person delights in associating with the messengers of Yama;
being foolish and lacking moral discipline, they give rise to intense distraction,
continuously committing various transgressions, and are not far from the hells.
If one delights in committing manifold evils, they will only bring harm upon themselves;
as the present fruit corresponds to past causes, why give rise to regret?
The river of sin is exceedingly deep and vast, its waves and surges ever surging and turbulent.
All those sinful people who drift and drown endure various sufferings day and night;
if they depart from that pure morality, they abandon the white and pure dharmas,
and even if they later obtain a human body, their minds will constantly give rise to negligence.
Those who completely violate the precepts, who harbor increased envy toward the virtuous and good—
such evil bhikṣus will certainly fall into the evil realms.
But those who delight in upholding the pure precepts and constantly traverse the path of goodness, [shall attain liberation].
Such a person will, before long, attain the true and eternal bliss that transcends the world.
By firmly upholding the precepts of the fast, reciting the various sutras,
their mind remains ever tranquil, free from association with afflictions.
Within the ocean of the three realms of existence, take the precepts as your boat and raft;
by practicing according to the teachings, you shall be able to reach the other shore.
Constantly wearing robes made of discarded rags, you shall possess only a single broken bowl.
Eating the fruits, roots, and melons of the forest—such is the joy praised by the Buddha.
With body, speech, and mind purified, one should practice right livelihood;
delighting in the cultivation of various meditative concentrations, one will not be far from awakening.
Always dwelling in the wilderness, with a mind free from negligence,
solely purifying the holy life, one is not far from awakening.
Turning one's back on the five desires, contented and without longing, one attains liberation.
Constantly giving rise to a mind of tranquility, one is not far from attaining bodhi.
Not practicing wrong livelihoods, and being free from the dust and defilements of afflictions,
with a mind equal to space, one is not far from attaining bodhi.
Regarding the various laws and teachings spoken by the Buddha, they do not give rise to love or joy in their hearts;
they do not cultivate that holy life (brahmacarya) and slander the path of tranquility.
Associating with inferior persons, they distance themselves from the precepts and the Dharma.
Abandoning true right view, one takes no pleasure in cultivating the various meditative concentrations.
Because of that restlessness, the mental application is destroyed;
being devoid of the remedial dharmas, by what means could one attain dhyāna?
Abandoning one's own wholesome qualities and delighting in the activities of false teachers—
both of these lead to ruin, and one will certainly fall into the evil realms.
Casting off the appearance of a bhikṣu and changing into the dress of a layperson,
They will be held in contempt by others and shall always live in poverty in this world.
Those base and foolish ones, boasting of their own learning,
abandon their own wholesome deeds and delight in practicing what is unrighteous.
By returning to secular life for one's own sake,
one loses a good reputation and is cast aside like mere straw by those virtuous people.
By delighting in the commission of various evil deeds, one destroys right view.
These monks who destroy the Dharma, their minds ever deceitful and fraudulent;
constantly craving exquisite food and drink, they delight in and cling to sensual matters.
These monks of evil conduct are called thieves wearing the saffron robe.
They exhaustively study the calendar, celestial phenomena, and the stars, and discourse on matters such as divination and physiognomy;
these are worldly bhikṣus who delight in associating with kings.
They practice medicine and the art of painting, and engage in the construction of improper affairs.
This wicked bhikṣu constantly devotes himself to clothing and food;
he loathes the recitation of sūtras and the practice of meditative concentration, greedily craving gain, offerings, and fame.
This bhikṣu in name only will, before long, bring about his own ruin.
Those who associate closely with evil friends and seek alchemical arts to transmute gold are unrighteous bhikṣus; they bring about their own ruin.
If one abandons such desires and practices, one will distance oneself from all evil friends.
Content with a mere portion of roasted flour, he likewise gives rise to no feverish distress.
When the objects of desire come to invade him, he abandons them as if they were a blazing fire;
such a bhikṣu who guards the precepts is like a stainless mani-jewel.
Pure both within and without, adorned with wisdom and virtue,
this bhikṣu of brahma-conduct is covered by the robes of precepts.
Unattached to worldly dharmas, he is as immovable as Mount Sumeru.
This tranquil bhikṣu is honored by all;
When entering cities or villages, he does not stay more than three days and nights.
This liberated bhikṣu always delights in dwelling among mountain crags and valleys.
Extremely fearful of the fault of desire, he cultivates concentration to eliminate distraction;
this solitary bhikṣu remains tranquil with an unmoving mind.
Having distanced himself from evil associates, he has utterly severed craving and attachment.
This bhikṣu who is free from defilement does not cling to any conditioned activities.
Always remaining far removed from kinsmen and friends, he practices meditative concentration or recites the scriptures.
This bhikṣu who has renounced the world shall thus be liberated from all suffering and hardship.
Having few desires and knowing contentment, Diligently practicing without indolence—
Such a bhikṣu of vigor Is able to destroy all demonic deeds.
The bhikṣu dwells in mountain valleys, Far removed from all greedy seeking.
How can one wear the saṃghāṭī robe yet live like a slave?
Furthermore, though such a person maintains the precepts, devas and nāgas always show them respect;
yet, lacking any wholesome dharma to rely upon, they are like geese departing from a dried-up pond.
If one can be free from desire, one will forever be without faults or afflictions;
yet to delight in associating with kings and ministers gives rise to various anxieties and fears.
Whether in a forest hermitage, a wilderness, or among the graves, [one remains at peace].
Amidst the wisteria vines within the mountain valleys, one should settle the mind and sit in tranquil meditation.
If one does not cultivate meditative concentration but only busies oneself seeking food and drink,
you should know that such a person is no different from the hungry ghosts.
Concentration is the joy free from defilement, as taught by the wise;
apart from meditative concentration, there is no other joy whatsoever.
Those of inferior intelligence and deluded persons are unable to cultivate it.
Attached to worldly food and drink, they deceive themselves;
led astray by the realm of desire, their minds give rise to further craving and delight.
They increase unwholesome dharmas and destroy the conduct that leads to rebirth in heaven.
If a person, toward the Dharma teacher, With faith and resolve, abandons self-conceit,
Arouses a mind of diligence, And maintains it so as not to forget;
Because they have heard this Dharma, They rely upon what has been thus taught.
Furthermore, they are able to cause others not to give rise to the conceit of "I am.
Being skilled in discerning and explaining the characteristics of pride and excessive pride,
and knowing themselves and others as they truly are, such a person is a wise bhikṣu.
With a mind distracted by ignorance, harboring the poison of pride and anger,
and intoxicated with the arrogance of fame and profit— how could such a person possess tranquility?
Only when one’s name accords with one’s conduct, abiding well within the realm of wisdom, can true peace be found.
Fearing the faults and afflictions of birth and death, one possesses the fruits and benefits of renunciation.
By abiding in the realm of wisdom, one comprehends self-nature and other-nature,
as well as what is the path and what is not the path, and the retribution of wholesome and unwholesome karma.
Having abandoned the two extremes of pleasure and pain, and not practicing that which is not the Path,
one casts off the fetters of the household life and dwells in peace, free from sorrow and suffering.
Yet when a bhikṣu resides in a monastic dwelling, distraction arises within him.
If one does not differ from worldly people, one ruins the Dharma of the śramaṇa.
If one dwells in mountain forests, one will not be slandered by others;
by constantly practicing meditative concentration and upholding the sūtras, the mind will be free from distraction.
If one delights in dwelling in monastic quarters, Greedy for acquisition and hoarding,
With a mind that finds no moment’s rest, One eventually brings about the destruction of one's life.
Failing to realize that life is not firm, One's happiness likewise diminishes accordingly.
Disregarding present causes, one seeks happiness in future lives;
yet when the mind does not give rise to such longing, one is a person free from greed.
Having few desires and knowing contentment, such a one attains the fruit of the śramaṇa.
Delighting in dwelling among mountains and forests, Cultivating all the various meditative concentrations,
And constantly praising the virtues of concentration, One is able to leave behind all faults and afflictions.
Detached from all worldly associations, One is not led astray by sensory objects.
Having well severed that craving, like fire consuming dry wood,
if one delights in dwelling in tranquility, then one fears the ocean of the three realms of existence;
this bhikṣu of purified body is not burdened by dwellings.
If one delights in dwelling in a monastic cell, it only increases craving;
in this life and in future births, by what means could one achieve liberation?
If one delights in dwelling in a monastic cell, one will mostly seek out acquaintances.
Those who constantly commit various evils will later fall into the evil realms.
If a person possesses clear wisdom and can abandon the notions of enemy and friend,
they will be free from such dualistic opposition, and their mind will remain ever tranquil.
All evils are like mud; one should not be stained by even a small portion of them.
One should dwell alone in the mountain forests, abandoning delusion to seek tranquility.
By skillfully cultivating stainless conduct, one then destroys all defilements.
Relying solely upon solitude, one can transcend the realm of desire.
Regarding both mundane and supramundane phenomena, being free from defilement and without attachment,
knowing suffering and pleasure with equanimity— this is called tranquility.
Having abandoned the five desires, being content and free from longing,
living a pure life— this is called tranquility.
Always remaining far from the clamor of the world, one does not frequent improper places.
Practicing alone by oneself—this is called tranquility.
Having forever severed craving and desire, one is then free from all sorrow and joy;
with body, speech, and mind purified—this is called tranquility.
Regarding phenomena that are superior or inferior, the mind does not give rise to high or low;
observing with the equality of wisdom—this is called tranquility.
Regarding wholesome and unwholesome actions, one fully knows their karmic retributions.
Not clinging to worldly phenomena— this is called tranquility.
Arousing right wisdom and constantly reflecting on the faults of desire,
Thoroughly understanding that which arises from sensation— this is called tranquility.
Well-taming all the sense faculties, Knowing the proper time to teach the Dharma,
And fearing the causes of saṃsāra— This is called tranquility.
Thoroughly understanding the characteristics of one's own body, One eliminates the distractions of the sense faculties.
Constantly relying on mountain forests— this is called tranquility.
Abiding in right mindfulness and diligence, always contemplating the departure from all evils,
and not sporting in gardens and groves— this is called tranquility.
Having severed all afflictions, like fire consuming a forest of trees, one is called a śramaṇa; such a person does not cling to any desires.
If one delights in worldly affairs and constantly dwells among the villages, [one is not a śramaṇa].
The deluded deceive others while claiming to dwell in accordance with the Dharma;
yet they feel no love or joy for the pure araṇya.
This is a realm inhabited only by those who are free from craving.
If one is addicted to the five desires and delights in worldly discourse,
you should know that such a person cannot go there.
Those whose minds delight in emptiness and stillness, who single-mindedly cultivate the various meditative concentrations—
Those brahmins and śramaṇas dwell well upon the path of peace and security.
If a person cultivates meritorious deeds, they shall obtain a most excellent reward;
therefore, one should practice extensively, for without merit there is no wealth.
Merit is the most supreme treasure; merit is called an inexhaustible storehouse.
Merit is like that bright lamp; merit is equal to parents.
Merit can give birth to the heavens; merit can lead one to superior realms.
When humans cultivate meritorious deeds, they experience results that accord with their wishes.
If one cultivates those meritorious deeds, one will certainly attract wealth and happiness;
one should understand well that without merit, there is no happiness.
Merit is beneficial throughout the three periods of time; its intrinsic nature is lovely and delightful.
Like a shadow that always follows, it is never abandoned for even a moment.
When the merit of the gods diminishes, they will before long fall into decline.
Therefore, regarding meritorious deeds, one should practice them continuously.
Without merit, there is much hardship; one is constantly born in inferior states.
Without virtue, one hopes for pleasant fruits as if seeking butter from sand.
Fools are deceived by their own minds and are constantly estranged from meritorious deeds;
since they do not cultivate wholesome dharmas, their evils increase ever more.
If one cultivates various virtues in the present life, merit will arise following those actions.
By these causes and conditions, one will later be born among the devas.
If one delights in cultivating meritorious deeds, one will be honored and revered by all people;
the body will be free from all oppression, and the mind will always be tranquil.
When virtuous people practice wholesome dharmas, they obtain the most excellent joy within all joys;
through those pure causes, they shall attain the path to enlightenment.
Therefore, all sentient beings should diligently cultivate meritorious deeds.
Suddenly impermanence arrives, and [the body] will certainly belong to another.
If one repeatedly cultivates and practices sublime meritorious deeds,
then according to their various causes, one will receive their respective fruits.
In all worlds, the dharmas of good and evil are the masters;
one should diligently cultivate wholesome dharmas, for they alone can provide protection.
If one abandons wholesome dharmas and delights in committing various evils, [one will surely fall].
For this reason, one undergoes the sufferings of hell.
As long as life has not yet ended and the limbs of the body remain intact, one should strive with diligent effort; such a person is endowed with great wisdom.
If a person skillfully expounds the Dharma, able to awaken others and lead them to the city of Nirvana,
where they dwell in peace, free from sorrow and fear; if,
regarding that True Dharma, they speak even a single four-line verse—
Revealing the path of renunciation, he is the foremost refuge and protector.
Skillfully proclaiming the True Dharma, one can swiftly attain the Buddha-way;
though Śakra possesses few causes, how could great wealth ever bring it about?
If one is greedily attached to worldly wealth, the wisdom of the Dharma will not increase;
precious jewels may be scattered and destroyed, but the wealth of the Dharma is inexhaustible in its use.
Only the wholesome dharmas one cultivates will follow one through hundreds of thousands of lifetimes.
Of all the wealth and possessions one owns, not a single step follows one when departing.
Furthermore, water, fire, and thieves can deplete one's riches;
yet the wholesome Dharma within the mind cannot be taken away even in the slightest degree.
Even if one experiences immeasurable sensual pleasures for many long eons, they will inevitably perish;
therefore, one must earnestly seek the True Dharma.
This alone is the single wholesome dharma that one should diligently protect.
By performing good, life is prolonged; by creating evil, it is swiftly extinguished.
One should draw near to wholesome dharmas and practice according to the teachings;
then all sufferings will not arise, and one will obtain supreme bliss.
If one delights in committing unwholesome deeds and constantly practices what is contrary to the Dharma,
one will later fall into hell and undergo immeasurable, extreme suffering.
Throughout immeasurable eons, one should always take refuge in the Triple Gem.
First one experiences the pleasures of the heavens, and later attains the fruit of tranquility.
Observing that the meritorious rewards received in the present all arise from prior karma—
whether they be causes for pleasure or suffering— each occurs without the slightest deviation.
One should steadfastly maintain pure precepts and extensively cultivate meritorious deeds,
continuing day and night without interruption, like a river that never ceases.
If a person abandons wholesome dharmas, this present life will have been spent in vain.
If one does not neglect the causes of virtue, one will obtain the happiness of humans and devas.
If one’s meritorious conduct is perfected and one skillfully protects and upholds the True Dharma,
such a person is the most supreme and peerless in the world.
It is better to lose one's body and life than to transgress the True Dharma;
for those who depart from the True Dharma will wander through the various currents of evil.
Fools, attached to sensual pleasures, cast aside the Eye of the True Dharma.
Their present life is spent in vain, like rain falling upon the ocean.
Failing to guard their prohibitive precepts and delighting in the commission of various evils,
the seeds of virtue in the field of the mind have no means by which to grow.
One should observe with single-mindedness the most supreme and pure Dharma;
having reached the state of non-extinction, there shall be no more suffering.
If the sense faculties are unrestrained and one remains attached to sensory objects, [suffering will follow].
Then one will be entangled by them, revolving without rest.
If one does not cling to sinful dharmas, like molten gold blazing brightly,
one leaves behind the perils of the three realms of existence and attains ultimate tranquility.
Endowed with pure wisdom, they always revere the True Dharma;
having heard it from those teachers of the Dharma, they are able to believe and accept it.
They constantly make offerings to the Triple Gem and serve their parents with filial piety.
One is able to reach the city of Nirvāṇa, Abiding in the most supreme peace and security.
Possessing the outward form and deportment of one who has gone forth, Skillfully proclaiming the True Dharma,
And diligently cultivating the holy life, One attains the most excellent and wondrous bliss.
Among all forms of giving, the gift of Dharma is unsurpassed;
Arisen with courageous diligence, one cultivates the various meditative concentrations.
Such a teacher of the Dharma is praised by the Tathāgata.
If one does not give rise to pure faith, one is no different from the animals.
Always delighting in the peaceful Dharma taught by the various sages and saints,
one should cultivate the three fields of merit to seek liberation.
Toward that Dharma-preacher, one should give rise to the highest reverence;
for the sake of seeking the True Dharma, the mind shall not grow weary.
Observing the objects of the five desires, one realizes they are truly not happiness.
Even if one sees them, one should not grasp at them; this is the admonition of the Muni.
Those who delight in practicing the True Dharma will see the path free from defilement;
they shall enjoy the bliss of the Dharma, which even the gods cannot attain.
The wholesome deeds performed in the present abide like a burden upon one's back;
therefore, with a single mind, one should always remain close to that goodness.
Observing with the eye of wisdom, one sees the various bitter retributions of the future.
The fool delights in committing evil, while the wise person’s mind is ever fearful of it.
Because they possess that right wisdom, they perceive all evils as perilous and difficult;
always remaining in accord with the wholesome, they attain liberation from all afflictions.
If one indulges in that folly, Delighting only in the realm of desire,
When pleasure perishes and suffering manifests, One will labor in vain,
giving rise to regret and distress. As long as life lasts, Let the mind not give way to distraction.
By constantly cultivating meritorious deeds, one can escape the evil realms.
Life passes away swiftly, and the retribution of merit does not endure long;
therefore, you should embrace the True Dharma to become a Lord of the Heaven of Contentment.
If one abandons wholesome qualities, one will give rise to negligence;
furthermore, failing to cultivate meritorious deeds, one shall before long fall away and perish.
Each [should reflect] while one is still robust and while the limbs of the body are unimpaired.
Extensively cultivating various meritorious deeds, one will later have no sorrow or regret.
If one does not cultivate the causes of merit but delights only in heedlessness,
know that such a person is the very root of the suffering of hell.
Although they possess all the sense faculties, they take no delight in the True Dharma;
how can they seek a livelihood and raise a large retinue?
Day and night, one should always hold the True Dharma within the mind.
By associating with a teacher of the Dharma, one becomes far removed from all defilements of sin.
Through the observance of precepts, one is born in heaven and enjoys various sensual pleasures;
yet the fool who neglects meritorious deeds will before long fall away and perish.
Delighting in the arising of pure wisdom, adorning the body with the jewel of ethical discipline,
and constantly fearing the serpent of desire, one is praised by all the devas.
Because of their love for and delight in wholesome dharmas, the devas always pay them respect.
If one gives rise to perverted thoughts, one will be poor and lack merit and wisdom.
Wholesome dharmas are like a bridge; by upholding the precepts, one can cross over.
If one does not cultivate those virtuous practices, by what means could one cross the ocean of suffering?
By practicing wholesome deeds in accordance with the Dharma, one will certainly attain wholesome fruits;
even through hundreds of thousands of koṭis of eons, those virtues cannot be destroyed.
Constantly cultivating the dharmas of generosity and ethical discipline, one should guard them with wisdom.
May all who have any requests take refuge in the Triple Gem.
By skillfully practicing the three kinds of giving, they can remedy the three faults;
through being free from those faults, they shall attain pure merit.
Delighting in the perfection of pure precepts, Giving rise to resolute and right faith,
One destroys the suffering of the three realms of existence, Just as the sun dispels the veil of clouds.
If one is endowed with the True Dharma, All the devas will show them respect.
This person shall attain the supreme state of tranquility.
