Compiled by the Venerable Master Guānwúwèi,
Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven Translation Bureau, Cháo-sàn Dàfū:
If a person cultivates manifold virtues, with a pure mind and upright character,
One shall be born among the devas, as the Muni has declared.
Those who delight in giving and kind speech, whose minds are ever conjoined with loving-kindness,
and who protect and cherish all sentient beings— this is the true cause.
Because their minds are pure, they serve as a basis for wholesome qualities;
they experience the bliss of the celestial realms, and light issues forth from their bodies.
This light is most excellent, continuing on without interruption.
Just as one who possesses the light of a lamp in this world does not fall into various perils and difficulties,
so too if a person’s mind is pure— like a stainless mani-jewel—
and they are always equanimous and humble, they shall be born among the devas.
If the mind is well-tamed, and one maintains the precepts and cultivates various meditative concentrations,
becoming pure like refined gold, one will be born among the devas.
Toward all sentient beings, one should always give rise to a heart of compassion.
By refraining from the sin of killing, one is reborn among the devas.
With a body of radiant purity while dwelling in the world,
untainted by any sinful dharmas and free from all harm, one is reborn among the devas.
Seeing the objects of desire as poison, Regarding gold and jewels as mere grass,
One leaves behind the afflictions of craving and greed, And is reborn among the devas.
If a person is free from craving and greed, Their mind will not be dragged away by sensory objects.
Having escaped from fear and perilous difficulties, one is born among the devas.
Having distanced oneself from kinsmen and associates— who are mutually entangling bonds—
one practices alone and is born among the devas.
Fully endowed with sublime conduct, dwelling securely in pure wisdom,
and having well subdued desire, one is born among the devas.
With the three karmas free from transgression, one delights in cultivating the various meditative concentrations.
Praised by the multitude, one is reborn among the devas.
Having abandoned evil associates and distanced oneself from the poisoned arrow of craving,
not bound by the snares of women, one is reborn among the devas.
Skillfully detached from the entanglements of craving, like a sword severing a rotten rope,
one dwells in peace, free from all fears, and attains rebirth among the devas.
With the power of wisdom most firm and courageous, one should always single-mindedly seek the True Dharma.
By practicing generosity, ethical discipline, and meditative concentration, one attains birth among the various devas.
Furthermore, those sentient beings who extensively cultivate virtuous conduct experience the fruition of being born within the heavens, where the devas always pay them respect.
When humans perform good deeds they are born as devas; when devas cultivate merit they become humans.
Always relying upon the True Dharma, they possess the power and capability to assist one another.
Some fall away from the celestial realm, while others from other destinies are reborn among the devas.
If one is separated from those wholesome karmas, one will then proceed to the three evil realms.
All dharmas of tranquility and goodness are the fundamental cause of happiness;
therefore, even in one's dreams, one should not abandon wholesome dharmas.
Wholesome dharmas extinguish unwholesome ones; truth subdues falsehood.
The gods defeat the asuras, and wisdom destroys ignorance and dullness.
Wholesome dharmas serve as a staircase, which the wise are able to ascend and tread upon.
One proceeds toward the realms of the gods, experiencing supreme and wondrous bliss.
By refraining from the sevenfold transgressions of body and speech, such as killing and stealing—
these seven serve as a ladder by which one attains birth in the celestial realms.
Adorned by pure karma, their bodies are radiant and most lovely,
just like those bright lamps emitting light from their own forms.
Therefore, all gods and humans take the precepts as their foundation.
Constantly giving rise to a heart of joy, one experiences inexhaustible bliss.
Attended by celestial maidens like the myriad stars surrounding the moon,
one sports within the heavens— all this is obtained through virtuous causes.
According to one's desires and following the mind, Having obtained [it], there is no decrease or loss;
That joy constantly increases, All of which is obtained through virtuous causes.
Practicing the perfection of giving well, One feels compassion for all sentient beings.
Endowed with a mind of loving-kindness, one shall be born in the heavens.
Having distanced oneself from the transgression of killing and not harming any living beings,
being endowed with virtuous conduct, one shall be born in the heavens.
Staying far away from taking what is not given, Delighting in the practice of giving,
And being without stinginess regarding even small things, One will be born in the heavens.
Abandoning sexual misconduct, Always relying upon that right path,
With a stainless mind and tranquility, one is reborn in the heavens.
By abandoning the fault of drinking alcohol, the mind does not become deluded;
one is not ridiculed by others and is reborn in the heavens.
Though the devas enjoy happiness, they should not give rise to negligence;
they should seek the bliss of tranquility, for therein lies eternal peace.
Having experienced the exquisite desires of the heavens and the most excellent palaces, [they must still strive for liberation].
Moment by moment, all is impermanent; before long, it shall come to an end.
Even Mount Meru, most lofty and sublime, can be surpassed by wholesome karma;
even to the Ultimate Heaven, how could one reach it without virtue?
Never satiated with the objects of desire, the gods become even more distinguished therein;
yet as craving increases further and further, how can they attain tranquility?
Because of their craving, the gods cling to pleasure without rest.
Constantly burned by the fire of craving, how can one find happiness?
There are three grades of wholesome deeds; these three types serve as the three causes.
Through the manifestation of the three realms of existence, the three karmas bring about the three fruits.
Because you delighted in wholesome dharmas, practicing generosity, patience, and non-violence, and were in accord with true conduct, you have attained birth in the heavens.
You are fully endowed with supreme adornments: flower garlands and precious necklaces.
Experiencing bliss within the heavens is entirely obtained through virtuous karma.
Furthermore, regarding the sublime pleasures in the heavens, there are distinctions of superior, middling, and inferior;
these three grades of causes manifest according to the fruits of one's merit.
By practicing those virtuous deeds accordingly, one does not lose the two kinds of retribution;
whether among humans or in the heavens, one shall experience happiness.
You have cultivated meritorious karma in the past and well guarded the sevenfold precepts.
Now having come to this celestial realm, they personally enjoy the fruits of their merit.
There are exquisite lotus ponds where pure, cool, and fragrant breezes arise;
within these wondrous and precious pavilions, the various devas sport together.
The most exquisite mountain of gold, with peaks of lapis lazuli,
abounds with jewel-trees laden with flowers and fruit, where the devas sport together.
There stands a forest of supreme karpāsa silk, its branches and leaves all flourishing and lush.
Clear springs encircle its center, where all the devas sport together.
Furthermore, there are mountains of the seven treasures, surrounded on four sides by flowing rivers;
golden sand is spread across their beds, where all the devas sport together.
The exquisite fragrance of blue lotuses, groves of *mandārava* flowers,
and the wondrous songs of flocks of birds— there the gods sport together. Furthermore,
there are other superior places, all consisting of forests of various precious trees.
The palaces are adorned with jewels, where the devas sport together.
With the subtle sounds of the five musical instruments and the most excellent singing and dancing, all who hear them find delight; the devas sport together.
Precepts are its seed, from which all fruits of happiness are born;
regarding the five sublime sensual pleasures, one enjoys them according to one's heart.
The celestial radiance and garlands are extraordinary, pure, and stainless.
Even all forms of happiness are produced by virtuous causes.
Sporting with the various devas, one experiences immeasurable joy;
such are the causes of this happiness, yet these causes were not created by me.
In a most excellent and wondrous pavilion, adorned with various jewels,
he dwells in peace by virtue of wholesome causes planted in the past;
though he enjoys the five vast sensual pleasures, he gives rise to no mind of defiled attachment.
By being freed from the three kinds of bonds, one becomes a Śakra, King of the Devas.

If a person’s mind is upright and honest, and they cultivate meditative concentration to eliminate distraction, they will be reborn in this celestial realm; their own karma will be directly realized there.
Having extensively cultivated various wholesome deeds, one experiences continuous succession of happiness;
realizing that this is the fruit received now due to causes practiced in the past,
one cultivates goodness in this present life, just like planting a forest of trees.
Causing the continuum to flourish and thrive— such a person is a wise one.
In whatever place they are born, whether they perform good or unwholesome deeds,
they each receive various retributions according to their respective causes.
If a person cultivates wholesome causes, they will be reborn among the gods;
if they create unwholesome causes, they shall fall into hell.
A foolish person, attached to desire, abandons what is good and performs what is unwholesome.
They feel no fear at the time of death, yet they bring about their own ruin.
The retribution for wholesome and unwholesome karma grows from each seed according to its kind;
the fool is attached to pleasure and never abandons it even for a moment.
By practicing the three grades of wholesome karma, observing the seven branches of body and speech,
and liberating oneself from those three poisons, one attains birth among the devas.
Unmoved by the objects of desire, one likewise does not give rise to praise for them.
Abiding in the purity of detachment from passion, one attains birth among the devas.
By skillfully practicing various forms of giving, one subdues that stingy mind;
transcending all places of suffering and hardship, one attains birth among the devas.
Not harming the lives of sentient beings, but always giving rise to love and protection,
abiding in a mind of tranquil compassion, one attains birth among the devas.
Staying far away from taking what is not given, one’s mind is like a blazing fire.
Abiding in right reflection, one is reborn among the gods.
Unstained by the mire of desire, seeing the forms of others as one’s own mother,
and observing well with wisdom, one is reborn among the gods.
The fires of hell are harbored within one’s own mind, ignited from the fuel of the tongue;
this arises from speaking false words. By abstaining from this, one is born among the devas;
for the tongue lacks truth, pointing to the void while claiming existence.
By leaving behind deceitful and ornate speech, one is born among the gods.
Always staying far from divisive talk, loving and respecting one another with a compassionate heart,
and refraining from words that cause estrangement, one is born among the gods.
Harsh speech is like a sword or a staff; the wise should keep far from it.
By always uttering beautiful words, one will be reborn among the gods.
By well-guarding these seven precepts, one can be born in the various heavens.
The wise should understand this as taught by all the Buddhas:
Adorned with manifold virtues, one is reborn in the heavens;
yet if one neglects former practice, one will surely feel regret.
In the heavens, there are wondrous groves of creepers, With long tendrils spreading in all four directions;
Adorned with beautiful flowers and fragrances, The devas rest beneath them.
If one cultivates various virtuous deeds, One shall surely obtain all manner of happiness.
They proceed toward the celestial realms, where they obtain such fruits as these.
Furthermore, those hosts of devas experience three grades of happiness;
each, according to their prior karma, attains their respective results.
Because cause and effect resemble one another, yet people are unwilling to cultivate the cause;
if one thoroughly understands cause and effect, one shall obtain a portion of happiness.
Regarding the sublime objects of the five desires, the gods give rise to attachment and delight therein.
The minds of fools are deluded by ignorance; they do not perceive the great terrors that lie ahead.
Craving sublime sensual pleasures and seeking superior realms, they fail to cultivate the causes for the fruits they desire; thus, their folly increases.
If one desires the fruits of that happiness yet does not maintain pure precepts, it is like a person dwelling in darkness who seeks light without a lamp.
Without seeds there is no fruit; without a lamp, how can there be light?
Without morality, one is not born in heaven; without wisdom, there is no liberation.
Pleasure is summoned by karma, and all such things are defiled and turbid.
One should therefore give rise to a resolute mind and seek stainless bliss.
If a person abandons sensual pleasures and forever cuts off all seeking,
they will have no mind of craving or attachment and will skillfully eliminate the grasping at "mine.
In the time it takes to bend or extend one's arm, they shall be reborn in the Yāma Heaven.
The hosts of devas vied with one another to welcome him; his bodily radiance shone constantly.
Like Mount Meru, the king of mountains, adorned and polished by myriad jewels, he emerged from that great ocean and dwelt suspended in space.
Jewel trees produce cool breezes, where birds and deer dwell together;
celestial maidens reside amidst red lotuses, sporting with one another.
With exquisite and wondrous garlands of jewels, they engage in various songs and dances to their heart's content.
The devas and their goddesses all made offerings and paid him homage.
Amidst the universally radiant garlands and the lovely, clear rivers,
they heard the exquisite sounds of the five types of music and realized that dependent origination is illusory.
Immeasurable hosts of devas, all together sporting and playing,
receiving three grades of happiness according to the causes they cultivated in the past.
Having long practiced giving and precepts, their resolve and mindfulness remain ever firm.
By being fully endowed with those practices, one is born in that heaven.
Constantly following the Buddha’s words, cherishing and protecting all sentient beings,
and abiding in a tranquil mind— one is born in that heaven.
Endowed with loving-kindness and patience, having eradicated the deep-seated roots of enmity,
and always remaining in accord with a compassionate mind— one will be born in that celestial realm.
If a person’s mind is tranquil and they do not cling to the three realms of existence, [they shall likewise be reborn there].
By having well-tamed that mind, one is born in that heaven.
Speaking only words of truth, taking no pleasure in much empty talk,
and remaining far removed from what is unbeneficial, one is born in that heaven.
Having realized the nature of old age, sickness, and death, and fearing the wandering of saṃsāra,
those who joyfully seek the bliss of nirvāṇa will be reborn in that heaven.
Dwelling among rocky valleys, forests, and springs, or in cemeteries or beneath trees, they find their home.
Those who deeply cultivate the various meditative concentrations will be born in that heaven.
Those who possess wondrous eloquence and preach the Dharma knowing the proper time and place,
And who always abandon evil associates, will be born in that heaven.
Not wandering to visit or enjoy the sights of villages and cities,
but dwelling only in solitary seclusion— one such as this will be born in that heaven.
Constantly observing one's own body, taking its impurity as the fundamental basis.
Moments do not abide for long; those who understand the nature of all phenomena,
who know that these phenomena abide in their own place,
and who do not cling to saṃsāra— such people will be born in that heaven.
Knowing all sensations as they truly are—how they give rise to grasping—one’s mind does not produce craving; such a person is born in that heaven.
Understanding all phenomena to be like illusions, like a city of the gandharvas,
One who has well tamed their own mind will be born in that heaven.
Even the aggregates such as form are, in their sole nature, emptiness;
one who aspires to nirvāṇa will be born in that heaven.
Toward men and women alike, one should conceive the thought of them as one's own parents;
by viewing all sentient beings with equanimity, one will be born in that heaven.
By abandoning the fault of double-tongued speech and delighting in the utterance of kind words, [one attains this state].
With a mind always upright and sincere, one will be born in that heaven.
Free from mental arrogance, viewing the body as mere clay or wood,
Contented and ever humble, one will be born in that heaven.
Throughout those days and nights, their minds do not give rise to weariness;
delighting in the diligent cultivation of all virtues, such people are born in that heaven.
As for restlessness, dullness, sleep, and indolence—
Those whose minds constantly give rise to detachment will be born in that heaven. Those who,
due to the distraction of the five faculties, repeatedly seize upon various objects,
but skillfully guard themselves with wisdom, will be born in that heaven.
Having well cultivated the four means of integration, clearly understood the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths,
and possessed vast knowledge and vision, such a person is born in that heaven.
Regarding the cause of suffering, the fruit of suffering, and the ultimate limit of the cessation of suffering—
Those who understand all things with true clarity will be born in that heaven.
Even when encountering the most perilous hardships, they do not abandon the various wholesome dharmas;
because their minds are tranquil, they will be born in that heaven.
Not delighting in exquisite garments, but always wearing robes of coarse wool,
subsisting on alms through a pure livelihood— one is born in that heaven.
With a mind that delights in practicing meditative concentration, sitting as still as a piece of withered wood, one is born in that heaven.
Those who well cultivate the practice of renunciation will be born in that heaven.
Whether the food and drink they obtain be exquisite or coarse,
if their minds give rise to neither delight nor aversion, they will be born in that heaven.
Using the earth as one’s bedding, with a tree beneath as one’s pavilion, their mind is ever serene; such a person is born in that heaven.
With the faculties always tranquil, they are not led astray by sensory objects.
Free from the defilement of distraction, such a person is born in that heaven.
When the eye perceives objects such as forms, understanding that their characteristics are all empty,
and thus possessing such correct knowledge, such a person is born in that heaven.
Whether reviled or praised, their minds remain unshaken upon hearing it;
free from the association of afflictions, such people are born in that heaven.
Having understood that good and evil karma inevitably result in their respective retributions, they abide in certainty.
One should cultivate that holy life; such a person will be born in that heaven.

One should abandon the faults of greed and the like; having committed deeds that invite evil retribution and constantly fearing all forms of suffering and affliction, such a person will be born in that heaven.
Such great benefit and profit are the causes of that bliss;
one should practice all virtues, for by doing so one is born in that heaven.
It is surely a forest of merit, the most supreme and pure happiness.
It can lead one to enlightenment, just as a calf follows its mother.
If one newly cultivates the causes of happiness, one can eliminate old suffering;
if one newly creates the causes of suffering, one will destroy old happiness.
Like bitter gall coated with honey, or like poisoned food mixed with delicacies, because good and evil are intermingled, a sweet flavor cannot be found.
True happiness does not arise from craving; this happiness is exclusively pure.
One who can proceed upon the path to tranquility is no longer subject to the names of the three poisons.
This bliss is unsurpassed; being virtuous in the beginning, middle, and end, the heart of craving and attachment will never arise again.
The minds of fools are distracted; they cannot realize selflessness.
Amidst objects of suffering and pleasure, they constantly seek those sensual delights.
If a person is free from defiled desire, they will sever the cause of saṃsāra.
By relying on pure karma, one can reach the further shore.
That defiled craving is not bliss; it is associated with greed and hatred.
By relinquishing the faults of greed and the like, one attains stainless happiness.
Though they experience the pleasures of the heavens, they do not give rise to delight;
seeking liberation with excellence, they have no attachment to craving.
If one is caught by the snare of craving, that entanglement is truly not happiness.
To reach the state of non-extinction is ultimate bliss.
If pleasure arises from desire, it is not what the wise delight in;
to be free from the conditions of defiled desire is the supreme bliss.
Not delighting in the practice of tranquility and abandoning the forest hermitage (araṇya),
how can one remain without sustenance, like a vulture at a lotus pond?
Due to negligence, the gods do not delight in relying upon tranquility.
Seeking cool light from the sun is a perversion, for it is not appropriate;
if one delights in being free from craving, then one can be liberated from all suffering.
This bliss is unsurpassed, yet it is unknown to the foolish.
Skillfully cultivating the various meditative concentrations, one can eliminate mental distraction;
thus, free from the shame of craving, this bliss is unsurpassed.
When the wise dwell in the forest, they constantly contemplate tranquility.
Having attained freedom from that greedy mind, the joys of the devas cannot compare.
All pleasures of the five desires are ultimately not enduring;
not giving rise to greed for them—this joy is the most supreme.
If one dwells in forests and wilds, one attains the highest peace and security;
yet all causes of suffering have greed as their root.
Enveloped by greed, one takes pleasure in food, drink, and clothing.
Such a person will be unable to sit in meditative seclusion within the forest;
yet by constantly observing with wisdom and relying upon wholesome objects,
one will always delight in the forest, cultivating practices such as non-attachment.
If a person’s mind is tranquil, they will not give rise to distraction;
always delighting in the forest, they attain freedom from defiled craving.
If a person is free from deluded conduct, they are without the faults of the three realms of existence.
Always delighting in the forest, one attains the supreme tranquility;
because the mind is tranquil, there are no further desires.
Always delighting in the forest, one cultivates the various meditative concentrations.
In cities and villages, let the mind not give rise to attachment;
relying solely on secluded places, settle the mind in meditative seclusion.
If a person engages in wrong reflection, they will be surrounded by craving and the like.
If one does not delight in dwelling within the forest, by what means can one exhaust all outflows?
If one stays near the clamor and bustle of the world, then distraction will arise;
therefore, one should distance oneself from such things, for this is praised by the wise.
One should know that dwelling in the forest is the most excellent and pure joy;
free from the turbidity of greed and other defilements, the wise always draw near to it.
If one takes up residence in the forest, the sense faculties will remain constantly at ease and delighted.
Even though Śakra, Lord of the Devas, does not equal them in their joy;
for they constantly practice meditative concentration and abide securely in the pure Dharma,
whereas those gods of the Yāma heaven, being attached to pleasure, are unable to practice it.
If one indulges in the pleasures of the five desires, one will constantly give rise to various sufferings and afflictions;
being shrouded by ignorance and craving, how could such pleasure endure?
Constantly seek the wealth of the sublime Dharma and do not commit the three types of unwholesome actions.
One should know that such a person, though possessed of delusion and craving, cannot be bound by them.
Regarding the wholesome dharmas they practice, their mind constantly maintains protection;
out of compassion for all sentient beings, they lead them to a place of peace and security.
If the mind becomes distracted, wholesome dharmas do not appear before it;
since those wholesome causes are absent, future happiness cannot be attained.
The wise constantly observe all sentient beings in the world:
All things are suffering, empty, and impermanent; thus, one does not give rise to craving or attachment.
One delights in practicing the dharma of tranquility, diligently seeking the wisdom of the Buddha, always uttering words of truth, and thereby attaining the end of suffering.
Far removed from the single dharma of craving, and from the two kinds of suffering and pleasure, one who understands the faults of the three periods of time attains a share of happiness.
The fruit of happiness arises from causes; once it has arisen, it immediately diminishes.
Those causes of tainted pleasure, If not cultivated, will not increase.
One who does not give rise to attachment toward such pleasure Is one who has abandoned craving;
Having skillfully crossed the ocean of the three realms of existence, They are able to reach the further shore.
Furthermore, those tainted pleasures do not endure for even a moment;
therefore, one should distance oneself from them and diligently seek the bliss of the immovable.
One should not grow weary of suffering, nor should one give rise to craving for pleasure.
Being unattached to these two, one can proceed upon the path to enlightenment.
The fool is attached to pleasure and lacks the means for renunciation;
it is like seeking oil from sand—it can never be obtained.
With a deluded and distracted mind, one gives rise to hundreds of thousands of thoughts;
constantly creating various causes of evil, one possesses not even a fraction of goodness.
If a person desires happiness, they should always rely upon the True Dharma.
Those who delight in practicing what is unrighteous will undergo all manner of suffering and affliction.
Having created the causes of their own suffering, how could they perceive happiness?
Since suffering and happiness each depend upon their respective causes, one should understand this and cultivate all forms of goodness.
Worldly pleasures are not tranquil; the power of impermanence is vast.
When stained by those cravings, they are like fine food mixed with poison.
By relying on sublime bliss, the virtuous reach the state of non-extinction.
Free from craving and having eliminated afflictions, one has no conflict of ice and fire within the heart.
Pleasure arises from female form; this is said to be nothing but suffering.
It is the seed of all evils, leading inevitably to rebirth in the evil realms.
If that which is pleasant brings about suffering in the future, how can it be called pleasure?
Ordinary people do not understand this, and thus they themselves undergo its bitter retribution.
When one indulges in those sensual pleasures, they are swept away by the passage of time.
Just as the sun does not remain for long, its radiance likewise fades away.
If a person, amidst suffering and pleasure, does not allow their mind to be swayed by them,
being neither afraid nor attached— such a one is a possessor of true wisdom.
Having experienced the fruits of merit cultivated in the past, yet failing to perform new wholesome deeds,
their pleasure gradually diminishes and great terror is about to arrive.
Furthermore, those gods and humans who enjoy supreme and wondrous happiness—
This pleasure is not firm; it is destroyed by impermanence.
If one does not awaken to that pleasure—which is like an illusion, a bubble, or the moon reflected in water—then for one thus attached to pleasure, all bodily bliss will scatter and perish.
This world is a great terror, from which no skillful means can provide escape.
The power of the Lord of Death is swift; once he has departed, there is no turning back.
Life and all pleasures are utterly dispersed and destroyed.
Bound by the snares of karma, they are dragged to other evil realms.
Having experienced vast and manifold pleasures in the past, how could one possibly describe them?
Why, then, do those deluded people never feel weary or satisfied?
The pleasure experienced in the present is intermingled with the poison of craving;
it is conditioned and impermanent, and all such things fall away.
The happiness of the three realms of existence is not something the wise delight in.
Able to intoxicate all the devas, by what means can they escape their feverish affliction?
Their time is not long; it passes as swiftly as a flash of lightning.
Those devas who are attached to pleasure are like dry wood being added to a fire.
All pleasures have already passed; one should cultivate various virtues with the mind, so that at the time of death, no sorrow or regret shall arise later.
Throughout hundreds of thousands of births, one has enjoyed all manner of happiness.
How long can the fool remain?
And where does his pleasure go?
The fool never tires of pleasure; it is like throwing fuel into a fire.
Therefore, one should abandon them; that pleasure is not ultimate.
Knowing the faults and perils of the five desires, one should leave behind craving.
Cultivating dhyāna to eliminate distraction—this is the most pure happiness.
If a person is attached to sensual desire, what they obtain is not true happiness;
it produces the causes for saṃsāra, like honey mixed with poison.
Therefore, one should never give rise to craving or delight in the five objects of desire.
That pleasure is not peaceful; one should seek ultimate bliss.
Having well subdued the sense faculties and not being disturbed by sensory objects, the wise person who possesses such knowledge does not allow the mind to follow after objects.
Fools, lacking even a modicum of wisdom, falsely perceive suffering as pleasure;
giving rise to delusion and perversion, they wander through the five realms of existence.
The wise always praise the supreme bliss of tranquility.
If one delights in sensual pleasures, one does not fear future dangers and hardships.
One must counteract all future sufferings with wisdom;
since suffering arises from transgressions, by not committing them, there will be no fault.
One who, through mutual regard for self and others, encourages one another to distance themselves from all evils,
and is able to provide protection in times of difficulty— such a person is called a kalyāṇamitra (spiritual friend).
They constantly speak words of benefit, bringing peace and happiness to both themselves and others.
If one delights in committing various evils, that person is not one's friend.
If one associates with evil companions, they will give rise to suffering and affliction;
by relying on virtuous and noble persons, one is forever freed from all woes and anxieties.
The practices cultivated by those two are known as defiled and pure;
regarding these two types of friends, the wise exercise careful discernment.
One should distance oneself from all evils and devote oneself exclusively to the cultivation of various virtues.
Since the causes of suffering no longer exist, one obtains only a share of happiness.
If one draws near to virtuous friends, one gains offerings and praise;
but if one associates with those who are unwholesome, one immediately falls into peril and hardship.
Distant from that conceit of "I," fearing all transgressions,
skillfully uprooting the very roots of sin, and eliminating faults such as greed;
firmly establishing all wholesome deeds, one stands in opposition to those who are evil.
One who increases meritorious conduct, And gives rise to no indolence;
Who is endowed with right view, Whose mind is firm and unshakable,
Whose courageous heart is disciplined and gentle— Such a person is called a true friend.
One should know that such a person is rare in the world;
all those who possess wisdom should draw near to them.
By distancing oneself from evil associates, one will attain a good reputation.
Thus, having understood this well, one should rely on [the Dharma] to seek liberation.
If a person relies on their noble lineage, wealth, or physical beauty,
they will gallop like a rutting elephant, fearing no deep pit.
With a mind constantly uplifted and the faculties perpetually distracted,
you should know that such a person is held in contempt by the world;
fearing no retribution for future suffering, they blindly commit manifold transgressions.
Since prior causes are not easily obtained, why do they disparage themselves?
Though they possess various meritorious deeds, if they do not cultivate wholesome conduct now,
those ignorant fools will once again drift and sink in the ocean of suffering.
Those treasures of the spiritual lineage, as well as all other forms of happiness,
are entirely impermanent and cannot be protected by anyone.
If one possesses such wise understanding and does not forsake pure ethical discipline, [one shall attain liberation].
Seeking birth within a noble lineage, one thus dwells in well-being.
Know that the dharma of pure precepts is like a cool, deep abyss;
it can dispel the heat of afflictions, and the mind remains ever serene.
Fully endowed with all sublime practices, Truly wealthy and prosperous,
associated with noble lineages, The mind does not give rise to renunciation.
Constantly drawing near to the wise, One is never born into low castes.
Diligently cultivating that merit and wisdom, one dwells well within a noble lineage.
If a king practices the True Dharma, his ministers and attendants will all be pure;
with his faculties well-subdued, he shall receive the protection of the devas.
Always practicing the conduct of patience, speaking with loving words and free from anger or joy,
that king is revered by all the people in the world.
Paying taxes at the proper time and enjoying wealth in accordance with the True Dharma, he reigns.
That king, free from a greedy mind, shall become the Lord of the Yāma Heaven.
Pure and without partiality, and devoid of notions of enemy or kin,
that king with an impartial mind shall surely attain the status of Lord of the Gods.
Regarding what was bestowed by a former king, one does not give rise to the intent to seize it;
by not afflicting sentient beings, one shall become a lord of devas.
Joyfully and diligently practicing generosity and ethical discipline, one always utters words of truth.
Regarding all sentient beings with equanimity, one shall become a lord of devas.
Delighting in virtuous and noble persons, casting out evil associates,
and guarding the true Dharma, one shall become a lord of devas.
Delighting in loyal and upright ministers, not becoming attached to female beauty,
with a mind free from defilement and tranquil, one shall become a lord of gods.
Not listening to the words of flatterers, one delights in what is spoken by righteous persons.
Like the excellence of ambrosia, one shall become a lord of devas;
Always delighting in hearing the True Dharma, not clinging to worldly treasures,
And being liberated from the defilement of craving, one shall become a lord of devas.
Always giving rise to right view, Not relying on those false teachings,
With a pure and unshakable mind, One shall become a lord of gods.
Endowed with precepts and wisdom, Delighting in courageous practice of giving,
One who gains the praise of the people shall become a lord of gods;
Always employing gentle speech and cherishing all living beings,
Acting in accordance with truth, one shall become a lord of gods.
Unafraid of the increase or decrease of wealth, And never having been stingy or miserly,
With a mind like Mount Sumeru, One shall become a Lord of Devas.
Or when enemy troops invade with violence, Knowing who is brave and fierce and who is timid and weak—
Through the peace of skillful means and wisdom, one shall become a Lord of Devas;
within those three realms, the Three Jewels are supreme,
and by being able to cause them to flourish through power, one shall become a Lord of Devas.
Issuing commands at the proper time for the benefit and happiness of all living beings,
causing them to leave behind peril and hardship, one shall become a Lord of Devas.
Free from the faults of defiled desire and taking no pleasure in excessive sleep, one attains this state.
Always in accord with wisdom, one shall become a lord of devas;
With a firm mind and diligent effort, never giving rise to weariness,
One crosses the torrential flood of the three realms of existence and shall become a lord of devas.
In all undertakings, one acts with careful discernment and without error;
cherishing one’s ministers, one shall become a lord of gods.
One does not utter harsh words and takes no pleasure in those who are evil.
Only through benevolence, forbearance, and peace Shall one become a lord of gods.
By committing no sinful evils, And by not groundlessly giving rise to joy or anger,
With a mind free from such defilements, One shall become a lord of gods.
When one has reached a definitive resolution through reflection, and subsequently acts accordingly,
practicing in accordance with the True Dharma, one shall become a lord of devas.
Not craving various foods and drinks, one should always delight in the True Dharma.
Attaining pure pliancy, he is the wisest among the wise.
By understanding that True Dharma, he nurtures his subjects with love;
that king, endowed with merit and wisdom, is constantly protected by devas and nāgas.
Saṃsāra is exceedingly long-lasting, like a continuous thread;
if one enters into understanding the True Dharma, one will skillfully transcend it.
Regarding that which was spoken by the Tathāgata, the ten wholesome and true dharmas—
That king was able to practice and uphold [the Dharma], governing the world according to the law;
he thoroughly understood the principle of dependent origination, as well as meritorious and non-meritorious karma.
Seeing forms, he remained free from craving, constantly giving rise to great awakening.
By offering these most excellent things to the Tathāgata,
one thereby attains rebirth among gods and humans, where one is constantly honored and revered.
With a pure mind free from defilement, one protects the queen, the consorts, and the retinue.
Staying far removed from such false and improper ways, one who is content knows no sorrow or affliction.
While ordinary people are dragged away by sensory objects, the wise have minds free of defilement;
they should take joy in practicing right conduct and be able to guard their precepts.
Staying far from those who violate the precepts, Having compassion for all virtuous people,
Abiding in right view and reflection, One always delights in the joy of the Dharma.
Ruling the country with the True Dharma, One protects the ministers and the people.
That king in this world is no different from the gods;
because the king cultivates pure virtue and his ministers rely on righteous conduct,
the common people are all purified, like the moon beautifying the autumn sky.
Having thoroughly understood the nature of cause and effect, there will be no mutual conflict or punishment;
all places will be auspicious, and both self and others will attain peace and security.
I take refuge in the Perfectly All-Knowing One, the Father of the World.
Able to sever the bonds of the three realms of existence, Causing one to ascend the path to enlightenment.
I take refuge in the eye of pure wisdom, Which can shatter all darkness of doubt,
Skillfully crushing all heterodox arguments, And causing one to abide in right view.
Taking refuge in the excellent field of merit, It causes all fruits of virtue to flourish;
Free from the afflictions of the three poisons, It brings about stainless purity.
Taking refuge in supreme wisdom, One dwells in the sublime samādhi.
With the most supreme jewel of the Dharma, he reveals it for the sake of sentient beings.
He praises the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and his marks, signs, and various merits;
this enables all who see him to find joy and have their minds purified.
If a person’s mind is pure, constantly paying homage to all Buddhas,
they shall obtain the most supreme auspiciousness and be freed from all fears.
If a person’s mind is pure, they shall skillfully expound the subtle and wondrous Dharma.
One can reach enlightenment and attain ultimate peace and security.
If a person’s mind is pure and they constantly give rise to right reflection,
they will board the boat of wisdom and be able to cross to the other shore.
The eye of wisdom is most pure, able to illuminate both the hidden and the manifest;
regarding the minds of self and others, as well as sentient and insentient things, it pervades all without exception.
If one is free from faults such as greed, the mind will not give rise to dullness or turbidity.
Just as in that pure lapis lazuli, everything is clearly perceived;
yet all those non-Buddhists do not behold the light of wisdom.
One should therefore use words of truth and skillful means to reveal it to them.
Only the Buddha can deliver those beings who are utterly heedless, leading them to the further shore; he is hailed as the Supreme Man.
Among all worlds, the Buddha acts as the foremost refuge and protector.
May those who are not yet at peace find peace; may those who have not yet crossed over be delivered.
For as long as one has wandered in the beginningless cycle of saṃsāra, obscured by ignorance, one can sever it through the Buddha’s words, just as the sun dispels the darkness.
Constantly reflecting on these words, the wise are able to transcend and reach the place of non-extinction, attaining supreme tranquility;
through the inexhaustible wisdom of the Dharma, they produce a vast and great radiance.
The merit is difficult to measure; it is the most supreme among the noble ones.
